1.  INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is one of the three 
Departments of the Ministry of Science and Technology. It was established in 1985, for the 
promotion of industrial research through indigenous technology promotion, development, 
utilization and transfer. The Department is entrusted with the following allocation of business:-  
(i) All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR). 
(ii) All matters relating to National Research Development Corporation (NRDC). 
(iii) All matters relating to Central Electronics Limited (CEL). 
(iv) Registration and Recognition of R&D Units. 
(v) Matters relating to UNCTAD and WIPO. 
(vi) National Register for Foreign Collaborations. 
(vii) Matters relating to creation of pool for temporary placement of Indian Scientists and 
Technologists. 
1.2. DSIR plays an instrumental role in accelerating the development of cutting-edge 
technologies by encouraging industries to significantly increase their investment in research and 
development. By facilitating the swift commercialization of laboratory innovations, DSIR 
effectively bridges the divide between scientific discovery and practical, real-world applications, 
ensuring that India remains at the forefront of technological progress. 
1.3. DSIR also functions through its attached autonomous institution, Council for Scientific and 
Industrial Research (CSIR) and the two public sector undertakings, National Research Development 
Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) to facilitate scientific and industrial 
research in the country. It also provides institutional host facilities to Asian & Pacific Centre for 
Transfer of Technology (APCTT). 
1.4. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in its meeting held on 20th February, 2025.

2.2  The Committee notes from the above table 2024-25 R.E. allocation of the Department 
decreased under all the heads except a marginal increase under the head National Laboratories 
(CSIR). The Committee also observes that average utilization of R.E. allocation of the Department 
during 2024-25 is just 71.71%. The performance in respect of the Central Sector Schemes - 
‘Industrial Research & Development’ is far from satisfactory. The Department could spend an 
abysmal 45.76 % of its revised allocation under this head.  
2.3 The Committee notes with concern the sub-optimal utilization of funds under the 
Central Sector Scheme - ‘Industrial Research & Development’, as over half of the allocated 
funds remain unutilized as the current financial year enters its final quarter. In light of this, 
the Committee emphasizes the critical need for the Department to expedite expenditure and 
ensure the optimal deployment of resources within the remaining timeframe of the financial 
year. To preempt such inefficiencies in subsequent years, the Committee strongly advocates 
for the institutionalization of robust quarterly monitoring mechanisms. 
2.4 The Committee sought details of the budgetary allocation proposed by the Department vis-à-
vis the amount actually allocated to it for the year 2025-26. The Department informed that against a 
proposal of ₹ 7283.24 crore, an amount of ₹ 6657.78 has been allocated, which is about 8.59% 
lesser than its budgetary demand. Thus, here is an overall shortfall of ₹ 625.46 crore in the actual 
allocation to the Department. 
2.5 In response to a query about the likely impact of this shortfall in actual allocation over the 
proposed budget and the strategy of the Department for dealing with the challenges arising thereof, 
the Department submitted that:– 
 The B.E. demanded for IRD Scheme, [Promoting Innovations in Individuals, Start-ups and 
MSMEs (PRISM)] was ₹ 3.10 crore for the Financial Year 2025-26. However, only ₹ 1.50 
crore have been allocated under the scheme. This would substantially impact the operation 
of the scheme as the Department needs to fulfill the commitment of ongoing projects from 
the previous years and fund new projects. 
 
  CSIR constituent laboratories across the country have been grouped under the Theme based 
Clusters to perform their activities and synergize to achieve the objectives of bringing in 
sector-specific industry focus, align to stakeholder needs and enhance business focus. 
Although reduction in the projected allocation and actual budgetary allocation may 
potentially affect financial planning and participative performance of R&D projects in 
general and new future plans, CSIR internal resources would be utilized to supplement CSIR 
driven R&D projects. Further CSIR is collaborating with other Departments/ Ministries for 

3 
 
sponsoring its projects. 
 Budget reductions can have a significant impact on the implementation of various activities 
under the two schemes of NRDC, Programme for Inspiring Inventors & Innovators (PIII) 
and Programme for Development of Technologies for Commercialization (PDTC). Under 
PIII scheme, most of the funds are utilized for technology development and the projects 
have already been sanctioned and any delay in release of funds, which is done milestone-
wise, can result in delay of completion of the projects and may even lead to reduction in 
operation and achievement of targets.

2.8 During the meeting, the Department informed the Committee that in 2024-25, 62% of the 
allocated funds were spent on pensions and salaries, leaving only 38% for R&D and infrastructure. 
Within this, 7% supports capacity-building initiatives such as Junior Research Fellowships (JRF), 
Senior Research Fellowships (SRF), and PhD programmes. Therefore, only 31 per cent is available 
for research. This leaves minimal scope for addressing infrastructure deficits or scaling innovation. 
The Department has introduced new schemes to optimize resource use, including pilot plants for 
industry-ready technologies, repayable facility creation projects, and prioritized equipment 
upgrades. Despite these efforts, a funding shortfall persists, exacerbated by ageing infrastructure 
across CSIR’s 70 year old laboratories, necessitating urgent investments in R&D blocks, staff 
quarters, guest houses, and renovation of Director’s residences. The Department also informed that 
it projected a requirement of ₹7,210 crore but was allocated ₹6,600 crore, resulting in a deficit of 
₹600 crore. Of this, ₹363.92 crore has been identified as a bare minimum additional requirement to 
sustain critical R&D activities and infrastructure projects, with ₹350 crore earmarked for CSIR and 
₹16 crore for DSIR, NRDC, and CEL. However, the desirable allocation for the Department would 
be ₹600 crore to fully address the infrastructure gaps, support pilot plants for proof-of-concept 
initiatives, and establish next-generation research facilities.  
2.9 The Committee finds merit in the Department’s request for an additional budgetary 
allocation to the tune of ₹ 363.92 crore, over and above the provision made in B.E. 2025-26. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may seek the requisite 
additional allocation from the Ministry of Finance at the R.E. stage.

CLAIM (CSIR League for AI based Industrial Manifestation), CSIR Hydrogen Mission

CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES  3.1 The Department has two umbrella schemes, viz., ‘Industrial Research and Development’ and ‘Assistance to PSEs’.  The Committee was informed that, under Industrial R&D, the Department implements the following sub-schemes:- (i) Promoting Innovations in Individuals, Start-ups and MSMEs (PRISM), wherein financial assistance is extended to independent innovators for converting innovative ideas into demonstrable working models/prototypes/processes that may take the form of new or improved products, processes, or services and assist them to become incubatees/techno-entrepreneur.  (ii) Patent Acquisition and Collaborative Research and Technology Development (PACE), wherein support is provided to industries and institutions for development and demonstration of innovative technologies. (iii) Building Industrial R&D and Common Research Facilities (BIRD-CF), wherein support is provided for creation of Common Research and Technology Development Hubs (CRTDH) for use by entrepreneurs and industries.

3.3 In response to a query of the Committee, the Department submitted that some of the 
achievements of these schemes during the year are:– 
 Two new technology development and demonstration projects were approved under PACE 
during FY 2024-25 and a tripartite agreement was also signed.  
 500 TRL 6 + level technologies were scouted and assessed and published as four 
compendiums as part of A2K+ studies. 
 Under PRISM, 10 new proposals were supported, 11 projects were successfully monitored 
and completed & 3 start-ups & incubatee firms were generated. 
3.4 The Committee expresses concern over the substantial gap between budgetary 
estimates and actual expenditures. The Committee observes that in several instances, the 
actual expenditure remains significantly lower than the budget estimates and even the revised 
estimates, indicating underutilization of allocated funds. Such underutilization may hinder 
the intended impact of these schemes and delay the realization of their objectives. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department take proactive measures to ensure 
effective fund utilization by addressing administrative bottlenecks, streamlining project 
approvals, and enhancing monitoring mechanisms. 
3.5 The Committee appreciates the achievements made under these schemes. However, the 
Committee believes that a more robust approach is necessary to scale up these achievements 
and expand the reach of these schemes. The Department should consider increasing outreach 
efforts to encourage wider participation from start-ups, MSMEs, and research institutions, 
ensuring that more innovators benefit from these programs. 
3.6 Under the umbrella scheme ‘Assistance to PSEs’, the Department provides support to 
NRDC and CEL. NRDC, established in 1953, is mandated to commercialize the technologies 
developed by all the research laboratories and institutes of CSIR and other public funded research 
institutes, universities including autonomous research institutions. It undertakes 
programmes/activities under two promotional schemes, viz., Programme for Inspiring Inventors & 
Innovators (PIII) and Programme for Development of Technologies for Commercialization 
(PDTC). PIII is planned to encourage the innovators in developing new innovative technologies & 
products as well as rendering technical and financial assistance for protection of inventions by filing 
IPR in India and abroad. To achieve this Corporation carries out various activities like awarding 
meritorious inventions, conduct awareness programmes, protection of IP’s, evaluation of 

8 
 
technologies, set up incubation facilities, conduct EDP programmes, etc. The major objective of 
PDTC is to provide support to lab scale technologies for making it acceptable by the industry 
through value-addition, dissemination of information of such developed technologies to industries 
and provide part of capital as seed fund.

3.8 In response to a query, the Department informed that NRDC has proposed to take-up a new 
scheme viz. Start-up driven Technology Scale-up Initiative (TSI). By fostering collaboration 
between startups and Research Institutes (RI), the scheme aims to leverage existing research to 
catalyze the development and commercialization of new technologies. The proposed scheme will 
have the following two major components:  (i) Technology Development Facility (TDF) (ii) 
Generic Startup Support Facility (GSSF). Through initiatives like the Technology Development 
Facility (TDF) and the Generic Startup Support Facility (GSSF), the scheme will provide crucial 
resources and expertise to address the unique challenges faced by startups and women-led 
enterprises. By offering financial support, access to research facilities, mentorship, and intellectual 
property assistance, the scheme will seek to facilitate the seamless transition of innovative ideas 
into market-ready products.

3.12 The Committee acknowledges the vital role played by NRDC in facilitating the 
commercialization of technologies developed by CSIR, public-funded research institutions, 
universities, and autonomous research bodies. However, the Committee notes with concern 
the disparity between budgetary allocations, revised estimates, and actual expenditures across 
multiple financial years, particularly in the PIII scheme, where the actual expenditure has 
remained consistently lower than the allocated amount. The Committee recommends that the 
Department take necessary measures to ensure the optimal utilization of funds by enhancing 
project execution efficiency, streamlining approval processes, and addressing any institutional 
challenges that may be causing delays. 
3.13 The Committee welcomes the NRDC’s proposal to launch the Start-up Driven 
Technology Scale-up Initiative (TSI) with its two major components, namely, the Technology 
Development Facility (TDF) and the Generic Startup Support Facility (GSSF). Given the 
critical role of start-ups in driving technological innovation and economic growth, the 
Committee emphasizes the importance of fostering stronger linkages between research 
institutions and start-ups to accelerate the commercialization of innovative technologies. The 
Committee recommends that the Department provide adequate financial and infrastructural 
support to ensure the successful implementation of this initiative, particularly in addressing 
the unique challenges faced by start-ups and women-led enterprises.  
3.14 CEL is another PSE under the administrative control of the DSIR. It was established in 1974 
with an objective to commercially exploit the indigenous technologies developed by National 

10 
 
Laboratories and R&D Institutions in the country. It is carrying out commercial production as well 
as R&D in four fields: (i) Solar Photovoltaics (SPV) (ii) Railways Electronics (iii) Strategic 
Electronics (iv) Security & Surveillance Systems. It is the pioneer and leading manufacturer of SPV 
cells, modules and systems and Railway Safety Signaling Equipment. In the field of strategic 
electronics, it is the only indigenous manufacturer of phase control modules, which is a key element 
of phased array radar. 
 
3.15  The Committee enquired about the current product portfolio of CEL. The Department 
informed that CEL specializes in end-to-end manufacturing of technical ceramics, particularly 
ferrite-based components such as Phase Control Modules (PCMs), which are integral to defence 
systems like the Swathi Weapon Locating Radar and Troop Level Radar, with cumulative supplies 
exceeding ₹850 crore over 15 years. The company’s expertise extends to advanced defence 
applications, including the production of ceramic radar domes (radomes) for missile systems, which 
are placed on missile nose to primarily protect underlying electronics while maintaining technical 
requirement of the whole system. CEL further distinguishes itself through the indigenous 
development of critical import substitutes such as isolators, circulators, and Piezo Ceramics (PZT) 
for ammunition and civil applications, alongside strategic materials like Cadmium Zinc Telluride 
(CZT) substrates for advanced imaging systems in collaboration with DRDO. 
3.16 In the railway sector, CEL competes with private entities in manufacturing and upgrading 
digital axle counter systems, having supplied over 12,700 Single Section Digital Axle Counters 
(SSDAC), 6,100 High Availability SSDACs, and 10,700 detection points for Multi-Section Digital 
Axle Counters (MSDAC) since 2002. The company’s collaboration with Indian Railways includes 
the development of a Broken Rail Detection System for Delhi Metro, with potential for nationwide 
deployment. Concurrently, CEL has expanded its footprint in IT and smart infrastructure, delivering 
Integrated Security Solutions, IoT based systems for power and water management, and Blockchain 
driven recruitment automation platforms implemented in institutions such as AIIMS Delhi, UP 
Police Recruitment Board, and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC). Notably, CEL has 
operationalized Smart Classrooms in 709 schools in Uttarakhand and established a production line 
for 65 and 75 inches Smart Boards, positioning itself as the sole PSU in this domain. Additionally, 
CEL’s legacy in renewable energy is marked by its pioneering role in developing country’s first 
solar cells and modules. The company continues to support the renewable sector through 
Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) services for solar projects, Project Management 
Consultancy, and maintenance of existing installations. 
3.17  The Committee also sought details of CEL's plans for technology development and 
innovation to maintain its competitiveness in the market. The Department informed that CEL has 
outlined a strategic roadmap for technology development and innovation to sustain its market 
competitiveness, anchored in proactive adaptation to emerging trends and collaborative 
partnerships. Recognizing the risk of technological obsolescence, particularly in defence 
applications, CEL is transitioning from legacy systems such as Passive Electronically Scanned 
Array (PESA) to advanced solutions like Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA). This 
includes collaboration with a defence PSU to develop Transmit-Receive modules for AESA, which 
will replace the existing Phase Control Modules (PCMs) in phased manner, ensuring alignment 
with next-generation radar systems. To bolster innovation, CEL is strengthening ties with academic 
institutions and research organisations for technology transfers and joint development initiatives, 
particularly in defence and railway sectors. This collaborative framework supports the indigenous 
upgradation of existing products and the creation of new solutions tailored to dynamic market 
demands. In the IT domain, CEL is enhancing its Integrated Security and Surveillance Solutions 
through AI driven advancements, such as facial recognition, behaviour analysis, and real-time threat 
detection systems for smart cities, critical infrastructure, and corporate security. Concurrently, the 
company is expanding IoT-based security applications for power plants, transport hubs, and 
government facilities, alongside modernising CCTV technologies with higher resolution, cloud-

11 
 
based monitoring, and encrypted data protocols. Further, CEL is scaling its Smart Education 
portfolio by integrating AI-powered learning analytics into its smart board manufacturing line, 
enabling interactive and customized digital classrooms for educational institutions and corporate 
training programmes. The company is also prioritising e-learning platform development to broaden 
access to advanced educational tools.  
3.18 The Committee enquired regarding major challenges being faced by CEL and strategies 
being implemented to address these challenges. The Committee was informed that CEL had the 
mandate to commercialize technologies developed in the national laboratories. However, absence of 
any corresponding provision in the relevant guidelines/rules/provisions pertaining to those national 
laboratories creates an anomalous situation putting CEL in a disadvantageous situation. In the field 
of renewable energy, CEL despite being a promising initial player in the field of solar 
photovoltaics, has suffered huge losses to the tune of ₹ 280 crore cumulative in the last 10-11 years. 
Technological advancement in the area coupled with cheaper import products has dented the 
profitability and adversely affected the returns from the sector. While CEL’s defence, railway, and 
IT/security verticals remain profitable, these face risks of technological obsolescence, slow growth, 
and rising costs, exacerbated by competition from private and multinational entities. Despite 50 
years of operation, CEL’s turnover remains modest (₹150–340 crore), necessitating urgent strategic 
recalibration to avoid stagnation.  
 
3.19 To mitigate these challenges, CEL is pursuing a multipronged strategy. This includes 
deepening collaborations with national laboratories (CSIR, DRDO), defence PSUs (BEL, HAL), 
and State Governments to align with market needs and access emerging technologies. The company 
is diversifying its portfolio, leveraging its recent Mini Ratna status to expand into new domains 
such as AI driven surveillance systems, IoT based infrastructure solutions, and smart education 
technologies, including scalable smart board manufacturing with potential applications in IT 
hardware. Strategic partnerships with academia and industry aim to counter obsolescence through 
joint R&D and process modernization. CEL is transitioning from component manufacturing to 
subsystem and system-level supply to enhance revenue, while exploring Public Private Partnerships 
(PPP) for ventures like Tier III data centers. A proposed subsidiary is under consideration to 
streamline CSR activities, fostering community engagement in health, education, and skill 
development. Additionally, plans for public listing of shares, pending approvals, aim to raise capital 
for establishing an in-house R&D centre, ensuring sustained innovation. 
 
3.20 In its presentation during the meeting, the Department provided a brief overview of the 
financial turnaround of the company. CEL’s sustained operational excellence and improved fiscal 
performance were recognized through its elevation to "Mini Ratna" (Category-I) status. Over the 
period spanning FY 2019–20 to FY 2023–24, the company demonstrated robust growth, with its 
turnover rising from ₹246 crore to ₹344.03 crore, and projections indicating a further increase to 
₹500 crore in the current fiscal year. Concurrently, Profit Before Tax (PBT) surged from ₹6.36 
crore to ₹78.88 crore, reflecting enhanced operational efficiency and profitability. The net worth of 
the company also witnessed a substantial rise, escalating from ₹80.76 crore to ₹193.64 crore during 
the same period. In FY 2023–24, CEL contributed ₹11.87 crore as dividend to the Government of 
India, underscoring its renewed financial viability. Additionally, the company settled longstanding 
employee liabilities, disbursing ₹18 crore towards arrears of interest linked to the 2007 wage 
revision. These milestones collectively underscore CEL’s successful strides in stabilizing its 
financial health, aligning with national objectives of public sector revitalization and accountability. 
3.21 The Committee commends the Department for the successful revival of CEL, which 
was once a struggling PSU on the brink of disinvestment. The remarkable transformation of 
CEL stands as a testament to the potential of strategic interventions in revitalizing public 
sector enterprises. The Committee expresses its optimism that CEL will continue on this 
trajectory of growth and excellence, eventually attaining Maha Ratna status. CEL’s 

12 
 
resurgence serves as an exemplary model of how a well-executed turnaround strategy can 
reinvigorate a PSU, reinforcing its role in advancing national technological and industrial 
capabilities.  
3.22 In view of CEL’s strategic significance, the Committee strongly recommends that the 
Department provide consistent policy and financial support to enable CEL to overcome its 
current challenges and capitalize on growth opportunities. The Department should ensure 
that CEL receives adequate institutional backing to secure its position as a leading player in 
defence electronics, railway electronics, IT-enabled smart infrastructure, and renewable 
energy. The Committee further advises the Department to submit a detailed roadmap 
outlining the steps required to enhance CEL’s operational efficiency, financial viability, and 
technological competitiveness. Strengthening CEL’s capabilities will not only contribute to 
national self-reliance in critical technology sectors but also reinforce India’s public sector 
enterprises as key drivers of innovation and industrial growth. 
4. COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR)  
 
4.1  CSIR, established in 1942, functions as an autonomous entity under the administrative 
purview of the Department. Renowned for its pioneering Research and Development (R&D) 
capabilities across diverse domains of science and technology, CSIR operates as a modern R&D 
institution with a pan-India footprint. Its infrastructure comprises a robust network of 37 national 
laboratories, 39 outreach centres, 1 Innovation Complex, and 3 specialized units, reflecting its 
extensive engagement in scientific advancement. 
4.2 CSIR has two non-central sector schemes, viz., (i) National Laboratories Scheme; and (ii) 
Capacity Building and Human Resource Development. While the former covers a wide range of 
R&D and S&T aspects, latter deals with human resources and different awards.

 4.4 The Committee recognizes the pivotal role played by CSIR in driving research, 
innovation, and technological advancements across diverse domains. As one of the premier 
research organizations in the country, CSIR has contributed significantly to scientific 
breakthroughs, industrial applications, and the development of indigenous technologies that 
have strengthened national self-reliance. Its extensive research network, spanning multiple 
disciplines, has facilitated advancements in healthcare, engineering sciences, environmental 
sustainability, agriculture, and emerging technologies, thereby supporting India’s economic 
and strategic objectives. 
4.5 However, the Committee notes with concern that CSIR has substantial overlaps in 
research activities with other scientific institutions, including the Ministry of Earth Sciences, 
the Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, etc.. 
This duplication of research efforts leads to fragmentation of resources, inefficiencies in 
execution, and a lack of cohesive direction in national scientific pursuits. The Committee 
strongly recommends that CSIR undertake a comprehensive restructuring to optimize its 
research priorities, ensuring a sharper focus on projects that are highly critical, have a 
substantial impact, and align with the country’s strategic interests. The Committee urges 
CSIR to realign its research portfolio by concentrating on areas of national importance where 
it can deliver unparalleled expertise and breakthrough innovations. Rather than engaging in 
research that overlaps with other institutions, CSIR should collaborate with relevant 
Ministries and research organizations to ensure synergy rather than redundancy. By 
leveraging its strengths in cutting-edge technologies, translational research, and industrial 
applications, CSIR can maximize its contribution to India's scientific and economic 
development. The Committee also recommends that CSIR establish a clear roadmap to 
prioritize high-impact research, streamline its organizational structure, and enhance its role 
as a leader in addressing national challenges. A well-defined and strategic approach will not 
only enhance CSIR’s efficiency but also position it as a key driver of India’s scientific and 
technological advancement in critical sectors.

nine sector-specific theme based clusters, with each cluster under a separate directorate. The list of 
these thematic clusters is as follows:-

4.8 The Department informed the Committee that it requires ₹100 crore in FY 2025-26 to 
execute these nine projects. Additionally, it is working on 12 need based R&D projects, for which 
₹120 crore is needed. The Department is also constructing two Science Experience Centres in 
Ahmedabad and Hyderabad, requiring ₹80 crore. Furthermore, it plans to establish four pilot plants 
for translational and industrial-scale demonstrations—one for Engineering Sciences, two for 
Chemical Sciences, and one for Biological Sciences. These pilot plants aim to support start-ups, 
MSMEs, and industries, particularly in advancing indigenous technologies, with an estimated 
requirement of ₹100 crore. 
4.9 The Department is advancing next-generation benchmark facilities through five critical 
initiatives, requiring a consolidated investment of ₹500 crore. First, it is prioritizing the 
establishment of a secured and centralized data center to safeguard CSIR’s research data, ensuring 
robust storage and cyber security. Second, it is driving the development of nuclear batteries in 
alignment with national objectives related to Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and Indo-US nuclear 
collaborations. CSIR has already initiated work on all-solid-state batteries and is seeking funding to 
accelerate progress in this technology. Third, it is setting up an indigenous chip fabrication facility 
focused on micro-LED displays. The Department has proposed collaborating with the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, aiming to match contributions and secure a total 
investment of ₹1,000 crore to strengthen India's global competitiveness in semiconductor 
manufacturing. Fourth, CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (NPL) is leading efforts in Indian 
meteorology and standardization by enhancing atomic clock precision, advancing quantum 
computing, and developing “Bharatiya Nirdeshak Dravya”—customized Indian standards for 
materials and measurements. Lastly, the Department is working on developing animal-free organoid 
models to replace animal testing with human cell-based alternatives, in line with ethical R&D 
practices and global trends. Despite CSIR’s existing capabilities, this project remains on hold due to 
funding constraints.

4.12 In its presentation during the meeting, the Department informed the Committee about the 
urgent financial requirements of the National Aerospace Laboratory (NAL) in Bengaluru, which has 
recently made significant strides in indigenous aerospace technology. During the Aero India event, 
NAL successfully demonstrated the flight of the Hansa-NG, a two-seater aircraft. Given the 
laboratory’s contributions, the Department emphasized the need to strengthen and equip it 
adequately. The Department highlighted the necessity of establishing a National Wind Tunnel 
Facility to replace the 63-year-old wind tunnel, which has played a key role in testing satellites, 
including Chandrayaan-3. While the existing open trisonic wind tunnel remains operational, India 
still relies on foreign countries for satellite testing and certification, which risks exposing sensitive 
information. To eliminate this dependence, the Department proposed developing a closed-circuit 
trisonic wind tunnel within the country at an estimated cost of ₹3,100 crore. Both the Indian Space 
Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), 
which regularly use the current facility, have supported this initiative. Although a cost-sharing 
model has been suggested, where each entity would contribute a portion of the funds, the 
Department recommended allocating the entire amount to a single organization such as CSIR to 
expedite the project. To emphasize its strategic importance, the Department removed this proposal 
from the regular budget and introduced it as CSIR-Aerospace Projects of National Importance 
(CSIR-APNI). 
4.13 The Department also requested ₹898 crore to develop the Saras Mk2, a 19-seater commuter 
aircraft, which has generated growing interest from Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and the 
Indian Air Force (IAF). Additionally, it sought ₹759 crore to advance electric aerial vehicles, 
including converting the Hansa aircraft into an electric variant, e-Hansa, and establishing facilities 
for urban air mobility solutions such as the urban air taxi. The Department pointed out that while 
India has successfully electrified agricultural machinery like e-tractors and e-tillers, similar 
advancements in the aerospace sector require financial support. Furthermore, the Department 
proposed ₹1,021 crore for the development of indigenous civil and military systems in vehicles, 

18 
 
including four-seater aircraft and Regional Transport Aircraft (RTA), which are becoming 
increasingly necessary. The total financial requirement for all these projects amounts to 
approximately ₹5,800 crore.

testing, including for Chandrayaan-3. The continued reliance on foreign facilities for satellite

5.3 The Committee also sought details of the staff hired on contractual basis. The Department

on the performance. As per NRDC, this approach is economical, provides for skill shortages, helps 
overcome unforeseen vacancies and bring in specialized knowledge and expertise. Similarly, CEL 
hired approximately 116 contractual employees since 2019.  
5.4 The Committee is shocked to witness such a staggering number of vacancies in the 
Department, particularly in Group-I category of CSIR. It is concerning to contemplate how 
CSIR continues its research with such a skeletal workforce. Expecting optimal results from an 
understaffed organization is unrealistic. Human resources are the most important asset of any 
scientific organization and CSIR is critically lacking precisely in that. The Committee 
strongly recommends that the Department urgently fills up all vacant positions, particularly 
the Group-I vacancies in CSIR, in mission mode.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
BUDGET ANALYSIS 
 The Committee notes with concern the sub-optimal utilization of funds under the 
Central Sector Scheme - ‘Industrial Research & Development’, as over half of the allocated 
funds remain unutilized as the current financial year enters its final quarter. In light of this, 
the Committee emphasizes the critical need for the Department to expedite expenditure and 
ensure the optimal deployment of resources within the remaining timeframe of the financial 
year. To preempt such inefficiencies in subsequent years, the Committee strongly advocates 
for the institutionalization of robust quarterly monitoring mechanisms.                      (Para 2.3) 
 The Committee finds merit in the Department’s request for an additional budgetary 
allocation to the tune of ₹ 363.92 crore, over and above the provision made in B.E. 2025-26. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may seek the requisite 
additional allocation from the Ministry of Finance at the R.E. stage.                            (Para 2.9) 
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES 
 The Committee expresses concern over the substantial gap between budgetary 
estimates and actual expenditures. The Committee observes that in several instances, the 
actual expenditure remains significantly lower than the budget estimates and even the revised 
estimates, indicating underutilization of allocated funds. Such underutilization may hinder 
the intended impact of these schemes and delay the realization of their objectives. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department take proactive measures to ensure 
effective fund utilization by addressing administrative bottlenecks, streamlining project 
approvals, and enhancing monitoring mechanisms.                                                        (Para 3.4) 
 The Committee appreciates the achievements made under these schemes. However, the 
Committee believes that a more robust approach is necessary to scale up these achievements 
and expand the reach of these schemes. The Department should consider increasing outreach 
efforts to encourage wider participation from start-ups, MSMEs, and research institutions, 
ensuring that more innovators benefit from these programs.                                         (Para 3.5) 
 The Committee acknowledges the vital role played by NRDC in facilitating the 
commercialization of technologies developed by CSIR, public-funded research institutions, 
universities, and autonomous research bodies. However, the Committee notes with concern 
the disparity between budgetary allocations, revised estimates, and actual expenditures across 
multiple financial years, particularly in the PIII scheme, where the actual expenditure has 
remained consistently lower than the allocated amount. The Committee recommends that the 
Department take necessary measures to ensure the optimal utilization of funds by enhancing 
project execution efficiency, streamlining approval processes, and addressing any institutional 
challenges that may be causing delays.                                                                            (Para 3.12) 
 The Committee welcomes the NRDC’s proposal to launch the Start-up Driven 
Technology Scale-up Initiative (TSI) with its two major components, namely, the Technology 
Development Facility (TDF) and the Generic Startup Support Facility (GSSF). Given the 
critical role of start-ups in driving technological innovation and economic growth, the 
Committee emphasizes the importance of fostering stronger linkages between research 
institutions and start-ups to accelerate the commercialization of innovative technologies. The 
Committee recommends that the Department provide adequate financial and infrastructural 
support to ensure the successful implementation of this initiative, particularly in addressing 
the unique challenges faced by start-ups and women-led enterprises.                         (Para 3.13) 

22 
 
 The Committee commends the Department for the successful revival of CEL, which 
was once a struggling PSU on the brink of disinvestment. The remarkable transformation of 
CEL stands as a testament to the potential of strategic interventions in revitalizing public 
sector enterprises. The Committee expresses its optimism that CEL will continue on this 
trajectory of growth and excellence, eventually attaining Maha Ratna status. CEL’s 
resurgence serves as an exemplary model of how a well-executed turnaround strategy can 
reinvigorate a PSU, reinforcing its role in advancing national technological and industrial 
capabilities.                                                                                                                         (Para 3.21) 
 In view of CEL’s strategic significance, the Committee strongly recommends that the 
Department provide consistent policy and financial support to enable CEL to overcome its 
current challenges and capitalize on growth opportunities. The Department should ensure 
that CEL receives adequate institutional backing to secure its position as a leading player in 
defence electronics, railway electronics, IT-enabled smart infrastructure, and renewable 
energy. The Committee further advises the Department to submit a detailed roadmap 
outlining the steps required to enhance CEL’s operational efficiency, financial viability, and 
technological competitiveness. Strengthening CEL’s capabilities will not only contribute to 
national self-reliance in critical technology sectors but also reinforce India’s public sector 
enterprises as key drivers of innovation and industrial growth.                                   (Para 3.22) 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
 The Committee recognizes the pivotal role played by CSIR in driving research, 
innovation, and technological advancements across diverse domains. As one of the premier 
research organizations in the country, CSIR has contributed significantly to scientific 
breakthroughs, industrial applications, and the development of indigenous technologies that 
have strengthened national self-reliance. Its extensive research network, spanning multiple 
disciplines, has facilitated advancements in healthcare, engineering sciences, environmental 
sustainability, agriculture, and emerging technologies, thereby supporting India’s economic 
and strategic objectives.                                                                                                      (Para 4.4) 
 However, the Committee notes with concern that CSIR has substantial overlaps in 
research activities with other scientific institutions, including the Ministry of Earth Sciences, 
the Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, etc.. 
This duplication of research efforts leads to fragmentation of resources, inefficiencies in 
execution, and a lack of cohesive direction in national scientific pursuits. The Committee 
strongly recommends that CSIR undertake a comprehensive restructuring to optimize its 
research priorities, ensuring a sharper focus on projects that are highly critical, have a 
substantial impact, and align with the country’s strategic interests. The Committee urges 
CSIR to realign its research portfolio by concentrating on areas of national importance where 
it can deliver unparalleled expertise and breakthrough innovations. Rather than engaging in 
research that overlaps with other institutions, CSIR should collaborate with relevant 
Ministries and research organizations to ensure synergy rather than redundancy. By 
leveraging its strengths in cutting-edge technologies, translational research, and industrial 
applications, CSIR can maximize its contribution to India's scientific and economic 
development. The Committee also recommends that CSIR establish a clear roadmap to 
prioritize high-impact research, streamline its organizational structure, and enhance its role 
as a leader in addressing national challenges. A well-defined and strategic approach will not 
only enhance CSIR’s efficiency but also position it as a key driver of India’s scientific and 
technological advancement in critical sectors.                                                                  (Para 4.5) 
 The Committee commends the selection of key projects under Viksit Bharat, the 
establishment of pilot plants supporting start-ups and MSMEs and the initiatives taken for 

23 
 
creation of next-generation benchmark facilities. The Committee strongly recommends that 
the Department proactively seek additional financial resources to complete these projects 
without interruption.                                                                                                         (Para 4.11) 
 The Committee acknowledges the significant advancements made by the NAL, 
Bengaluru in the field of aerospace technology. Recognizing the strategic importance of 
NAL’s contributions, the Committee concurs with the Department on the need to strengthen 
and adequately equip the laboratory to further its research and development efforts. The 
Committee also notes the critical necessity of establishing a National Wind Tunnel Facility to 
replace the existing 63-year-old wind tunnel, which has played a pivotal role in satellite 
testing, including for Chandrayaan-3. The continued reliance on foreign facilities for satellite 
testing not only incurs financial costs but also exposes sensitive technological information. The 
Committee, therefore, supports the Department’s proposal to develop a closed-circuit trisonic 
wind tunnel within the country at an estimated cost of ₹3,100 crore. Given the regular use of 
this facility by ISRO and DRDO, the Committee recognizes the national importance of this 
project and agrees with the proposal to allocate the full financial outlay to a single 
organization, such as CSIR, to expedite its implementation.                                        (Para 4.15) 
 The Committee acknowledges the Department’s request for funds to develop Saras 
Mk2, e-Hansa, urban air mobility solutions, and indigenous civil and military aviation 
systems, including Regional Transport Aircraft. Recognizing the growing need for regional 
connectivity, electrification in aerospace, and defense preparedness, the Committee 
emphasizes the importance of expediting these projects with adequate financial support. 
(Para 4.16) 
  
     Given the total financial requirement of approximately ₹5,800 crore for these critical 
projects, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department seeks the necessary funds 
to ensure their seamless execution. Additionally, the Committee recommends that the 
Department closely monitor the progress of these projects, ensure effective coordination 
among stakeholders, and provide periodic updates on their implementation. Prioritizing these 
projects will not only enhance India’s self-reliance in aerospace technology but also contribute 
significantly to the nation’s scientific and industrial advancement.                            (Para 4.17) 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE CHALLENGES 
 The Committee is shocked to witness such a staggering number of vacancies in the 
Department, particularly in Group-I category of CSIR. It is concerning to contemplate how 
CSIR continues its research with such a skeletal workforce. Expecting optimal results from an 
understaffed organization is unrealistic. Human resources are the most important asset of any 
scientific organization and CSIR is critically lacking precisely in that. The Committee 
strongly recommends that the Department urgently fills up all vacant positions, particularly 
the Group-I vacancies in CSIR, in mission mode.                                                          (Para 5.14)

1. INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Science & Technology (DST) stands as the premier nodal agency in 
India dedicated to fortifying the nation's Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) landscape. It 
plays a pivotal role in identifying critical gaps within the S&T sectors, formulating strategic plans 
and policies to address societal needs, and fostering emerging areas of science and technology to 
meet future demands. DST acts as a vital bridge, connecting the science and technology domains 
with various Government horizontals and verticals, academia, Research and Development (R&D) 
laboratories, institutions, and industries, ensuring a cohesive and collaborative ecosystem. 
1.2 With the overarching goal of enhancing India's S&T capacity and capability, DST 
spearheads the largest extramural R&D support in the country. This is achieved through three 
comprehensive umbrella schemes: (i) Science and Technology (S&T) Institutional and Human 
Capacity Building, (ii) Research and Development, and (iii) Innovation, Technology Development, 
and Deployment. These schemes are designed to empower scientists across diverse institutions and 
disciplines through a competitive framework, thereby reinforcing India's education system, 
scientific and industrial R&D. 
1.3 In a significant move to streamline operations and enhance flexibility in fund allocation, 
these three umbrella schemes have been consolidated into a single, unified initiative named ‘Vigyan 
Dhara’. This integration ensures a more efficient and adaptive flow of resources across programs, 
fostering greater innovation and impact. 
1.4 DST remains steadfast in its mission to strengthen the national STI ecosystem, positioning 
India as a global leader in science and technology. By driving positive transformations, DST aims 
to contribute to a safer, more secure, and prosperous society, while proactively preparing for future 
challenges and disruptions. Through its relentless efforts, DST continues to catalyze advancements 
that not only address current societal needs but also pave the way for a sustainable and 
technologically advanced future. 
1.5 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Science & Technology in its meeting held on 19th February, 2025.

reinstated for 2025-26. The Committee enquired the Department for reasons. The Department 
submitted that the provisions of the ANRF Act were notified on 5th Day of February, 2024 and

budget allocation of ₹2000 crore (BE 2025-26) would be utilized fully for funding the schemes 
already initiated and the new schemes to be introduced during the year 2025-26, under the 
guidance/directions of EC, ANRF.

3. RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT & INNOVATION FUND 
3.1 In the Interim Budget for the fiscal year 2024-25, a ₹1 lakh crore corpus was announced to 
promote private sector research and innovation in deep tech and sunrise sector. This corpus was 
intended to provide long-term financing or refinancing at low or zero interest rates through a 50-
year interest-free loan. 
3.2 Building on this initiative, the Budget for FY 2025-26 introduced the Research, 
Development, and Innovation (RDI) Fund with a budgetary allocation of ₹20,000 crore. This fund 
is designed to facilitate long-term financing or refinancing with extended tenors and minimal or 
zero interest rates for science, technology, and other research-driven initiatives. The objective is to 
incentivize the private sector to expand its research endeavors and position India as a global leader 
in research, development, and innovation within emerging domains. The fund aims to support 
programs that leverage the potential of India's youth and technological advancements. 
3.3 Under this scheme, a Special Purpose Fund would be set up and implemented by 
Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) for funding Startups and private sector 
corporates. The focus and coverage of RDI Scheme is envisaged to be in sunrise sectors which are 
likely to have transformative and strong ripple impact on the economy, besides having potential for 
high growth and commercial success. The identification of sectors and sub-sectors, for the purpose 
of funding, will also account for the Indian context including the economic landscape, level of 
technological advancement and the societal needs. The relevance for global value chain integration 
as well as potential for creating market access shall also be considered. 
3.4 The Department submitted that the specific sectors and sub-sectors to be supported by the 
Scheme would be identified upfront.  Some of the sunrise sectors have been identified for 
consideration of funding under the Scheme which may  subject to further refinement include 1) 
Energy security/transition and climate action 2) “Deep Technology” including quantum 
computing, robotics and  space  3) Artificial Intelligence and its application to Indian problems 
including  in agriculture, health, and education  4) Biotechnology, biomanufacturing, synthetic 
biology, pharma, medical devices  5) Digital economy including Digital agriculture, technologies 
whose indigenization for strategic reasons or for economic security and any other sector or 
technology where it is deemed necessary in  public interest. 
3.5 The Department plans to allocate ₹20,000 crore as a 50-year interest-free loan to a special 
purpose fund. This fund will be managed by second-level fund managers, including alternate 
investment funds, fund of funds, and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs). These managers 
will invest in deep tech sectors such as clean energy, bio-manufacturing, quantum computing, AI, 
sustainable agriculture, gene therapy, and computational drug discovery, either through loans or 
equity investments in start-ups and private companies. A key condition is that private sector

5. NATIONAL QUANTUM MISSION (NQM)  
5.1 The Department informed the Committee that one of the thrust areas for the year 2025-26 is 
National Quantum Mission (NQM). It was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19th April 2023 at a 
total cost of ₹6003.65 crore for a period of eight years from 2023-24 to 2030-31.  
 
5.2 Under the Mission, four Thematic Hubs comprising of 14 Technical Groups having 17 
Project Teams across India, involving nearly 152 researchers from 43 institutions have been 
established, each dedicated to a specific technology vertical:  
(i) Quantum Computing at IISc. Bengaluru; 
(ii) Quantum Communication at IIT Madras in association with C-DOT, New Delhi; 
(iii) Quantum Sensing & Metrology at IIT Bombay; and 
(iv) Quantum Materials & Devices at IIT Delhi 

10 
 
5.3 The Mission objectives include developing intermediate-scale quantum computers with 20-
50 physical qubits in 3 years, 50-100 physical qubits in 5 years and 50-1000 physical qubits in 8 
years in various platforms like superconducting and photonic technology. Satellite-based secure 
quantum communications between ground stations over a range of 2000 kilometers within India, 
long-distance secure quantum communications with other countries, inter-city quantum key 
distribution over 2000 km as well as multi-node Quantum networks with quantum memories are 
also some of the deliverables of the Mission. The National Quantum Mission will focus on 
developing magnetometers with high sensitivity in atomic systems and atomic clocks for precision 
timing, communications, and navigation. It will also support the design and synthesis of quantum 
materials such as superconductors, novel semiconductor structures, and topological materials for the 
fabrication of quantum devices. Single photon sources/detectors, and entangled photon sources will 
also be developed for quantum communications, sensing, and metrological applications. The 
Mission would greatly benefit various sectors including communication, health, financial, energy 
with applications in drug design, space, banking, security etc. The Mission will also provide a huge 
boost to National priorities like Digital India, Make in India, Skill India and Stand-up India, Start-
up India, Self-reliant India and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG). 
5.4 The Committee enquired about the physical achievements of the Mission, and was informed 
that IIT Bombay has established the section – 8 Company in the area of Quantum Sensing & 
Metrology namely Qmet Tech Foundation in October 2024. Similarly, IIT Madras in association 
with C-DoT, New Delhi has established IITM CDOT Samgnya Technologies Foundation in 
December 2024 in the area of Quantum Communication. 
5.5 The Committee notes that the ₹ 427 crores were allocated in B.E. 2024-25 which were 
significantly reduced to ₹ 86 crores and Department could spent only 64.30 per cent of the 
R.E. till 31st January, 2025. Even after such gross under-utilization of funds, ₹ 600 crores has 
been allocated for this Mission in B.E. 2025-26. The Committee enquired about the increased 
budget allocation for the National Quantum Mission (NQM) in B.E. 2025-26 and the 
Department informed that the increased allocations will play a pivotal role in expanding and 
scaling up ongoing initiatives while accelerating the development of a robust quantum 
technology ecosystem in India. A significant portion of this funding will be dedicated to 
strengthening the four established Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs), each focused on a key vertical—
Quantum Computing, Quantum Communication, Quantum Sensing & Metrology, and 
Quantum Materials & Devices. The enhanced funding will empower these T-Hubs to fulfill 
their mandates effectively by: Technology Development, Human Resource Development, 
Entrepreneurship Development and Industry Collaborations and International 
Collaborations. 
5.6 The Committee acknowledges that the launch of a dedicated Mission for research in 
Quantum Technologies is a strategic and forward-looking initiative, aligning with global 
technological advancements. However, the underutilization of allocated funds raises concerns 
about the Department's commitment and operational efficiency. The Committee emphasizes 
the need for the Department to adopt a more proactive and results driven approach to ensure 
the Mission's success. Rather than merely playing catch-up to Google’s Willow and 
Microsoft’s Majorana 1, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department adopt an 
ambitious vision to position India as a global leader in Quantum Technology.

A. Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences & Technology (SCTIMST), 
Thiruvananthapuram 
Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute of Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) is actively 
contributing to biomedical technology development and its translation, creation of intellectual 
property, collaboration with industries and other institutions, academic activities, and patient care. 
As the outcome of its research and development activities, the following products were launched in 
the market: 
 National Launch of AG Chitra Tuberculosis Diagnostic Kit: SCTIMST launched a new 
innovative open isothermal amplification kit for the early diagnosis of pulmonary 
tuberculosis. The AG Chitra TB diagnostic kit was developed with funding received through 
the Technical Research Centre Scheme of DST. This kit was developed as an open platform 
for affordable, fast, and accurate diagnosis of pulmonary Tuberculosis. The technology was 
licensed to M/s. Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kochi, Kerala. Following the successful 
validation, the Central Standard Drug Control Organization (CDSCO) approved the kit for 
manufacturing and commercialization.  

14 
 
 Titanium Nitride (TiN) coated coronary stent: This implant device is intended for the 
treatment of coronary artery disease and consists of the following components: (a) L605-
based metal stent platform and (b) TiN ceramic coating. The technology transfer agreement 
was signed with M/s. Invasive Technologies Pvt. Ltd., Kerala on 23rd September 2024. 
 Automatic contrast injector: This device is meant for the automatic delivery of contrast 
agents for facilitating coronary angiography and angioplasty. The device consists of a 
handheld power drive and a disposable manifold. The disposable manifold directs the 
contrast to the catheter during delivery and sucks the contrast agent from the reservoir. The 
technology was transferred to M/s. Cyrix Healthcare Pvt. Ltd., Kerala. 
 Automated trolley e-drive: This device is a universal electric trolley puller/pusher 
designed to be attached to any type of patient trolley so as to convert it to an electrically 
powered trolley. The technology was transferred to M/s. Quasys Software and Consultancy 
Pvt. Ltd., Kerala.

D. Raman Research Institute (RRI), Bengaluru 
The Raman Research Institute (RRI) was founded by Indian Science Nobel Laureate Sir C V 
Raman in 1948, marking 2023 as its Platinum Jubilee Year (PJY). The research at the Institute 
spans mind-boggling spatial and temporal scales from the very large- galaxies, galaxy clusters and 
beyond, to the very small – on the scale of atoms; from processes that happen over millions and 
billions of years to ultrafast processes that occur in attoseconds. The Institute has designed and built 
POLIX, world's first instrument designed to operate in the medium X-ray band of 8 to 30 kilo 
electron Volt (keV) energy. It was launched onboard XPoSat mission by ISRO on 1st January, 2024. 
It is designed to detect the scattered X-rays, enabling X-ray polarisation measurements. After initial 
calibrations and tests, the first light was obtained in early February and since then, the instrument 
has been making scientific observations. 
6.12 The Committee commends the Raman Research Institute (RRI) for its outstanding

atomic physics.

7.2 On the issue of staff shortage, the Department informed that it time and again approaches 
and follows up with the cadre controlling authority concerned for filling up the vacancies and the 
recruitment/ promotion agencies concerned for expediting the recruitment process. The Department 
also informed that manpower shortage may directly impact the outcome of scientific research and 
for time being the required manpower is being managed through the outsourced manpower and 
short-term contract appointments to achieve the scientific aims. 
7.3 The Committee also sought details of the staff hired on contractual basis. The Department 
apprised the Committee that 113 employees are working on contractual basis in DST Headquarters 
whereas 1149 employees are engaged on contractual basis in various AIs. 
7.4 The Committee expresses deep concern over the significant number of vacancies in the 
Department, as well as in the Autonomous Institutions (AIs) under its administrative control. 
It is particularly dismayed by the persistent reliance on contractual appointments as a 
stopgap measure to address short-term manpower shortages. The Committee firmly believes 
that a highly skilled and dedicated workforce is the cornerstone of any scientific institution’s 
success and output. Therefore, it strongly recommends that the Department adopt a mission-
mode approach to expeditiously fill all vacant positions. This will ensure the availability of a 
competent and stable workforce, essential for advancing scientific research and institutional 
excellence. 
7.5 The Committee also enquired how the Department ensures ample opportunities for its staff 
to enhance their skills and capacities. The Department submitted that it has the following activities 
for ensuring capacity building of its staff: 
I. Training programmes under the scheme "National Programme for Training of Scientists & 
Technologists working in Govt. Sector" on yearly basis. 
II. Encourage all the employees to complete the available digital courses through weekly 
Announcements for Learning Hour.  
III. Identified 07 Mandatory Courses. 
IV. All Heads of Autonomous Institutions/Statutory Boards/Professional Bodies have been 
requested to comply with the Karmayogi Guidelines vide DO letter from Secretary, DST. 
V. Two Immersion programmes for newly recruited scientists have been conducted. 

19 
 
VI. Quarterly incentive for top three karmayogis has been introduced. 
VII. Conducted multiple workshops for enhancing skills of its Office. 
7.6 The Committee observes that the existing provisions for capacity building and skill 
enhancement are inadequate in effectively cultivating scientific talent. To address this gap, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department formulate a comprehensive policy 
dedicated to capacity building programs for its staff. This policy should focus on structured 
training initiatives, skill development, and continuous learning opportunities. Additionally, 
the Department should actively explore and establish collaborations with internationally 
renowned scientific institutions to facilitate knowledge exchange, exposure to global best 
practices, and advanced research training.

RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT & INNOVATION FUND 
Although the Committee acknowledges the bold initiatives undertaken by the 
Department to encourage private sector participation in cutting-edge research in deep tech 
and sunrise sectors, it also recognizes certain concerns. These include the potential risk of 
fund misallocation, the competence of fund managers in identifying suitable recipients and 
impactful projects, implications for national security, the limited rate of return on investment, 
the possibility of private entities benefiting disproportionately at the Government's expense, 
and the extent to which the outcomes of such research will ultimately benefit the common 
citizen. The Committee is also concerned that such a substantial allocation of funds could 
have yielded a significant impact if directed towards government institutions. Therefore, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department should consider these apprehensions 
while formulating the detailed framework and guidelines to implement this scheme. (Para 3.6)

National Research Foundation (ANRF) as a significant and progressive initiative to 
strengthen research and innovation in the country. However, the Committee is of the view 
that the Department could have demonstrated greater foresight in expediting the procedural 
formalities and operationalization of the ANRF. With better planning and timely execution, a 
portion of the allocated funds could have been effectively utilized during the financial year. 
The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to ensure a more structured and time-bound 
approach in the future to optimize the utilization of budgetary allocations, thereby facilitating 
the timely implementation of research initiatives under ANRF.

1 
 
REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Government of India has set up the Space Commission and the Department of 
Space (DOS) in 1972. Department of Space is responsible for implementing the policies 
framed by the Space Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research 
Organisation (ISRO), Indian National Space Promotion & Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe) 
and the Grant-in-aid institutions viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National 
Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-
SAC), Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and 
Technology (IIST). 
1.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located 
in Bangalore. The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall 
programmes like Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation, Earth Observation, Space 
Transportation Systems, Space Science and Planetary Exploration, Climate & Atmospheric 
Programme, Disaster Management Support, National Natural Resources Management System 
(NNRMS), International Co-Operation, Capacity Building, Media & Public Relations, 
Budget & Economic Analysis and Human Resources Development. 
1.3 The activities of Department of Space (DOS) are broadly organized under four 
umbrella schemes namely 
 Space Technology - development of launch vehicles, satellites, manned space mission, 
R&D in Space Technology such as propulsion, navigational satellite systems, 
indigenization of Space materials & components, etc.  
 
 Space Applications - major Projects/activities such as Earth Observation Navigation 
Missions, Tele-medicine, Tele-education, Disaster Management Support, etc are 
undertaken. 
 
 Space Sciences - projects towards Space sciences and planetary exploration are 
undertaken. Major projects undertaken under the scheme include Indian Lunar Mission - 
Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1 mission, XPoSat, Space Docking Experiment.  
 
 INSAT Satellite Systems- This programme is envisaged to provide satellite based 
communication services in the country.  
1.4 Major Centres / Units of DOS/ISRO: 
a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the 
technology base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development 
b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities located at Bangalore and 
Thiruvananthapuram, is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and 
cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles 
c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the 
spaceport of India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles.  Also, 
it provides the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors 

2 
 
d) Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) is created with the responsibility to act as the 
lead centre for Human Space Flight Program. This centre is responsible for the 
execution of Gaganyaan programme that envisages sending a crew of astrounauts to 
space and bring back safely to earth.   
e) U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bangalore, is entrusted with the prime 
responsibility for development of satellites     
f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad 
g) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data 
acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision 
support for disaster management 
h) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bangalore  
i) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), Mahendragiri  
j) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC) 
k) Master Control Facility (MCF), Hassan 
l) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun  
m) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram  
1.5 Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid: 
a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution 
supported mainly by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences. 
b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near 
Tirupati, conducts atmospheric research. 
c) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) established as an 
autonomous body under the Department of Space provides space technology inputs 
for developmental activities in the North-Eastern Region.  
d) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body 
under the Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to 
suit the requirements of state-of-art space research programme.    
1.6 Government Companies under DOS:  
a) The Antrix Corporation Limited, Bangalore, established in 1992, is a wholly owned 
Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
b) The NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bangalore, is another commercial arm of 
Indian Space Research Organization, with the primary objective of enabling Indian 
industries to scale up high-technology manufacturing and production base for Indian 
space programme.  
1.7 Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (INSPACe) 
Recently, the space sector was opened up to promote, handhold, regulate and 
authorise private enterprises and start-ups to undertake space activities by creation of an 
independent nodal agency under Department of Space - the Indian National Space Promotion 
and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe). This will enhance the contribution of space 
technology towards boosting space economy within the country.

Space Applications 
3.8 The Committee notes that the allocation for Space Applications has increased 
from ₹1,527.97 crores in R.E. 2024-25 to ₹1,706.79 crores in B.E. 2025-26. The 
Committee inquired about the details of major projects under the Scheme. The Department 
replied that under the scheme- “Space Applications”, significant progress have been made 
under Earth Observation, Disaster Management and Communication & Navigation 
Applications. 
Earth Observation Applications 
The Department informed the Committee that it has established a data-sharing 
mechanism under the Indian Space Policy-2023, providing free access to EO data above 5m 
resolution and regulated access for finer resolutions. INSAT-3DS, EOS-06 (Oceansat-3), and 
EOS-04 satellites are actively supporting weather forecasting, ocean monitoring, vegetation 
mapping, and disaster response. Some of the key achievements under the application include: 
 Automated crop mapping for Kharif and Rabi seasons. 
 Soil moisture and hydrological modelling for water resource management. 
 National land-use mapping and geospatial services through the Bhoonidhi and 
Bhuvan portals. 
 Recognition for excellence – Bhoonidhi Portal received the Geospatial Excellence 
Award at GeoSmart India 2024. 
Disaster Management Support 
The Department provided over 300 flood maps across 16 states and implemented a 
flood early warning system for the Godavari and Tapi rivers. Other initiatives include: 
 Landslide early warning models for pilot sites in Kerala, West Bengal, and 
Uttarakhand. 
 Daily forest fire alerts integrated with FSI for real-time monitoring. 
 Lightning observation system for national weather forecasting. 
 Support for 41 international disaster relief requests under Emergency & Disaster 
Management. 
 Satellite-based analysis of the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) in Sikkim, 
determining the cause and assessing the damage. 
 19 capacity-building programmes for Government disaster response agencies. 
Communication & Navigation Applications 
The NavIC satellite system continues to provide positioning, navigation, and timing 
(PNT) services, with four active satellites and five repurposed for safety-of-life messaging. 
Some of the key achievements under the application include: 
 Tele-education expansion in Northeast India and Jammu & Kashmir. 
 Telemedicine connectivity for defence establishments. 
 NavIC-based messaging services for fishermen safety. 
 Vessel tracking and monitoring systems for the fishing industry. 
 Real-time train tracking for Indian Railways using NavIC signals. 
 Continued support for satellite-based search and rescue operations.

sponsored research activities at academia. The Department informed that The Aditya-L1 
spacecraft was successfully placed at the designated halo orbit around the first Sun-Earth 
Lagrangian point on January 6, 2023. So far, the spacecraft has completed more than two 
orbits. The mission has yielded important science results on the Coronal Mass Ejection 
dynamics and UV signatures from the solar disc. The maiden set of scientific data from 
Aditya-L1 was released to the global scientific community on January 6, 2024. The 
Chandrayaan-3 mission life of fourteen Earth days have been completed in September 2023, 
which has yielded significant scientific results on the lunar surface elements at the Southern 
lunar latitudes, validating the Lunar Magma Ocean (LMO) Hypothesis. The data sets from 
Chandrayaan-3 were released to the global scientific community on August 23, 2024. The 
Department further elaborated that the XPoSat mission is about to complete its Payload 
Verification (PV) phase and scientific data from the mission will be released to the research 
community shortly. On planetary exploration initiatives, the Department informed that 
recently, Government has approved planetary missions like Venus Orbiter Mission, 
Chandrayaan-4 and Chandrayaan-5 mission and the approval for Mars Lander Mission is in 
advanced stage. ISRO is playing active role in community building in the domain of 
planetary exploration, and space science in general.

4.1    IN-SPACe 
  The Department in a written reply informed the Committee about the vision, mission 
and objectives of INSPACe. IN-SPACe aims to boost private sector participation in space 
activities, strengthen India’s space economy, and promote self-reliance in space technology. 
As a single-window agency, it facilitates start-ups, MSMEs, industries, and academic 
institutions in innovation and commercialisation within the space sector. Its key functions 
include:  
 
(i) Enabling private sector involvement in launch vehicle and satellite development. 

20 
 
(ii) Granting access to ISRO’s infrastructure for research, manufacturing, and testing. 
(iii) Overseeing the establishment of new space facilities by private players while ensuring 
compliance with safety and statutory guidelines. 
(iv) Facilitating launch campaigns and satellite registration for Indian private entities. 
(v) Encouraging technology sharing and collaboration to strengthen India’s space 
ecosystem. 
(vi) Managing an integrated launch manifest to align priorities of ISRO, public sector 
units, and private entities. 
(vii) Providing affordable access to ISRO’s high-tech facilities for private sector research 
and   development. 
The Department further informed that IN-SPACe actively promotes skill development 
and talent acquisition through short-term training courses in satellite technology, propulsion, 
and space communications to bridge industry skill gaps; academic partnerships with IIT 
Roorkee and universities to integrate space technology education; Pre-Incubation 
Entrepreneurship (PIE) Program, launched in June 2024, to mentor and support early-stage 
start-ups and recognition by NCVET as an awarding body, setting industry standards for 
space-related vocational education and training. 
4.2 The Department of Space highlighted the following key initiatives/actions under taken 
to support & enable the private-sector engagement in space activities:  
i. Regulatory and Policy Framework for Indian Space Sector 
Indian Space Policy – 2023 (ISP-2023) was brought out in April 2023, has identified 
the range of Space Activities undertaken by private players that require Authorization 
by IN-SPACe. 
Subsequently, IN-SPACe has brought out the Norms, Guidelines and Procedures 
(NGP) document for streamlining the authorization processes. 
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy provisions for the Space sector have been 
liberalized in prescribed sub sectors/activities, to attract potential foreign investors to 
invest in Indian companies in space sector.

IN-SPACe enables & facilitates NGEs to access ISRO’s capital intensive testing 
facilities and launch infrastructure. IN-SPACe also facilitates NGEs to access & 
utilize standard test facilities at the IN-SPACe Technical labs established exclusively 
for developing and testing their technologies. All these facilities are offered to the 
Start-up and MSME at a price support. 
IN-SPACe in collaboration with ISRO, facilitates the opportunity to host payloads on 
POEM (PSLV orbital experimental module) platform to strengthen / complement the 
space-based research activities taking place in industry/academia within the country. 
IN-SPACe has also setup mechanisms to provide expert mentorship, and guidance to

5.3   National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL)  
NARL conducts advanced research in atmospheric and space sciences, focusing on 
monitoring atmospheric processes, high-resolution weather modelling, and scientific 
observations to support space missions and other applications. It has developed high-power 
radio and optical instruments, many of which have been patented and transferred to industry. 
The Department informed that observatories in Hyderabad and Kolkata have been established 
to study key national issues, while the Venus Advanced Radar and Differential Absorption 
Lidar have been developed for planetary and atmospheric studies. NARL has also introduced 
AI/ML-based techniques for weather forecasting and atmospheric data analysis, built GNSS 
receiver networks for ionospheric and meteorological research, and improved rocket launch 
weather forecasting models. The airglow laboratory in Hyderabad and spectrograph in 
Gadanki contribute to studying atmospheric dynamics and space weather. Over 6.8 TB of 
climate data has been shared with scientists, and 184 research papers have been published in 
peer-reviewed journals. The institute has produced 17 PhDs and 97 dissertations, with many 
faculty members receiving national and international honours, including recognition from 
Stanford University, INSA, and the International Commission for Optics. Looking ahead, 
NARL aims to expand its research facilities, setting up more observatories across the country 
and establishing a national-level observational network. It seeks to develop indigenous 

26 
 
ground-based and space-borne instruments, enhance weather forecasting through water 
vapour and ionospheric mapping, and study the impact of rapid urbanisation on atmospheric 
conditions. The institute is also committed to strengthening collaboration with academic and 
national laboratories to achieve significant advancements in atmospheric and space research.
