Similarly, Autonomous Bodies (NARL, NESAC, PRL) and IIST also face recruitment 
challenges, although to a lesser extent. 
7.2 The Committee inquired into the manner in which this shortage will affect the 
efficiency and performance of ISRO and its affiliated PSUs, CPSEs, and Autonomous Bodies 
and the measures being taken to ensure that the Department's missions and projects are not 
impacted due to manpower shortages. The Department acknowledges the pressing issue of 
manpower shortages across ISRO, PSUs, CPSEs, and Autonomous Bodies, which currently 
stands at 3,927 vacancies. The Department informed the Committee that this shortage has 
impacted the operational efficiency and timely execution of projects, particularly as ISRO 
gears up for major missions such as the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), lunar sample 
return, and human spaceflight to the Moon by 2027. The Department informed the 
Committee that the accumulation of vacancies was primarily due to disruptions caused by 
COVID-19, sectoral reforms, and recruitment policy revisions, leading to a one-year delay in 
hiring. Additionally, security concerns in examination halls led to a four-month halt in 
recruitment activities in 2023, further compounding the backlog. The Department highlighted 
the key measures taken to expedite filling of vacancies which are as follows: 

30 
 
(i) The Department has initiated actions to fill about 1,950 posts before June 2025, with 
written tests and interviews for 1,060 posts underway and reporting planned for 889 selected 
candidates. However, administrative vacancies remain significantly high (2,008 out of 3,062 
positions), indicating challenges in processing personnel recruitment. 
(ii) To  meet the rising demands of space exploration and mission complexity, ISRO has 
proposed augmenting its workforce by at least 500 additional S&T personnel and increasing 
IT personnel by 80 posts to strengthen cyber security monitoring. 
(iii) The Department has implemented a centralised recruitment process under which 
hiring for general disciplines is conducted annually, covering about 70% of staffing needs. 
Additionally, quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises have been introduced to identify and 
resolve bottlenecks in hiring. 
7.3 The Committee recommends expediting the recruitment process to ensure that 
vacant posts, particularly for Scientists/Engineers and technical staff, are filled within 
the next six months. A dedicated recruitment task force should be established to oversee 
hiring efficiency, identify process bottlenecks, and ensure compliance with recruitment 
timelines. The Committee recommends that the Department must develop a structured 
workforce planning model, forecasting staffing needs for the next decade in alignment 
with ISRO’s Vision 2047. The Committee is concerned about the high vacancy rate in 
NSIL and Antrix, as it may impact India’s growing commercial space sector. It 
recommends an industry-specific recruitment approach to attract talent from both 
public and private space technology domains, ensuring that PSEs remain competitive 
and capable of supporting ISRO’s missions. 
7.4 The Committee supports the Department’s plan to engage S&T personnel on a 
tenure basis but recommends that flexible hiring models be expanded to include 
project-based contracts for emerging space technologies. 
7.5 The Committee notes that the backlog in hiring was caused partly due to delays 
during the COVID-19 period and recruitment policy revisions. It recommends 
increasing the frequency of centralised recruitment drives to ensure that vacancies do 
not accumulate in the future. Quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises should be 
conducted to track hiring progress and address any procedural challenges.

for 1,950 posts are in progress, there is a pressing need to accelerate hiring, particularly 
for S&T roles. The Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) under DoS, such as Antrix and 
NSIL, also report a concerning vacancy rate (265 out of 323 sanctioned posts), which 
may hinder their efficiency in commercial space activities. Similarly, Autonomous 
Bodies (NARL, NESAC, PRL) and IIST also face recruitment challenges, although to a 
lesser extent.                                                                                                               (Para 7.1) 
 The Committee recommends expediting the recruitment process to ensure that 
vacant posts, particularly for Scientists/Engineers and technical staff, are filled within 
the next six months. A dedicated recruitment task force should be established to oversee 
hiring efficiency, identify process bottlenecks, and ensure compliance with recruitment 
timelines. The Committee recommends that the Department must develop a structured 
workforce planning model, forecasting staffing needs for the next decade in alignment 
with ISRO’s Vision 2047. The Committee is concerned about the high vacancy rate in 
NSIL and Antrix, as it may impact India’s growing commercial space sector. It 
recommends an industry-specific recruitment approach to attract talent from both 
public and private space technology domains, ensuring that PSEs remain competitive 
and capable of supporting ISRO’s missions.                                                          (Para 7.3) 
 The Committee supports the Department’s plan to engage S&T personnel on a 
tenure basis but recommends that flexible hiring models be expanded to include 
project-based contracts for emerging space technologies.                                     (Para 7.4) 
 The Committee notes that the backlog in hiring was caused partly due to delays 
during the COVID-19 period and recruitment policy revisions. It recommends 
increasing the frequency of centralised recruitment drives to ensure that vacancies do 
not accumulate in the future. Quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises should be 
conducted to track hiring progress and address any procedural challenges.     (Para 7.5)

REPORT  
INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change (MoEF&CC) is the nodal 
agency in the administrative structure of the Central Government for planning, promoting, 
coordinating and overseeing environmental, ecological, forestry and wildlife policies and 
programmes. Its main activities include conservation and survey of natural resources 
including flora, fauna, forests, wildlife, aquatic bodies and water resources and eco-systems, 
prevention and control of pollution and management of hazardous substances, protection of 
the environment and forests, including their biodiversity, mitigation and adaptation to 
climate change through measures that include afforestation, regeneration of degraded areas, 
and adoption of cleaner technologies, and promoting sustainable development and better 
environmental governance while protecting human, plants and animals life, health and 
welfare.  
1.2 These objectives are well supported by a set of legislative and regulatory measures, 
aimed at the preservation, conservation and protection of the environment. Besides the 
legislative measures, a National Conservation Strategy and Policy Statement on 
Environment and Development, 1992, National Forest Policy, 1988, a Policy Statement on 
Abatement of Pollution, 1992 and a National Environment Policy, 2006 also guide the 
Ministry’s work.  
1.3 The main tools used to discharge its mandate include, inter alia, conducting surveys; 
collecting, compiling and disseminating data and information; undertaking scientific 
research, extension services and analyses; carrying out impact assessment of developmental 
projects and programmes; regulating use of natural resources; undertaking regeneration 
programmes; extending technical, scientific, financial and administrative support to 
organisations and institutions in the subject fields; imparting education, training, building 
capacity and generating awareness among stakeholders and the public at large; and 
promoting international cooperation through bilateral, regional and multilateral initiatives in 
environment and ecology. 
1.4 The institutional set up of the Ministry includes a number of Directorates and 
Divisions assembled around the main thematic sectors of environment and ecology, forestry 
and wildlife, afforestation and eco-development. The Ministry has 20 Regional Offices; ten 
Attached/Subordinate Offices (e.g. Botanical, Zoological and Forests Surveys of India, 
Directorate of Forestry Education, Indira Gandhi National Forestry Academy, National 
Green Tribunal, Wildlife Crime Control Bureau etc.); Boards and Authorities (e.g. Central 
Pollution Control Board, National Biodiversity Authority, National Tiger Conservation 
Authority, Central Zoo Authority) and Autonomous Institutions (e.g. Indian Council for 
Forestry Research and Education, Wildlife Institute of India etc.). Provision has been made 
in the Demand for Grants for the year 2025-26 for its attached/ subordinate/ autonomous 
organisations and other bodies. 
FUNCTIONING AND ACTIVITIES OF THE MINISTRY 
1.5 The Mission of Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change is to plan, 
promote, co-ordinate and oversee the implementation of India’s environmental and forestry 
policies and programmes related to conservation of the country’s natural resources including 
its lakes and rivers, its biodiversity, forests and wildlife, ensuring the welfare of animals, 
and the prevention and abatement of pollution. The Ministry seeks to ensure inclusive 
economic growth guided by the principles of sustainable development and enhancement of 
human well-being.

5. CONTROL OF POLLUTION 
5.1 The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change administers the Central 
Sector Scheme-‘Control of Pollution’ to curb environmental pollution since 2018-19.  For 
the FY 2025-26, the total budget (under BE) of the scheme is Rs.853.9 crore.  The main 
objective of the Control of Pollution scheme is to monitor air quality across the country and 
take appropriate air pollution mitigation measures, besides monitoring water quality and 
noise levels in the country. The components under the scheme are as under: 
(a) Assistance for Abatement of Pollution to weaker SPCBs/PCCs-Under this 
component State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs)/Pollution Control 
Committee (PCCs) are supported to meet the expenditure requirements for taking 
pollution abatement activity including pollution assessment (Source monitoring, 
monitoring of ambient air, water and noise), technical studies for R&D, survey 
and documentation for creation of environmental database and consultation in 
the area of pollution abatement of air, water & noise, scientific research and 
studies on issues of waste management, inventorisation of wastes, training and 
mass awareness, education, seminars/workshops/conference, lab upgradation/ 
procurement of equipment,  E- Governance and IT applications including online 
consent management, online emission/effluent monitoring systems, development 
of IT infrastructure. 
(b) National Clean Air Programme (NCAP): The National Clean Air Programme 
(NCAP) was launched by Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change 
in January 2019 with an aim to improve air quality in 130 cities (Non-Attainment 
cities and Million-Plus cities) in 24 States/Union Territories (UTs) by engaging 
all stakeholders. The NCAP envisages reduction by 20-30% in PM10 
concentrations by 2024-25 over baseline in the year 2017-18. Target has been 
revised to achieve reduction in PM10 level up to 40% over baseline in the year 
2019-20 or achievement of national ambient air quality standards (60 
microgram/cubic meter) by 2025-26. Annual PM10 reduction target of 4-15% has 
been assigned to each city to improve air quality through implementation of City 
Action Plans. The Ministry has issued guidelines for release and utilization of 
funds under the sub-component. Further, in case of 48 Million-Plus cities /Urban 
Agglomerations funded under 15th Finance Commission Air Quality Grant, 15% 
reduction in PM10 concentrations and 15% improvement in good days (Air 
Quality Index<200) w.r.t. previous year have been considered.   
(c) Following Components come under Environmental Monitoring Network 
Programme:- 

12 
 
i. Operation and Maintenance of National Air Quality Monitoring 
Programme (NAMP) stations 
ii. Operation and Maintenance of Continuous Ambient Air Quality 
Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) 
iii. National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network (NANMN) – strengthening 
and establishment of New Stations in Million Plus Cities 
iv. National Water Monitoring Programme (NWMP)                      
(d) Research and Outreach Programmes - The Ministry is providing funds to the 
projects which have impact for prevention and control of pollution. Under 
this component of the scheme, the Ministry proposes to provide funds to the 
Research and Development (R&D) projects, which can advance emerging 
technologies and solutions in control and prevention of pollution and 
implementing decision support systems. This component also includes 
developing indigenous facilities for certification, testing and calibration of air 
quality monitoring equipment, and National Environmental Health Profile 
(NEHP) study. NEHP study aims to assess impact of air pollution on human 
health in selected cities across the country.

5.3 The Committee was surprised to observe that out of the RE 2024-25 allocation of 
Rs.858.00 crore for ‘Control of Pollution’, only an amount of Rs.7.22 crore was spent upto 
31.1.2025.  The Committee desired to know the reasons therefor from the Ministry.  In their 
reply, the Ministry informed that the utilisation of majority of the funds in the scheme for 
the financial year 2024-25 could not be made till now as the approval for the continuation of 
the ‘Control of Pollution’ scheme till FY 2025-26 is awaited. Planning for disbursement and 
utilization of the funds are already in place and will be executed as soon as approval is 
received.  Further, the Ministry intends to spend the budget of Rs.853.00 crore for FY 2025-
26 under Control of Pollution Scheme under various components of the scheme as per the 
approval. 
5.4 The Committee is of the view that pollution, whether it be air, water or noise, 
has gone beyond permissible limits during the last few years and has serious 
consequences for the health and well being of the citizens of the country. Air pollution 
has assumed gigantic proportions and has become a national issue.  Although Delhi has 
been in the news because of it ever-deteriorating air quality, other cities in the country 
are also not left behind and are experiencing high AQI levels.  In such a scenario, the 
Committee is shocked to note that amount to the tune of Rs. 858.00 crore allocated for 
‘Control of Pollution’, which is 27.44% of the annual RE allocation of the Ministry, 
remains unutilized since the approval for continuation of Control of Pollution Scheme 
till 2025-26, is awaited, even at the fag end of the financial year.  The rising 
environmental pollution in the country not only results into a number of pollution 
related human diseases and health conditions but negatively impact our ecology too.  
The scenario of air pollution in the country is indeed very grim and has been affecting 

13 
 
one and all.  At a time when the Ministry is required to address the grave and critical 
challenge of deteriorating air quality, the Ministry has not been able to decide the 
continuation of the concerned scheme, as a result of which not even 1% of the funds 
allocated for the scheme have been utilized so far.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry needs to introspect and take a serious note of the 
reasons for this gross underutilization.

Development of Wildlife Habitats 
6.3 The ‘Development of Wildlife Habitats’ (DWH) is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme. 
The overall objective of the scheme is conservation and management of PAs, recovery of 
endangered species, mitigating man-animal conflict, and voluntary relocation of families 
for creating inviolate space for wild animals, healthier ecosystem and repository as source 
for gene pool.  The Protected Area (PA) network in country comprises of 106 National 
Parks, 573 Wildlife Sanctuaries, 123 Conservation Reserves and 220 community reserves 
extending over an area of 1,78,640.69 sq.km., which is 5.43% of the geographical area of 
the country.  The components of the scheme are (i) Support to Protected areas, (ii) 
Protection of Wildlife outside Protected Areas and (iii) Recovery Programmes for saving 
Critically Endangered Species and habitats.  
Project Tiger & Elephant 
6.4 The Ministry provides financial assistance to the States/UTs under the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme Project Tiger & Elephant for the protection of elephants, their habitats & 
corridors, welfare of captive elephant and mitigation of human elephant conflict.

sponsored schemes such as Project Tiger and Elephant and the scheme for 
Development of Wildlife Habitats for the maintenance of protected areas notified

7.2 It was informed that India is on track to meet its global commitments towards global 
collective efforts to combat climate change and that some of the Targets under India first 
NDC, submitted in 2015, have been achieved ahead of stipulated timeline (2021-30). 
7.3 The Committee desired to know from the Ministry that given the commitments 
under India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) to the Paris Agreement, how 
does this budget support India’s goal of achieving a 45% reduction in emissions intensity by 
2030?  In response, the Committee was informed that India is a Party to three treaties 
governing the International Climate Regime; namely the United Nations Framework 
Convention on the Climate Change (UNFCCC), its Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement. 
Under the Paris Agreement of the UNFCCC, India has submitted and subsequently updated 
its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to the UNFCCC. India’s current NDC is for 
the period of 2021-2030. In addition, India has also submitted its Long-Term Low Carbon 
Development Strategy to reach net-zero by 2070. 
7.4 The Government earlier committed to finance India’s climate action, which cuts 
across various sectors important for our economy, through annual budget exercise.  On 
these lines, and like the previous budgets, Union Budget 2025-26 has provisioned series of 
measures including those for energy sector reforms, nuclear energy development, clean 
technology manufacturing, lithium-ion battery production, and increase in budgetary 
allocations for the Ministry of Power and the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy from 
the previous year and for enhancing climate resilience. Some of the salient announcements 
are as under:  
(a) A “National Manufacturing Mission” to cover small, medium, and large industries is 
announced. Recognizing our commitment to climate-friendly development, the 
Mission will also support Clean Tech manufacturing. The aim is to improve 
domestic value addition and build our ecosystem for solar PV cells, EV batteries, 
motors, and controllers, electrolyzers, wind turbines, very high voltage transmission 
equipment and grid scale batteries.  
(b) Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat: -The Budget recognizes the importance 
of nuclear energy in reaching to net-zero. Towards this, the Budget has provisioned 

18 
 
development of at least 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047. It is essential for our 
energy transition efforts. For an active partnership with the private sector towards 
this goal, amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and the Civil Liability for Nuclear 
Damage Act have been proposed. A Nuclear Energy Mission for research & 
development of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) with an outlay of Rs. 20,000 crore 
is proposed through which at least 5 indigenously developed SMRs will be 
operationalized by 2033. 
(c) The budget also emphasizes expanding the electric vehicle ecosystem, strengthening 
domestic battery manufacturing, supporting startups, and enhancing green financing 
for EV adoption and energy storage solutions. In the context of battery 
manufacturing; the Budget has announced Mining sector reforms, including those 
for minor minerals, including a policy for recovery of critical minerals from tailings. 
The Budget has also proposed to add to the list of exempted capital goods, 35 
additional capital goods for EV battery manufacturing, and 28 additional capital 
goods for mobile phone battery manufacturing. This is to boost domestic 
manufacture of lithium-ion battery, including those required for electric vehicles. 
(d) For enhancing the resilience of agriculture sector, the Budget has proposed Prime 
Minister Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana; 6-year Mission for Aatmanirbharta in 
Pulses; Comprehensive Programme for Vegetables & Fruits; National Mission on 
High Yielding Seeds; and Mission for Cotton Productivity. The Budget also 
proposes a framework for sustainable harnessing of fisheries from Indian Exclusive 
Economic Zone and High Seas.   
(e) To further enhance India’s action towards adapting to the climate change in water 
sector, the Budget has announced the extension of the Jal Jeevan Mission until 2028 
with an enhanced total outlay. 
7.5 The Committee is of the view that Climate change is a global concern and India, 
being amongst the most populous countries, needs to be concerned about that. Our 
National Action Plan for Climate Change (NAPCC) has missions in areas like solar 
energy, energy efficiency, water, human health, sustainable agriculture, Himalayan 
ecosystem, sustainable habitat, and strategic knowledge of climate change. We must 
cooperate with other countries globally, as climate summits, after the Paris Agreement, 
have shown slow progress.  While taking progressive steps, India must correlate her 
efforts with other countries. The Committee notes that the new U.S. administration's 
withdrawal from climate funding is a matter of concern, as they had committed to 
contributing $100 billion to the climate fund under the Paris Agreement.  Not only 
have they backed out, but even the international organizations, like, the WHO has 
shown its reservations. Under these circumstances, India, being a large country and 
being a major player in climate change mitigation, must take responsibility and work 
towards achieving its goals. 
7.6 During the meeting, the Committee also drew attention of the Ministry to the 
reports that in view of the recent climatic trends, the coming months of the year 2025-
26 are likely to see temperatures soaring to 1-3°C higher than the average 
temperatures recorded in the past across various cities and terrains of the country, 
especially Delhi where the temperature may be abnormally high during the summer 
season of 2026.  The Committee is extremely concerned over such alarming reports. 
The Committee is of the view that, if this happens, it will have devastating 
consequences for human habitats, birds, animals, and the environment.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest & 
Climate Change should immediately formulate and implement a national-level Heat 
Action Plan (HAP) to mitigate the heatwave conditions that the citizens of India are 
likely to face in the coming months.

BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 AND 
ALLOCATION FOR 2025-26 
 The Committee observes that the Ministry had been able to utilize more than 
96% of the allocated funds during the year 2022-23 and 2023-24.In 2024-25, against the 
BE allocation of Rs.3330.00 crore, a reduced RE allocation of Rs.3125.96 was made to 
the Ministry.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that the actual 
expenditure of the Ministry upto 31.1.2025 was only Rs.1712.48 crore which is merely 
54.78% of the RE allocation.  During the presentation made before the Committee on 
19.2.2025, the Secretary of the Ministry further informed the Committee that the 
Ministry has utilized 69% of the funds as on that date.  However, the Committee is of 
the view that the utilization of funds by the Ministry during 2024-25 is not satisfactory.  
With hardly 40 days left in the completion of the financial year, the Ministry is yet to 
make use of more than 30% of the funds allocated to it.  This is in sharp contrast to the 
utilization of funds by the Ministry during the past two financial years when the 
Ministry was able to utilize more than 96% of the budgetary allocations.  The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry must make proactive efforts to optimally 
utilize the funds made available to it during the financial year 2024-25.          (Para 2.3) 
 
BARE MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS IN BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 
SUSTAINING KEY PROGRAMMES 
 The Committee takes note of the challenges projected by the Ministry in Budget 
allocation in Key programmes and the bare minimum budgetary requirements 
projected by it for sustaining certain key programmes.  Though the Committee is in 
agreement with the requirements projected by the Ministry, the utilization of funds by 
the Ministry in 2024-25 are not encouraging enough for the Committee to make any 
positive recommendations in this regard.  The Committee would, however, like to 
recommend that in 2025-26, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change 
should make proactive efforts to ensure that the physical targets of the Ministry in 
respect of the above schemes/programmes are on schedule and the allocation made at 
BE is utilised to the maximum so that it is on a firm ground to seek additional funds at 
the Supplementary and RE stage in respect of the schemes/programmes stated above.  
(Para 2.5) 
MAJOR THRUST AREAS  
 The Committee is of the opinion that the launching of the campaign to plant 
trees on the occasion of World Environment Day is indeed laudable.  The Committee 
feels that the campaign to plant a tree in honour of a mother would certainly create a 
lasting legacy that nurtures both the environment and a greener, prosperous future.  
The Committee notes that 118 crore had already been planted as on 19th February 
2025 and hopes that the Ministry would be able to achieve its target of planting 140 
crore trees by 31st March 2025.                                                                              (Para 3.4) 
 The Committee would, however, like to point out that although a number of 
plantation activities are undertaken on various occasions, the mortality rate of such 
plants is very high.  There is a need not only to plant the trees but also to ensure that 
once planted, they are looked after well and continue to survive and grow.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should not only undertake 
plantation activities but should also ensure that the survival rate of these plants 
remains high so that they continue to contribute to the environment and the society. 
This also needs to be emphasized to the youth/children etc. when organizing 
workshops, exhibitions, campaigns, competitions etc. by the concerned 

20 
 
Central/State/UT authorities.  There is also a need for audit of the plantation activities, 
so that the allocations made in this regard are utilized optimally.                     (Para 3.5) 
The Committee is also of the view that Centrally-funded schemes are crucial 
because they provide funds to other States for improving their systems. Facilitating 
research and development and investing for the same are extremely important for the 
development of any nation and for a developing country like India, the critical 
importance of environmental education, awareness, Research and Development cannot 
be overemphasized, as education and awareness only can help finding practical 
solutions to problems of environmental protection and management and for developing 
policies, strategies, action plans and in better management and conservation of natural 
resources. The Committee feels that the allocation of Rs. 101.96 crore allocated for 
‘Environment Education, Awareness, Research and Skill Development’ is not adequate 
and the Ministry should consider allocating additional funds to this head.       (Para 3.6) 
NATIONAL COASTAL MISSION 
 The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by the Ministry with 
regard to the allocations made to the National Coastal Mission during the last few years.  
The allocation was reduced from Rs.196.00 crore (BE) to Rs.4.00 crore (RE) in 2022-23.  
In 2023-24, the allocation was increased from Rs.12.50 crore (BE) to Rs.43.30 crore 
(RE).  In 2024-25, the allocation was again reduced from Rs.50.00 crore (BE) to Rs.8.00 
crore (RE), out of which the Ministry has been able to spend only 13.8% i.e. Rs.1.10 
crore upto 31.1.2025.  These figures amply bring out that the funds under this scheme 
are being allocated and utilized in an adhoc and unplanned manner.  The Committee is 
of the view that, keeping in view the importance of the Mission, the Ministry should 
holistically plan the execution of the scheme and ensure that the funds are suitably 
allocated and optimally utilized.                                                                                (Para 4.4) 
CONTROL OF POLLUTION 
 The Committee is of the view that pollution, whether it be air, water or noise, 
has gone beyond permissible limits during the last few years and has serious 
consequences for the health and well being of the citizens of the country. Air pollution 
has assumed gigantic proportions and has become a national issue.  Although Delhi has 
been in the news because of it ever-deteriorating air quality, other cities in the country 
are also not left behind and are experiencing high AQI levels.  In such a scenario, the 
Committee is shocked to note that amount to the tune of Rs.858.00 crore allocated for 
‘Control of Pollution’, which is 27.44% of the annual RE allocation of the Ministry, 
remains unutilized since the approval for continuation of Control of Pollution Scheme 
till 2025-26, is awaited, even at the fag end of the financial year.  The rising 
environmental pollution in the country not only results into a number of pollution 
related human diseases and health conditions but negatively impact our ecology too.  
The scenario of air pollution in the country is indeed very grim and has been affecting 
one and all.  At a time when the Ministry is required to address the grave and critical 
challenge of deteriorating air quality, the Ministry has not been able to decide the 
continuation of the concerned scheme, as a result of which not even 1% of the funds 
allocated for the scheme have been utilized so far.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry needs to introspect and take a serious note of the 
reasons for this gross underutilization.                                                                 (Para 5.4)

 The Committee notes that the financial performance of the Ministry under this 
scheme had been satisfactory during the last three years.  The Ministry was able to 
spend 81% and 99.99% of the allocated funds during 2022-23 and 2023-24.  During 
2024-25, the Ministry has been able to spend nearly 75% of the funds upto 31st

sponsored schemes such as Project Tiger and Elephant and the scheme for

R E P O R T      
INTRODUCTION 
 
 Earth System Science deals with all the five components of the Earth 
System, viz., Atmosphere, Hydrosphere, Cryosphere, Geosphere, and 
Biosphere, and their complex interactions. The Ministry of Earth Sciences 
(MoES) holistically addresses all the aspects relating to the Earth System 
Science for providing weather, climate, ocean, coastal state, hydrological, and 
seismological services. The services include forecasts and warnings for various 
natural disasters like tropical cyclones, storm surges, floods, heat waves, 
thunderstorms, and lightning; alerts for Tsunamis and monitoring of 
earthquakes, etc. In addition, the ministry also has the mandate to develop 
technology for ocean surveys and exploration of living and non-living 
resources from the ocean and exploration of all three poles (Arctic, Antarctic, 
and Himalayas). The services provided by the ministry are being effectively 
used by different agencies and state governments to save human lives and 
minimize damages due to natural disasters. 
 
1.2 The mandate of the ministry includes overall policy, planning, 
coordination, implementation, evaluation and review of the schemes relating to 
meteorology, seismology, oceanography, ocean resources and technology, 
polar science, cryosphere and geosciences not specifically allocated to any 
other Department or Ministry.  The overarching vision of the Ministry is 
“Excelling in Earth System Science to make lives better through world class 
services for weather, climate, ocean, coastal and natural hazards; sustainable 
harnessing of ocean resources and exploration of the polar regions”.  The 
Objectives of the Ministry are as under :- 
i. To provide Weather and Climate Services for various sectors like 
disaster management, agriculture, aviation, water resources, power, 
tourism, health, air quality, public safety etc. 
ii. To undertake the Science of Climate Change- Regional Climate Change 
Scenarios. 
iii. To provide Early warnings for Hazards such as Cyclones, Heavy 
Rainfall, Heatwave, etc. 
iv. To provide Ocean Services, which include Tsunami warnings, Potential 
Fishing zone advisories, Ocean State Forecasts, Oil Spill Advisories, 
Coastal Research, and Coastal Protection. 
v. Harnessing of non-living ocean resources - Water, Energy and Minerals 
vi. Ocean living resources mapping, Marine biodiversity, Marine 
Biotechnology 

2 
 
vii. Survey and Exploration of Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental 
Shelf 
viii. Earthquake Detection and information, Deep Scientific drilling, Crustal 
Dynamics, Geoscience research. 
ix. Scientific exploration of the three poles (Arctic, Antarctic and 
Himalayas) and Cryosphere research. 
x. Develop deep sea technologies for sustainable use of ocean resources, 
and improve our understanding of deep sea. 
xi. R&D and development of technology leading to weather intervention 
xii. To support various Extra-Mural R&D activities, Outreach and 
Awareness activities and Capacity Building in the field of Earth 
Sciences. 
 
1.3 The policies and programs of the Ministry are being primarily pursued 
through its 10 Institutes viz., autonomous bodies, attached and subordinate 
offices.  The institutions dealing with atmospheric sciences are the India 
Meteorological Department (IMD), National Centre for Medium Range 
Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida and Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM), Pune.  The institutions related to ocean science and 
technology are National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR), Goa, 
National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai, Indian National 
Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad, Centre for 
Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi and National Centre 
for Coastal Research (NCCR), Chennai. The National Centre for Earth Science 
Studies (NCESS), Thiruvananthapuram and National Centre for Seismology 
(NCS), New Delhi conduct research on solid earth and earthquake monitoring. 
Each Centre of the Ministry has a well-defined mandate to conduct research 
and development in a specific area of Earth Sciences.

PERFORMANCE OF SCHEMES / PROGRAMMES 
5. Deep Ocean Mission 
5.1 As a Maritime nation with a coastline of about 7500 km and around 30% 
of the country's population living in coastal areas, oceans play an important 
role in the Indian economy. The Government of India’s Vision of New India by 
2030, enunciated in February 2019, highlighted the Blue Economy as one of 
the ten core dimensions of growth. With a view to exploring the deep ocean for 
resources, developing deep-sea technologies for sustainable use of ocean 
resources, and improving our understanding of the deep sea, the Government 
of India launched the “Deep Ocean Mission” at an estimated cost of Rs.4077.0 
crore for a period of 5 years. This mission mode project will support various 
priority areas illustrated in the Blue Economy policy document of the 
Government of India. Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) is the nodal 
implementing Ministry for this multi-ministerial, multi-institutional mission.   
5.2 Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) aims to explore deep-oceanic resources and 
develop technologies for their sustainable use. The Mission consists of six 
major themes, namely (i) Development of Technologies for Deep Sea Mining, 
Manned Submersible, and Underwater Robotics; (ii) Development of Ocean 
Climate Change Advisory Services; (iii) Technological innovations for 
exploration and conservation of deep-sea biodiversity; (iv) Deep Ocean Survey 
and Exploration; (v) Energy and freshwater from the Ocean and (vi) Advanced

6. Prithvi Vigyan (PRITHVI) 
6.1 Ministry of Earth Sciences is mandated to translate Science to Services 
for Society in providing services for weather, climate, ocean and coastal state, 
hydrology, seismology, and natural hazards; to explore and harness marine 
living and non-living resources in a sustainable manner for the country and to 
explore the three poles of the Earth (Arctic, Antarctic and Himalayas).  
PRITHVI Scheme deals with the study of various aspects of Ocean, Polar and 
Cryosphere with Special emphasis on the Antarctic, Arctic, Southern Ocean 
and Himalayas, Seismological and Geo-science as well as Research Education, 
Training and Outreach.  All the earlier schemes, viz. Ocean Services, 
Modelling Application, Resources and Technology (O-SMART), Polar Science 
and Cryosphere Research (PACER), Seismology and Geosciences (SAGE) and 
Research, Education, Training and Outreach (REACHOUT) have been merged 
together in the PRITHVI scheme.   
6.2 The overarching scheme of PRITHVI will holistically address all the 
five components of earth system to improve the understanding of the Earth 
System Sciences and to provide reliable services for the country.  The major 
Objectives of the Prithvi Scheme are:  
 Augmentation and sustenance of long-term observations of the 
atmosphere, ocean, geosphere, cryosphere and solid earth to record the 
vital signs of the Earth System and change 
 Development of modelling systems for understanding and predicting 
weather, ocean and climate hazards and understanding the science of 
climate change 
 Exploration polar and high seas regions of the Earth towards the 
discovery of new phenomena and resources;  
 Development of technology for exploration and sustainable harnessing 
of oceanic resources for societal applications 
 Translation of knowledge and insights from Earth systems science 
into services for societal, environmental and economic benefit.

7. Mission Mausam  
7.1 This scheme has been designed to enhance India's weather and climate 
forecasting capabilities across various critical sectors, including agriculture, 
aviation, urban planning, defense, sports, and disaster preparedness. The 
mission seeks to leverage cutting-edge technologies, high-performance 
computing, and advanced modeling techniques to revolutionize weather 
monitoring, prediction, and data analysis. By advancing weather surveillance, 
incorporating next-generation radars and satellites, and utilizing artificial 
intelligence and machine learning, Mission Mausam aims to provide more 
accurate and timely forecasts, addressing the challenges of extreme weather 
events and climate change. The program also focuses on building robust 
infrastructure, fostering innovation, and ensuring that weather-related 
information reaches the public effectively, contributing to national 
development, disaster management, and climate resilience. Through its 
comprehensive approach, Mission Mausam aims to establish an integrated 
framework for advanced weather and climate prediction in India.   
7.2 The Government of India has approved the Mission Mausam with a 
financial outlay of ₹ 2000 crore with Rs. 1500 crore being additional 
allocation, and the remaining Rs.500 crore is drawn from the PRITHVI scheme 
(ACROSS sub-scheme) of the MoES, which was approved earlier.

capabilities and improving weather management systems. With an increased

Mission Mausam is designed to provide highly accurate forecasts across 
multiple time scales: 
(i) Short-Term (up to 72 hours): High-resolution forecasts using data 
from advanced observation systems like radars, wind profilers, and 
satellites, combined with real-time computational models for rapid 
prediction. 
(ii) Medium-Term (3 to 15 days): Enhanced weather predictions utilizing 
advanced modeling techniques and HPC resources for greater 
accuracy. 
(iii) Long-Term (seasonal to annual): The integration of Earth system 
models, data-driven methods, and AI/ML to forecast large-scale 
weather and climate patterns over months or seasons.

management, and transportation, enabling better preparedness and more 
effective responses to climate and weather events. The mission’s integrated 
approach will help deliver more precise, timely, and actionable forecasts, 
thus contributing to improved safety, economic stability, and climate 
resilience for India. 
8. High-Performance Computing System 
8.1 The High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems deployed across 
various institutes of the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) in previous plan 
periods have been crucial in enhancing the accuracy of weather forecasts and 
advancing research and development over the past decade. These HPC systems 
have facilitated seamless data assimilation and the generation of precise 
forecasts with extended lead times from both global and regional Numerical 
Weather Prediction (NWP) models, leading to significant improvements in 
weather, climate, and ocean state predictions. The proposed scheme aims to 
establish a petaflops-scale HPC facility for MoES institutes to support 
numerical modelling for weather and climate forecasting, basic research, and 
data assimilation. It will also provide computational resources to the academic 
and R&D community, to undertake research and development and enable 
improvements in operational forecasting systems and enhance forecast skill.

visualization environment to support state-of-the-art Big Data Analytics and

11. Use of modern technologies  
11.1 The Committee enquired from the Ministry regarding the use of new 
technologies or innovations in weather prediction and how the Ministry was 
utilizing advanced and modern technologies such as Artificial Intelligence 
(AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Big Data to improve weather forecasting 
models.   The Committee also desired to know the role of supercomputing and 
high-performance computing in improving weather predictions? 
11.2 In response to the above, the Committee was informed that the Ministry 
has taken various steps to strengthen the observational and weather forecasting 
infrastructure across the country. The Ministry adopts new technologies at 
various stages, including the augmentation of observational networks, 
numerical/AI-ML modeling, forecasting methodology, visualization, and 
dissemination of forecasts/warnings to various stakeholders.  The Ministry 
explores integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into weather and 
climate forecasting systems, in addition to physics-based numerical models. 
The key initiatives, future plans, and innovative projects are as follows: 
(i) Virtual Center on AI/Machine Learning (ML)/Deep Learning 
(DL) at IITM Pune:   The Ministry has established a specialized 
virtual center at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) 
in Pune. This center focuses on leveraging AI, ML, and DL 
techniques for advancements in Earth Sciences, handling large-
datasets. It has already developed several AI/ML-based applications 
tailored for localized predictions and the analysis of weather and 
climate patterns. 
(ii) Collaborative Research Across Institutes: Institutions under the 
Ministry are actively working to incorporate AI/ML methodologies 
into their research activities and operational frameworks. This 
collaborative approach ensures a comprehensive application of AI 
technologies across Earth sciences. 
11.3 The Committee was further informed that the augmented HPC capacity 
will help in advancing the understanding of weather and climate, resulting in a 
better prediction and improved weather services for the nation. The major 
benefits include: 
 Improved weather and climate forecasts at a very high resolution and 
forecasts of extreme events at block level.  
 Carryout research to improve the indigenous dynamical models for better 
prediction. Leveraging the new HPC facility to develop models using the 
latest technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning 
(ML) to improve the last mile services to different stakeholders.   
 Improving short, medium, and long-range forecasts for monsoon.   
 Better forecast of Air Quality, and Fog forecasts for many cities in India 

21 
 
11.4 The Committee was also informed that there has been a 40 to 50 percent 
improvement in the forecast accuracy of all severe weather events like heavy 
rainfall, fog, heat/cold waves, and thunderstorms in the recent five years by the 
India Meteorological Department (IMD).  IMD has adopted new techniques 
and technology from time to time to detect, monitor, and provide timely early 
warnings for disruptive weather events. Initiatives and developments have been 
taken to improve the monitoring and forecasting of weather events by 
augmenting the observational network, numerical weather prediction models, 
and supercomputers.   Further, IMD utilizes a seamless forecasting system at 
seasonal to nowcast scale and implemented well-defined Standard Operating 
Procedures (SOPs) for monitoring & forecasting weather hazards. IMD uses a 
state-of-the-art dissemination system to share all severe weather information 
and early warnings with disaster management authorities and the general public 
through various platforms/channels for necessary preparedness and to support 
mitigation measures. It includes social media, Common Alert Protocol, Mobile 
Apps, WhatsApp, and APIs. As a result, the vulnerable population gets 
evacuated from the damage-prone areas on time to safe shelters, thereby 
reducing the human death toll to a bare minimum. 
11.5 Advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), offer 
potential for the development of solutions and improve environmental 
governance for more sustainable living.  AI algorithms process real-time 
data from weather sensors, radars, and stations, providing up-to-date 
information on weather conditions and help generate timely forecasts, 
allowing for rapid response and decision-making in various industries. 
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry to integrate 
artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into weather and climate 
forecasting systems, in addition to physics-based numerical models to 
predict extreme weather events with greater precision, enabling early 
warnings for disasters like cyclones, floods, heatwaves etc.   The 
Committee firmly believes that by combining AI, satellite data, and 
advanced analytics, the schemes of Ministry of Earth Sciences will 
improve and enhance the country's ability to make more accurate and 
efficient meteorological predictions, consequentially contributing to better 
disaster preparedness, resource management, and overall climate 
resilience.

OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.1 The Committee recommends that the DAE should adopt a more robust approach to 
financial planning and forecasting by incorporating detailed risk assessments and contingency 
allocations into the initial budget estimates. The Committee notes that the Revised Estimates 
have consistently exceeded the Budget Estimates. The Committee therefore urges the Department 
to implement regular internal and external audits and to ensure transparent reporting of any 
mid-year adjustments, with clear justifications for deviations from the initial allocations. 
Furthermore, it is recommended that standard operating procedures for urgent procurement and 
maintenance should be established to pre-empt emergency expenditures, while also integrating 
anticipated costs for global collaborations and new technologies into the budgetary framework. 
(Para 2.5 of the 387th Report) 
Action Taken  
1.2 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.3 The Committee recommends that the Department continue to streamline fund disbursal 
processes to ensure optimal utilization of allocated resources, particularly for multi-year atomic 
energy projects. The Committee also recommends that a more robust financial strategy be 
adopted, incorporating contingency planning to mitigate the impact of unexpected budget cuts. 
Additionally, the Committee urges the Ministry of Finance to consider the critical nature of the 
Department’s commitments, particularly those related to nuclear fuel procurement and 
international obligations, and to ensure that adequate funding is provided in a timely manner. 
The Committee urges upon the Department to implement these measures with immediate effect to 
restore the expenditure trajectory to match both the budget estimates and the requirements of 
multi-year projects.                                                                                                     (para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.6 The Committee observes with concern that the Research & Development (R&D) Sector is 
the most impacted amongst all, with the R&D sector suffering the largest reduction of 
Rs.3,289.60 crore, from a proposed BE of Rs.14,516.38 crore to the approved BE Rs.11,226.78

reactor safety, radioactive waste management, and new reactor technologies. The Mega Science

1.7 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends immediate action to restore essential

and medical applications. The Committee recommends urgent restoration of at least Rs.5,933.62 
crore, particularly for the R&D and I&M sectors, to ensure continued progress in nuclear 
technology development and fuel production.                                                         (para 2.13 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.8 As recommended by the Hon’ble Committee the additional funds for R&D and I&M 
Sector shall be sought at RE stage, to ensure continued progress in nuclear technology 
development and fuel production. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.9 The Committee supports DAE’s initiative to attract private investment. However, the 
Committee recommends that clear regulatory frameworks and risk mitigation strategies should 
be developed to ensure private sector participation in the critical and sensitive nuclear 
infrastructure projects. While the Committee acknowledges DAE’s efforts to optimize its 
expenditures, it recommends a detailed financial audit to ensure that budgetary constraints do 
not result in inefficient cost-cutting measures that could compromise long-term technological 
advancements.                                                                                                           (Para 2.14 ibid) 

4 
 
Action Taken  
1.10 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.11 The Committee recommends priority-based funding for R&D sector and the funding 
should be allocated strategically, with a focus on high-impact projects such as Fast Breeder 
Reactor (FBR) development, fusion research (ITER), and radio isotope production for medical 
applications. Considering the importance of fuel availability, the Committee recommends that 
additional resources should be allocated to AMD for increased uranium and rare metal 
exploration to secure a stable domestic supply of nuclear fuel.                              (Para 2.15 ibid)                                                
Action Taken  
1.12 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.13 The Committee observes from Chart 3 that the total budget allocation for the Department 
of Atomic Energy (DAE) in B.E. 2025-26 stands at Rs.37,482.93 crore, with Rs.22,668.29 crore 
earmarked for revenue expenditure and Rs.14,814.64 crore for capital expenditure. The 
Committee observes that while the proposed capital expenditure was Rs.16,468.59 crore, the 
approved allocation was Rs.1,653.95 crore lower, whereas the revenue allocation saw a steeper 
decline of Rs.4,279.67 crore from the proposed Rs.26,947.96 crore.                     (Para 2.18 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.14 As observed by the Hon’ble Committee there are budgetary cuts in the BE allocations. 
The current shortfall of Rs.5,933.62 crore alongwith any further additionality, based on the 
budgetary requirements, shall be sought at RE stage. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.15 The Committee notes a significant disparity in proposed budgetary allocations against 
the actual allocations for 2025-26, between capital and revenue expenditure across key sectors 
of the Department, particularly in I&M and R&D sectors. A comparative assessment of the 
proposed and approved allocations (Table-2) highlights that while capital expenditure across 
sectors has been significantly curtailed, revenue expenditure has remained relatively stable.       
         (Para 2.19 ibid) 
1.16 The Committee notes that the I&M sector saw a capital allocation reduction from the 
proposed Rs.6,386.07 crore, in BE 2025-26, to Rs.5,293.18 crore, reflecting a 17.1% shortfall, 
while the revenue allocation was curtailed by 22.9% from the proposed Rs.6,762.58 crore to 
Rs.5,217.27 crore. The Committee notes with concern that R&D sector experienced an even 

5 
 
substantial reduction in capital expenditure, reduced by Rs.560.89 crore, a reduction of over 
27.3%, while the revenue component saw a reduction of Rs.2,728.71 crore (21.9%), indicating a 
prioritisationof operational expenses over infrastructure investments. The Committee notes that 
the Power sector has faced only a marginal reduction in capital allocation, with the approved 
amount standing at Rs.8,028.84 crore against the proposed allocation of Rs.8,029.01 crore. 
Revenue allocation for the sector also remained largely unchanged at Rs.7,631.72 crore.             
                                                                                                                                  (Para 2.20 ibid) 
1.17 The Committee feels that capital expenditure disparity is expected to have a negative 
impact on several high-priority projects. The Committee observes that the reduced capital 
allocation to the R&D sector could affect long-term research initiatives under Bhabha Atomic 
Research Centre (BARC), Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), and Raja 
Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT), potentially delaying innovations in 
nuclear safety, reactor technology, and radioactive waste management. The Committee 
emphasizes that while operational (revenue) expenses are necessary for maintaining institutional 
stability, the underfunding of capital investments may hinder advancements in nuclear energy 
infrastructure and indigenous technology development. To address these concerns, the 
Committee recommends a reassessment of expenditure priorities within the DAE, advocating for 
a more equitable distribution of funds between revenue and capital components. (Para 2.21 ibid) 
Action Taken  
1.18 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.19 The Committee acknowledges that the predominance of revenue expenditure is partly due 
to salary commitments, facility maintenance, and recurring operational costs. However, it 
underscores the need for a balanced allocation to ensure continued infrastructure expansion and 
modernization of nuclear energy facilities.                                                       (Para 2.22 ibid) 
 
1.20 The Committee urges the Department to recalibrate its financial strategy by enhancing 
capital allocations and ensuring a robust implementation framework for major nuclear projects. 
The Committee notes that the underfunding of capital projects could result in execution delays

1.119 Below are some of the research studies that have made an impact on routine treatment 
guidelines of the cancer patients and provided evidence of high quality affordable treatment 
1) Low-Dose Immunotherapy in Head and Neck Cancer: A Randomized Study 
Immunotherapy treatment for treatment of cancer has been one of the key 
developments with two nobel prizes. Due to cost there are only 3-4 % of patients in 
India who can use it. With the research project done at Tata memorial Hospital the 
cost for this treatment has come down by almost one tenth of original cost which 
has led to use by the majority of patients of head and neck cancer. This also has 
opened the avenue to explore the similar concept and develop low dose cost 
effective immunotherapy in other cancers. This is part of routine care in our country 
and developing world. This paper had an editorial in JCO and was covered by NIH-
NCI, MEDSCAPE etc.  
2) Gefitinib vs Gefitinib Plus Pemetrexed and Carboplatin Chemotherapy in EGFR-
Variant Lung Cancer-Long-Term Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial:  Modern 
targeted therapy has improved outcomes in lung cancer with EGFR mutation but 
only 4-5% of patients in India can use it due to cost. Tata Hospital used an 
innovative approach of combining two relatively cost effective drugs and showed in 
a randomised study that their efficacy is similar to modern targeted therapy and 
accessible to almost every patient in India with lung cancer with EGFR mutation. 
This is part of international and national guidelines for lung cancer management eg 
- PAN ASIA ESMO guidelines, UpToDate guidelines, NCG guidelines etc. 
3) Low-cost oral metronomic chemotherapy versus intravenous cisplatin in patients 
with recurrent, metastatic, inoperable head and neck carcinoma: an open-label, 
parallel-group, non-inferiority, randomised, phase 3 trial: Chemotherapy is an 
integral part of treatment of Head and Neck cancer but has toxicities and is also of 
limited benefit. Tata Hospital used an innovative approach of low dose, oral 
administration of chemotherapy in head and neck cancer. TMC was able to prove in 
our research work that in platinum sensitive and resistant patients they are effective 
and also cost effective and almost every patient can use it and this also eliminates 
the IV administration of drugs. This research has been published in various 
prestigious journals. This is part of various guidelines - UpToDate, NCG etc. 
4) Late Toxicity After Adjuvant Conventional Radiation Versus Image-Guided 
Intensity-Modulated Radiotherapy for Cervical Cancer (PARCER): A Randomized 
Controlled Trial: This study was conducted by Tata Memorial Centre in women 
with cervical cancer who needed post-operative radiotherapy. It compared, in a 
randomized controlled trial, two techniques of giving radiotherapy to these women 
- intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) or conventional 3D conformal 
radiotherapy. The results showed that IGRT markedly reduced the radiotherapy 
related short-term and long term side effects on the bowel and bladder. Thus, 

26 
 
although it is more resource intensive, it is now accepted that IGRT is a better way 
of delivering radiotherapy to these patients. 
5) Evaluation of 1-Year vs Shorter Durations of Adjuvant Trastuzumab Among 
Patients With Early Breast Cancer: An Individual Participant Data and Trial-Level 
Meta-analysis:Targeted cancer therapies are effective but very expensive. Once 
such expensive targeted therapy for breast cancer patients is an antibody drug called 
trastuzumab. Ordinarily it is given for a duration of 1 year. An individual-patient 
data meta-analysis conducted by Tata Memorial Centre, involving about 12000 
patients from six randomized controlled trials which compared 3-6 months of 
Trastuzumab with 1 year of Trastuzumab showed conclusively that shorter 
durations of this drug resulted in similar long-term cure rates. Another study 
conducted in collaboration between researchers of Tata Memorial Centre and PGI 
Chandigarh showed that shorter durations of Trastuzumab were cost-effective but 1 
year of Trastuzumab was not cost-effevtive, at current prices of this drug, in India. 
As a result of this study the PMJAY has rolled out short duration Trastuzumab as 
the standard treatment regimen in this scheme. 
6) Effect of Peritumoral Infiltration of Local Anesthetic Before Surgery on Survival in 
Early Breast Cancer: Clinical researchers at Tata Memorial Centre conceptualized 
and led a study wherein they injected the inexpensive local anesthesia drug 
lidocaine all around the breast cancer tumor, just prior to surgical removal of this 
tumor. This was a randomized controlled trial in 1600 women with breast cancer, 
wherein half the patients received this injection prior to surgery and the other half 
underwent surgery without this injection. The results showed that the recurrence of 
cancer and death were substantially reduced by this simple intervention which costs 
less than Rs 100. The results of this recently published study have been 
implemented in TMC and many other centres in India and in some other parts of 
the world.

1.122 Accessibility to all sections of society- One of the problems of our country is accessibility 
of the treatment.  In order to overcome the problem TMC has offered hub and spoke model. This 
is a distributed model of cancer care to offer patients high quality cancer care at their doorsteps. 
Common and less complex cancer care should be provided close to patients’ homes (spokes) to 
create minimum disruption in their lives and that of their families. Treatment of uncommon 
cancers and those with complex treatment protocols require management in expert centres of 

27 
 
excellence (hubs). However, to avoid over-burdening the hubs, the spokes need to be reasonably 
capable of handling less complex and common cancer types in the region. With an aim to 
decentralize cancer care and to make it more affordable and accessible. TMC registered 1,28,000 
new cancer patients in 2024 (Calendar year) of which about 70% are in general and nominal 
charges category.

 AMD is an active member of various State Geological Programming Board (SGPB) and 
Central Geological Programming Board (CGPB) Committees, which aim to ensure 
synergy and close coordination between Central as well as State Geological Departments 
and the relevant ministries/organisations. The meetings facilitate communication and 
collaboration between different stakeholders involved in geoscience activities, preventing 
duplication of efforts and maximising resource utilisation. 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.22 The Committee observes that HWB has been allocated Rs.6,478.07 crore, for the 
financial year 2025- 26 with Rs.3,322.31 crore earmarked for capital expenditure and 
Rs.3,155.76 crore for revenue expenditure, a shortfall of Rs.513.37 crore from its originally 
proposed Rs.6,991.44 crore. The Committee observes that this reduction in allocation 
couldadversely impact the modernisation of heavy water plants, delay the expansion of nuclear 
solvent production, and slow down critical research on deuterium-based pharmaceuticals. Given 
that heavy water is a strategic material crucial for India’s nuclear power programme, ensuring 
adequate funding is essential for energy security, industrial applications, and medical research.                           
                                                                                                                                (Para 3.20 ibid) 
Action Taken  
 
2.23 Fund reduction / shortfall to HWB is impacting various activities like Modernisation and 
expansion of Heavy Water Plants, Expansion of Boron facilities, Supply of Deuterium Depleted 
Water (DDW) and R&D in Deuterium based applications in pharmaceuticals. While the supply 
of Heavy Water for requirement of our PHWRs has been ensured, additional funds for the other 
requirements will be sought during RE 2025-26 stage.

Nuclear Damage Act have been revised to facilitate private participation while ensuring safety

and security standards are met. However, the Committee notes that several key concerns still 
remain. The Committee observes that ensuring strict compliance with nuclear safety protocols, 
waste management regulations, and radiation protection measures is crucial to avoid potential 
hazards. The Committee expresses concern that regulatory uncertainties regarding liability and 
risk-sharing mechanisms could deter private investors.                                            (Para 6.2 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
2.25 In reference to “The Committee notes that the existing Atomic Energy Act and Civil 
Liability for Nuclear Damage Act have been revised to facilitate private participation while

2.30 Right from its inception, Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has paid considerable 
attention towards the induction and development of human resources for achieving excellence in 
the field of science and technology.  DAE has followed a comprehensive policy to develop 
competent scientists, engineers and technical personnel to support its programmes.  DAE has a 
detailed and streamlined procedure for Recruitment and Promotion of Scientific and Technical 
personnel and filling up vacancies arising due to their superannuation.   
2.31 Merit is the prime consideration for Recruitment and Promotion of candidates to 
Scientific and Technical posts who have to work in the advanced field of  
Science and Technology in DAE.  Hence, there is a possibility of posts remaining unfilled after a 
recruitment drive. Such vacancies are considered for filling in subsequent recruitment campaign.   
Sometimes, selected candidates are not willing to join due to remote places of posting/places far-
off from their home-town etc. 
2.32 Scientific personnel are recruited through flagship Programme Orientation Course for 
Engineering Graduates and Science Post Graduates (OCES) and DAE Graduate Fellowship 
Scheme (DGFS). The candidates selected for OCES Programme based on score of Graduate 
Aptitude Test in Engineering (GATE) or Computer Based Test (CBT) and technical interviews 
by Experts Panel undergo one-year training in nuclear science & technology at BARC training 
school. The DGFS candidates, who have already secured admissions in selected Indian Institute 
of Technology (IITs), pursue their M Tech. OCES and DGFS candidates are absorbed in various 
units of DAE viz., Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic 
Research (IGCAR), Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC), Atomic Minerals Directorate for 
Exploration and Research (AMD), Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT), Heavy 
Water Board (HWB), Directorate of Construction Services and Estate Management (DCSEM), 
as scientific officer after successful completion of training and MTech respectively. 
2.33 Technical personnel are recruited through Computer Based Test and Skill Test/Interview 
and the selected candidates undergo two-year stipendiary training scheme in areas related to 
nuclear science and technology.  On successful completion of training, Graduates in science and 
diploma holders in engineering are absorbed as Scientific Assistants and candidates having 
qualification of HSC (science) or SSC followed by ITI certificate are absorbed as Technicians in 
the various Units of DAE.

Recommendations/Observations 
2.36 The high vacancy rates across DAE institutions raise serious concerns about workforce 
planning, recruitment efficiency, and the overall sustainability of nuclear and research projects 
in India. The Committee expresses its concerns over these vacancies, especially in key 
operational areas such as nuclear power generation, research, and mineral exploration. The 
shortage of skilled personnel could lead to delays in research and development, inefficiencies in 
plant operations, and constraints in nuclear fuel production, ultimately affecting the country's 
nuclear energy programme. To address this issue, the Committee strongly recommends an 
immediate recruitment drive to fill the existing vacancies. It is imperative that recruitment 
processes be streamlined to ensure timely hiring of personnel in technical, scientific, and 
operational roles. A review of existing workforce policies should be undertaken to identify areas 
where delays occur in the hiring process, and necessary reforms should be implemented. The 
DAE must adopt modern human resource management strategies to attract and retain talent, 
ensuring competitive salaries, career progression opportunities, and research grants for 
professionals in nuclear science, energy, and advanced research.                           (Para 8.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
2.37 Department of Atomic Energy follows Merit based Promotion Scheme for Scientific and 
Technical personnel which is delinked from availability of vacancies and rewards them with time 
bound promotions. This merit-based career progression scheme is implemented through a well-
established mechanism of minimum residency requirements, performance assessment, screening, 
review and evaluation. The Merit Promotion Scheme has so far been regulated through norms 
and practices based on decisions taken by the Trombay Council and further approved by the 
DAE. 
2.38 In addition, the modern human resource management strategies as adopted by DAE, is 
followed in the Units to attract and retain talent by way of following measures: 

43 
 
i. Advance increments are given to the Scientific and Technical Personnel on their initial 
appointment. 
ii. Scientists are encouraged to carry out further studies like M Tech, MSc. Engg., PhD. After 
PhD, opportunities are also given to carry out Post-Doctoral Research works at reputed 
International laboratories.  
iii. DAE also grants Performance incentives in the form of Performance Related Incentive 
Scheme (Organization) [PRIS-O], Performance Related Incentive Scheme (Group) [PRIS-
G] and Performance Related Incentive Scheme (Individual) [PRIS-I] for timely completion 
of major activities related to DAE programmes. 
iv. DAE also grants Professional Update Allowance to Scientific / Technical Officers in the 
grade of SO/C and above, every year. 
v. DAE has collaboration with International Agencies like ITER/CERN Projects where they 
get opportunity to work on these projects on deputation. 
vi. To promote research and capacity building in the field of nuclear science and energy, 
grants are provided to young talented scientists for research projects and scientific events 
aligned with the departmental mandate through Board of Research in Nuclear Sciences 
(BRNS) an extramural agency of DAE through various schemes such as Young Scientist 
Research Project (YSRP) scheme, research fellowship for (JRF/ SRF/ RA) and DAE 
Graduate Fellowship Scheme (DGFS-PhD).  
2.39 In Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL), Policy changes have been proposed 
and approved for recruitment of Technicians on Fixed Term Appointment basis so that locals get 
the opportunity for employment on Fixed Term basis. 
2.40 Electronics Corporation of India Ltd (ECIL), is constantly reshaping policies such as 
Promotion Policy with better norms, Medical Insurance Policy with Cashless facility and 
Recruitment Policy with an aim to create a conducive work environment to employee group and 
in line with the market trends.  
2.41 Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), an Aided Institution,actively seeks out 
talented Indian nationals with proven high credentials in emerging areas of scientific research 
from around the world to apply for advertised positions through continuous engagement via 
visits, collaborations, and conferences. They are provided with competitive initial start-up grants 
based on the research program’s requirements and salaries consistent with other premier 
academic institutions in the country.   
2.42 Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) has robust Training & Developmentsystem. Medical & 
Scientific Staff are encouraged to attend conferences, workshops, research programmes in India 
and abroad.  They are also supported with extramural and intramural research grants for various 
projects. 

44 
 
2.43 In order to retain talented and experienced medical staff, TMC has taken up a proposal 
for increasing the age of superannuation in case of Medical Staff from 60 to 65 years. 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.44 The Committee observes with great concern contractual employment and temporary 
staffing, particularly in research institutions such as TIFR. The Committee urges a review of 
these employment practices and recommends converting long-term contractual positions into 
permanent roles wherever necessary. The Committee recommends that regularisation of 
employment will not only enhance job security for researchers and scientists but also ensure 
continuity in long-term research projects. Additionally, for institutions such as TMC, where 
medical professionals are in high demand, the Committee recommends expanding recruitment 
efforts and increasing budgetary support for healthcare staff and researchers.       (Para 8.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
2.45 With regard to employment on a contractual or short-term basis, it is stated that 
contractual appointments are made only for support services, execution of Plan projects for 
research activities and creation of assets and not for core scientific or technical roles. 
 
2.46 In Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), the contractual positions are primarily 
used for administrative tasks that are suitable for outsourcing. Short-term contractual positions 
for research-related tasks are only utilised for projects which have a specific time and scope 
delimitation. This is in keeping with standard practices being followed at all leading research 
institutions at the national and international levels. It is highlighted that temporary Research 
Associate / Research Fellow positions offer valuable training opportunities for fresh Ph.D. 
holders, enabling them to grow as independent researchers and thereafter take up tenured 
positions in academia/research institutions/industry while at the same contributing to advance 
scientific research in the Institute.

REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee 
contained in its ‘Three Hundred Eighty Eighth Report’ on “Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Biotechnology.  The Report was presented to/ laid on the Table of both the Houses 
of Parliament on the 25th March, 2025. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Department of Biotechnology in 
respect of all the 17 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three Hundred Eighty 
Eighth Report’. The replies of the Department of Biotechnology have been categorized as 
follows:- 
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos.:- 2.11, 2.15, 3.8, 3.9, 4.6, 5.5, 5.7, 5.8, 5.13, 5.16, 5.17, 
5.19 and 6.7  
 Total recommendations – 13 
Chapter II: Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies:  
  Para Nos.:- 4.8, 5.14, 5.22 and 5.23 
  Total recommendations – 04  
Chapter III:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: NIL 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: NIL 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
COMPARATIVE BUDGET ANALYSIS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee expresses deep concern over the sub-optimal utilization of funds by the 
Department, particularly in the context of the Central Sector Scheme, Bio-RIDE. This 
underutilization not only hampers the effective implementation of critical programs but also 
undermines the potential impact of the Department’s initiatives. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department take immediate and appropriate measures to address this issue 
and ensure the optimal utilization of funds allocated to it in the Budget Estimates (B.E.) for 2025-
26. The Department should conduct regular reviews and take corrective actions to prevent delays 
and inefficiencies, thereby maximizing the impact of its programs and achieving the desired 
outcomes in a timely and effective manner.  
(Para 2.11 of the 388th Report) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.2  The Department acknowledges the concern of the Committee.  In background, as per 
extant instructions of DOE, Ministry of Finance vide its O. M. F. No. 3/(06)/PFMS/2023 dated 
21st May, 2024, Department has closed its earlier revised funds flow system of CNA-02 
operations in December 2024 for its two Central Sector (CS) Schemes. In compliance to DOE 
O.M., following the merger of earlier two CS schemes along with a new component into newly 
Cabinet approved Scheme-Bio-RIDE, Department transitioned from earlier fund flow system 
(CNA-02) to new revised funds flow system of TSA-Hybrid (1A) in January, 2025. Department 
rolled out the fund utilization of Bio-Ride scheme through TSA-Hybrid system w.e.f. 29th 
January, 2025.   
1.3 Though overall RE budget utilization by the Department has been sub-optimal, the 
percentage (%) of assignments vs utilization in the new revised funds flow system was 84.8%. 
Department could not assign the full RE allocation to child agencies within such a short period of 
time (2 months) as several hundred implementing agencies could not onboard to new TSA-Hybrid 
system due to various reasons.  
1.4 The department has taken cognizance of the new funds flow system, and accordingly, 
necessary actions for the utilization of funds are being undertaken for maximal utilization of the 
budget for achieving the desired outcomes in the programs in a timely and effective manner in FY 
2025-26 and it will be ensured that 50% of the expenditure target is met by 30th September, 2025. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

3 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.5         Given the substantial allocation to Bio-RIDE, the Committee recommends that the 
Department must ensure optimal utilization of funds. Regular monitoring, timely implementation, 
and transparent reporting mechanisms should be established to avoid sub-optimal utilization and 
maximize outcomes. 
(Para 2.15 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.6 The Department has been taking all possible steps to ensure the optimal utilization of 
allocated funds in FY 2025-26 and the outcomes are being monitored regularly.
