CHAPTER – 8 
CONCLUDING OBSERVATIONS AND AN URGENT CALL FOR ACTION 
8.1 The Yamuna River in the National Capital Region is in a state of 
profound ecological collapse, representing one of the nation's most severe 
environmental and governance failures. Decades of plans, j udicial directives, 
and substantial financial investment have yielded negligible results, with the 
river biologically dead through its critical 22 -kilometer stretch in Delhi. This 
crisis stems not from a lack of effort, but from a flawed strategy —a systemic 
reliance on outdated, linear models of waste management and a critical 
disregard for the river's fundamental need for water. The Yamuna's plight is 
a symptom of a broader malaise where the river is viewed as a sewer rather 
than a living ecosystem.  However, this is not an intractable problem. H istory 
and global experience provide a clear path forward. The successful 
rejuvenation of rivers like the Thames in London, which was declared 
biologically dead in the 1950s but now supports thriving salmon populatio ns, 
and the Rhine in Europe, which recovered from severe industrial pollution, 
demonstrates that even the most degraded waterways can be restored.  
Domestically, the remarkable transformation of the Kham River in 
Aurangabad stands as a powerful testament to  what determined civic action 
can achieve. Through citizen -led efforts that focused on desilting, waste 
management, and the construction of check dams, significant improvements 
in water flow and quality were realized, demonstrating that community 
participation is not just beneficial but essential to sustainable river 
management. 
8.2 The path to rejuvenation  of River Yamuna  demands an urgent and 
fundamental paradigm shift. We must move beyond the obsolete model of 

 
60 
 
simply building treatment plants and discharging the effluent back into 
polluted drains. The new agenda must be the creation of a circular water 
economy, where every drop of wastewater is captured, treated according to its 
future use, and reused as a valua ble resource. This requires mandatory reuse 
for agriculture and industry, the formalization of the desludging tanker 
network, and rationalized treatment standards. Simultaneously, industrial 
pollution must be plugged through stringent enforcement, a cluste r based 
approach to zero liquid discharge, and a crackdown on unauthorized units. 
However, even the most advanced treatment will fail if the river is starved of 
water. 
8.3 The single most critical intervention is securing a scientifically 
determined environmental flow. The current token release is ecologically 
meaningless. The basin  States must reach a consensus on the scientifically 
recommended minimum flow. This must be coupled with aggressive demand 
side management in Delhi, including reducing the city's massive water losses 
and augmenting supply through reused wastewater. The impending revision 
of the Yamuna Water Sharing Agreement presents a historic opportunity to 
formally allocate a rightful share of water to the river itself, an essential 
stakeholder ignored for too long. 
8.4 Ultimately, the revival of the Yamuna is a test of our national 
commitment to sustainable development. It requires a unified command, 
breaking down the silos between numerous agencies. The rejuvenation of the 
floodplains, t hrough a ban on groundwater extraction, removal of toxic 
sludge, and large scale ecological restoration, is the fin al but vital piece of this 
puzzle.  

 
61 
 
8.5 The time for incrementalism is over. The Committee urges all 
stakeholders to embrace this comprehensi ve blueprint with the urgency and 
resolve that this national crisis demands, to transform the River Yamuna 
from a symbol of environmental failure into a testament of ecological renewal.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
 
CHAPTER – 2 
 
SOURCES OF WATER POLLUTION AND MONITORING OF WATER 
QUALITY 
The Committee observes that there is a severe degradation in water 
quality of River Yamuna between the Palla and Wazirabad locations, and 
then again after the meeting the Shahdara Drain. This indicates that major 
pollution loads are entering within these stretches. To precisely identify the 
specific drains and discharge points responsible, a denser network of 
monitoring stations should be established between Palla and Wazirabad, and 
immediately upstream and downstream of every major drain outfall. 
Furthermore, the monthly monitoring frequency is insufficient to capture the 
dynamic nature of pollution, especially from non -point sources and during 
non-compliance events. A shift to weekly or even c ontinuous automated 
monitoring at these critical points is essential to provide a more accurate, real-
time picture of pollutant loads and enable swift corrective action. 
(Para 2.18) 
The Committee also observes that  while BOD, DO, pH, and Fecal 
Coliform are  critical, they do not provide a complete picture of the river's 
health or the sources of contamination. The monitoring program should be 
enhanced to include parameters such as  Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD)  to 
distinguish between biologically degradable and  industrial waste,  heavy 
metals (like lead, mercury, and chromium) to track industrial 
pollution, ammoniacal nitrogen  which is a key indicator of raw sewage, 

 
63 
 
and phosphate and nitrate to assess nutrient loading that causes 
eutrophication. For groundwater, the consistent exceedance of Total Hardness 
and Total Dissolved Solids in Delhi warrants a mandatory and regular 
analysis of these parameters at all locations, moving beyond the current focus 
on nitrate and fluoride. This expanded parameter list will allow  authorities to 
fingerprint pollution sources more accurately and tailor remediation 
strategies accordingly. 
(Para 2.19) 
The Committee also observes that c urrently data is collected under 
different programmes (NWMP, DPCC monitoring) and assessed against 
different standards (Bathing Water Criteria, BIS Drinking Standards). There 
should be a concerted effort to harmonize the presentation of data, ensuring 
that all rive r water quality is consistently assessed against a single uniform 
standard. All this data — from the CPCB, DPCC, and other State Pollution 
Control Boards —should be integrated into a single, open -data portal with 
interactive maps and time-series analysis tools. This would allow for real-time 
tracking of compliance, easy identification of pollution trends, and better 
public accountability.  
(Para 2.20) 
The Committee also recommends that the practice of reporting only 
"min-max" ranges for annual data should be supplemented with the 
calculation and reporting of annual average values for each parameter at each 
location, as a single high BOD max value can be an outlier, while a high 
average confirms persistent pollution. 

 
64 
 
(Para 2.21) 
CHAPTER – 3 
 
SEWAGE MANAGEMENT IN DELHI NCR 
The Committee observes that there is lack of reliable data on actual 
waste water generated in the city. The current methodology simply assumes 
the wastewater generation to be 80% of the supplied water. Although the 
assumption is based on international stan dards but the data regarding the 
water supplied in the city is itself inaccurate in the first place as it did not 
account for large distribution losses. Therefore, the Committee recommends a 
comprehensive and independent audit of the real -time volume of wa ter 
supplied, accounting for all distribution losses, must be commissioned. This 
will generate a reliable baseline for wastewater generation. The Committee 
also observes that distribution losses in water supplied in the city is too high. 
The Committee, accordingly, recommends that Government should conduct a 
comprehensive study to determine the actual extant of these losses, the 
reasons behind this and corrective measures that should be taken to reduce 
these losses. The Committee also recommends that Govern ment should 
strengthen the water supply network in Delhi by replacing the old and 
damaged water carrying pipelines. 
(Para 3.31) 
The Committee further observes that a significant portion of Delhi's 
households lack connection to the underground sewerage network, relying 
instead on septic tanks and pit latrines. The waste from these systems is often 
collected by desludging tankers which, due to a lack of regulation and disposal 

 
65 
 
facilities, routinely dump raw sewage into open drains. Consequently, even as 
Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) process waste from sewered areas, a 
continuous flow of untreated waste from unsewered populations ente rs the 
same drainage system, completely bypassing treatment and undermining the 
entire infrastructure.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
Government must ensure mandatory mapping and formalization of the entire 
desludging tanker ecosystem. All deslu dging tankers should be registered, 
fitted with GPS tracking, and mandated to discharge their collected fecal 
sludge only at designated Sewage Treatment Plants or co -treatment facilities. 
This will ensure that the massive volume of waste from unsewered population, 
which currently bypasses the system, is captured and treated, effectively 
closing a major pollution gateway. 
(Para 3.32) 
The Committee observes that the significant investment in sewage 
treatment capacity by the Central and State Governments is  fundamentally 
undermined by the continued discharge of treated effluent back into the very 
drains it was meant to clean. The Committee therefore recommends that the 
Government should ensure mandatory reuse of treated wastewater.  The 
model exemplified by the Chilla plant, where treated water is discharged 
directly into the river, should be adopted wherever feasible to prevent re -
contamination. 
(Para 3.33) 
The Committee further recommends that in order to avoid 
underutilization of treated wastewater, the Government should take necessary 
steps to ensure that all treated effluent is utilized for non -potable purposes 

 
66 
 
such as agricultural irrigation, industrial cooling, gardening, and 
groundwater recharge. This would transform wastewater from a pollutant 
into a valuable resource, simultaneously conserving freshwater and 
preventing treated effluent from re -entering and overburdening the 
ecosystem. 
(Para 3.34) 
The Committee observes that uniformly applying stringent river-quality 
standards to all treated wast ewater is not the right approach . This forces 
unnecessary and costly removal  of nutrients like Nitrogen and Phosphorus  
from water that could be directly reused for agriculture, where those 
nutrients are beneficial, providing no environmental gain.  The Comm ittee, 
therefore, recommends that Government should revise its quality standards 
according to the end use of the treated waste water. 
(Para 3.35) 
The Committee also observes that the location and design of treatment 
plants should be driven by the potential for reusing the treated water and by 
the practicalities of reducing pumping costs by treating sewage close to its 
source. The Committee therefore recommends that Government should adopt 
a hybrid and pragmatic approach  that could leverage  both the large-scale 
centralized STPs and the smaller, localized solutions like fecal sludge 
treatment plants, particularly in densely populated, congested areas w here 
centralized interception is challenging. 
(Para 3.36) 
 

 
67 
 
CHAPTER – 4 
 
ROLE OF INDUSTRIES IN WATER POLLUTION OF DELHI NCR 
 
The Committee observes that there is a significant disconnect between 
installed treatment capacity and actual utilization. In Delhi,  the 13 Common 
Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs) have a combined capacity of 212.3 MLD 
but only receive 72.2 MLD of effluent, operating at a mere 34% capacity , 
which indicates that a large volume of industrial wastewater is being diverted 
elsewhere, likely  into the municipal sewer system or directly into drains, 
completely bypassing treatment. The Committee also observes that a vast 
number of industries have moved to unauthorized areas where their pollution 
is entirely unregulated and untreated  indicating that the actual pollution load 
entering the river remains unchecked. The Committee also observes that the 
data from Grossly Polluting Industries (GPIs) inspections, though showing 
improvement in Delhi's compliance rate from 72.1% in 2020 to 94.9% in 2023, 
reveals 49 GPIs still non-compliant in 2024. 
(Para 4.15) 
The Committee recommends that  the State Pollution Control B oards of 
Haryana and Delhi , in collaboration with their respective municipal 
corporations, must conduct a comprehensive Geographic Information System 
(GIS) based mapping of all industrial units, regardless of their location in 
"approved" or "unauthorized" areas. The Committee is also of the view that 
ignoring industrial units in dense, unauthorized clusters  will render all other 
efforts futile  and, hence , recommends that the Government should facilitate 
the establishment of decentralized, modular CETPs or provide targeted 
financial and technical assistance for small -scale, common treatment facilities 
in these areas. 

 
68 
 
(Para 4.16) 
The Committee al so recommends that CETPs must be mandated and 
supported to upgrade their infrastructure to handle tox ic pollutants like 
heavy metals and that the governance of CETPs should be strengthened 
through mandatory, frequent, and random third -party audits, the res ults of 
which should be made public.  
(Para 4.17) 
The Committee is also of the view that Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) is 
a far superior and more effective technology for wastewater treatment 
compared to CETPs, despite its higher cost. The Committee therefor e 
recommends that for MSMEs struggling with the high cost of ZLD system, the 
Government should create a dedicated green financing window with soft loans 
and subsidies to make ZLD systems financially viable for these smaller 
businesses. The Committee also r ecommends that the Government should 
promote cluster-based approach where industrial areas with similar types of 
effluent share a single, larger ZLD system. This collective model would make 
the crucial transition to this advanced technology technically man ageable and 
economically accessible for all. 
(Para 4.18) 
 
CHAPTER – 5 
 
ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW OF YAMUNA RIVER 
 

 
69 
 
The Committee would like to reiterate the recommendation made by the 
Department-related Standing Committee on Water Resources in its 27 th 
Report that the Department of Water Resources, River Development and 
Ganga Rejuvenation  should make concerted efforts to evolve consensus 
among the Yamuna basin States to maintain E -flow of 23 cumecs in the lean 
season as recommended by the NIH.  
(Para 5.9) 
The Committee observes that this is a critical situation characterized by 
inadequate environmental flows, inter -State disagreements, and severe 
ecological degradation. The Committee also observes that this situation 
demands a multi -pronged strategy where the p rimary objective must be to 
transition from ad -hoc, politically contentious water releases to a 
scientifically-grounded, collaboratively managed, and legally robust regime 
for environmental flows. The Committee, therefore, recommends reconvening 
the Yamuna  River Basin Board with a renewed mandate to achieve a 
consensus on the scientifically recommended environmental flow of 23 cumecs 
for the lean season, as established by the National Institute of Hydrology. This 
process should be facilitated by a neutral t echnical expert group and must 
incorporate a transparent water accounting system to build trust among basin 
states by clearly documenting water withdrawals, uses, and losses. The 
dialogue must shift from a perception of loss to a shared vision of securing the 
river’s health as a fundamental prerequisite for long -term water security for 
all stakeholders. 
(Para 5.11) 
 

 
70 
 
The Committee feels that the cleaning of any river is a two -step process. 
Firstly, we need to ensure that all discharges into the river are tre ated 
properly and secondly, the river has sufficient water all round the year to 
maintain its environmental flow. While a lot of emphasis is laid on the first 
aspect that is treatment of discharge into the river,  maintaining the 
environmental flow of the r iver is often ignored.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that a comprehensive reassessment of the entire river's flow 
requirements should be initiated, moving beyond the single metric of lean -
season flow. This assessment  should establish a dynamic envir onmental flow 
regime that specifies not only the minimum quantity but also the timing, 
duration, and quality of water required to mimic the river's natural 
hydrograph, including necessary pulses for fish migration and floodplain 
rejuvenation. This scientific blueprint could serve as the basis for future water 
allocation decisions.  
(Para 5.12) 
The Committee opines that a paradigm shift in urban water 
management is essential for Delhi. The Committee, accordingly, recommends 
that the Delhi Jal Board must augment its water supply through an aggressive 
strategy for the reuse of treated wastewater. A significant percentage of 
treated effluent, meeting stringent standards, should be used for non -potable 
purposes such as industrial cooling, horticulture, and groundwater recharge, 
thereby reducing the city's absolute dependence on freshwater withdrawals 
from the Yamuna and freeing up this water for the river's ecological 
functions. 
(Para 5.13) 

 
71 
 
The Committee also recommends that the State Government of 
Haryana and the State Government of NCT of Delhi should setup  a dedicated 
River Rejuvenation Fund , financed by a small levy on water -intensive 
industries discharging in the Yamuna River basin. This fund could be utilized 
for initiatives such as financing modernizat ion of irrigation canals to reduce 
water loss, implementing advanced sewage treatment technologies, thereby 
creating a sustainable financial model for the Yamuna's recovery.  
(Para 5.14) 
The Committee observes that the Yamuna River water sharing 
agreement of 1994 is due for revision in 2025 and talks have initiated amongst 
the States which are party to this agreement.  In light of the rapidly evolving 
socio-economic, demographic, and environmental factors, the Committee 
finds 30 -year duration for such a crit ical agreement to be fundamentally 
misaligned with contemporary realities.  The Committee recommends that 
future water sharing agreement should be made for a maximum period of 10 
years only and this period should be explicitly tied to the decadal census cycle, 
with revisions incorporating updated census data as a primary determinant 
for water allocation, thus ensuring that the agreement remains responsive to 
contemporary demographic and resource realities. 
(Para 5.15) 
 
CHAPTER – 6 
 
REJUVENATION OF YAMUNA FLOODPLAINS 
The Committee recommends that the proactive measures taken to 
combat encroachment and illegal dumping must be strengthened and 

 
72 
 
implemented consistently. The successful land recovery and waste clearance 
efforts in Delhi should be replicated across all S tates along the river. 
Furthermore, the patrolling and security infrastructure must be expanded 
beyond Delhi, with all States ensuring strict and  timely penalties for illegal 
dumping and construction in the Yamuna floodplain. 
(Para 6.7) 
The Committee also recommends that the unsustainable extraction of 
groundwater in the Yamuna floodplain must be immediately addressed to 
prevent the river from running dry. The planned drawing of an additional 190 
MLD from the floodplain must be revisited in light of the already exceeded 
sustainable yield. The Committee recommends that a complete ban should be 
enforced on groundwater extraction within the entire Yamuna floodplain.  
(Para 6.8) 
The Committee also recommends that a zero -tolerance policy must be  
implemented against illegal sand mining in the Yamuna floodplain . This 
requires coordinated raids and surveillance by revenue, police, and 
environment Departments to halt the illegal sand mining that is eroding the 
riverbed.  
(Para 6.9) 
The Committee furt her recommends that a comprehens ive sludge 
assessment must be commissioned to determine the full extent of heavy metal 
contamination in the Yamuna floodplain . Based on the findings, a targeted 
sludge removal plan should be implemented, starting from the mo st critically 
polluted stretches.

revival of the floodplains must be significantly scaled up. The successful 
planting of native trees and grasses should be intensified, aiming to cover the

biodiversity parks and wetlands, which have proven successful in  bringing 
back bird s and retain water, should be a primary focus of all restoration 
projects, transforming t he floodplains into thriving ecological hubs rather 
than just open spaces.

  INTRODUCTION 
 
 
           I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science 
and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change, having been authorized by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Four Hundred  Third Report on ―Review 
of the functioning of CSIR -Central Scientific Instruments Organization (CSIR -CSIO) and CSIR -
Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology (CSIR-IGIB)‖. 
 
2.  CSIR - Central Scientific Instruments Organization (CSIR -CSIO), a constitue nt unit of Council 
of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), is a premier national laboratory dedicated to research, 
design and development of scientific and industrial instruments.  Recognizing the rapidly 
growing global importance of the instrumentatio n sector, the Committee visited CSIR -CSIO, 
Chandigarh on 19th September 2025 as part of its study tour to Chandigarh and Mumbai from 19th 
to 22nd September 2025 to gain a comprehensive, first -hand understanding of CSIO’s pioneering 
research, innovative technologies, and ongoing challenges.   
 
3.     CSIR-IGIB is a premier Institute of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), 
engaged in research of national importance in the areas of genomics, molecular medicine, 
bioinformatics and proteomics.  As the work conducted at IGIB is critical not just for advancing 
the frontiers of science but also for its direct impact on public health, personalized medicine, and 
biotechnology in India, the Committee considered it imperative to witness the operatio ns in their 
state-of-the-art laboratories from fundamental genomic sequencing to the development of 
innovative diagnostic tools and to grasp the on -ground realities of scientific innovation. The 
Committee undertook a local study visit to CSIR-IGIB on 7th November, 2025 to understand, first-

CSIR-CENTRAL SCIENTIFIC INSTRUMENTS ORGANIZATION (CSIR-CSIO) 
Introduction 
1.1 CSIR- Central Scientific Instruments Organization (CSIR -CSIO), a 
constituent unit of Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), is a premier 
national laboratory dedicated to research, design and development of scientific and 
industrial instruments. It i s a multi -disciplinary and multi -dimensional apex 
industrial research & development organization in the country whose mission is to 
stimulate the growth of scientific and industrial instrument industry in India.  
1.2 CSIO has well equipped laboratories man ned by highly qualified and well 
trained staff with infrastructural facil ities in the areas of Agrionics, Medical 
Instrumentation and Prosthetic Devices, Optics and Cockpit based Instrumentation, 
Fiber/Laser Optics based Sensors & Instrumentation, Analytic al Instrumentation, 
Advanced Materials based Transducers etc. Large number of instruments ranging 
from simple to highly sophisticated ones, have been designed and developed by the 
Institute and their know -how has been passed on to the industry for commerci al 
exploitation. 
1.3 The primary R &D domains of CSIR -CSIO include optical instrumentation, 
biomedical instrumentation, Artificial Intelligence enabled systems, sensors and  
instrumentation technologies to support India’s strategic, societal and industrial  
sectors. The research areas of CSIR -CSIO are mainly focused on agrionics, 
medical instrumentation and prosthetic devices, optics and cockpit  based 
instrumentation, Fiber/Laser Optics based Sensors and Instrumentation, Analytical 
Instrumentation, Advanced Materials based Instrumentation and Devices. 
1.4 Currently, the organization structure of CSIR-CSIO comprises various R&D 
verticals, Centres of Excellence , S&T facilities, R&D Management and HRD 
support system. There are 6 primary R& D verticals at CSIR -CSIO namely 
Intelligent Machines and Computing Systems (IMCS), Applied Materials and 
Instrumentation (AMI), Optics & Photonics Instrumentation (OPI), Bio -medical 
Instrumentation, Advanced Engineering and Design, Energy Management & 
Instrumentation (Chennai Centre).The organization structure of CSIR -CSIO is as

1.12 Noting that the sanctioned strength and the in-position strength of CSIO for the 
year 2024-25 stood at 532 and 257 respectively, the Committee inquired about the

last few years. The prolonged CO VID-19 pandemic from early 2020 severely

restrictions, suspension of physical interviews, and reallocation of resources 
toward pandemic management led to unavoidable delays in hiring processes. 
ii. In the past, Scientific & Technical posts vacant for more than 5 years were not 
considered as deemed abolished by Department of Expenditure. Therefore, in 
order to avoid large number of recruitment/superannuation in one go only 10% 
of vacancies were  advertised in one recruitment cycle. This practice of 
staggered advertisement was followed to ensure smooth transition in Labs at

Finance Office Memorandum No. 7(1)/E.Coord -I/2017(Part.II) dated

Agrionics 
1.15 Agrionics, one of the research areas of CSIR-CSIO, is a multidisciplinary field 
that combines agriculture and electronics/instrumentation to enhance productivity, 
safety, precision and automation in farming and allied application areas. Agrionics 
involves the design, development and implementation of electronics, smart sensors, 
control circuit, transducers, embedded system and communication modules to 
monitor, control the operational parameters of agriculture such as soil moisture, 
temperature, hu midity, nutrients levels, pH and crop health. Such systems enable 
safety, precision agriculture with data -driven decisions to improve  yield, conserve 
resources and reduced human efforts.  
1.16 While briefing the Committee about the technological advancemen ts made by 
CSIR-CSIO, the Committee was also informed that  CSIR-CSIO has developed 
various technologies in the domain of agrionics. CSIR-CSIO has been at the forefront 
of developing advanced sensors and instrumentation technologies to support India’s 
agricultural sector. Recognizing the need for precision, sustainability, and efficiency 

8 
 
in farming practices, CSIR -CSIO has designed a wide range of Agri -instrumentation 
solutions that integrate sensors, associated electronics, and automation. These include 
soil nutrient and moisture sensors, crop health monitoring systems, electrostatic 
sprayers, post -harvest quality assessment tools, and technologies for detecting 
adulteration in food products. By enabling data -driven decision-making, improving 
resource utilization and ensuring quality control across the agricultural value chain, 
CSIR-CSIO’s innovations aim to empower farmers, enhance productivity, and 
contribute to national food security through indigenous, cost-effective technologies.  
1.17 The key achievemen ts of CSIR-CSIO in this field include  development of 
several technologies and their technology transfers to the relevant industries. The 
agricultural instrumentation technologies developed by CSIR -CSIO, are poised to 
significantly enhance the safety, susta inability, and productivity of India’s 
agricultural ecosystem. Sensitive bio (chemo) sensing strips, portable electrochemical 
sensor arrays, and pocket colorimeters for multi  parameter testing enable rapid, on -
site detection of pesticides, antibiotics, myc otoxins, and adulterants, ensuring food 
safety and protecting public health. Affordable IoT -enabled water service delivery 
and monitoring systems for rural deployment strengthen water management practices, 
ensuring equitable distribution and efficient util ization of this critical resource in 
farming communities. Advanced sensing methods for detecting gluten adulteration 
and edible oil contamination, along with SERS -based analytical platforms, directly 
contribute to quality assurance across the food supply chain.  
1.18 Post-harvest innovations, such as edible coating materials, biodegradable 
electrostatic coatings  and novel preservation technologies, extend the shelf life of 
perishable crops, reduce wastage, and improve farmers’ income. Region -specific 
smart agro-technologies, coupled with aerial electrostatic spraying systems for locust 
and pest control, bring precision agriculture closer to reality, reducing chemical use 
while increasing crop protection efficiency. Collectively, these indigenous, 
affordable, and field -deployable solutions empower farmers with actionable data, 
enhance rural resilience, promote sustainable practices, and support India’s food 
security and self-reliance goals.  
1.19 The Committee commends CSIR -CSIO for its outstanding and sustain ed 
contribution to the emerging field of agrionics.  The Committee notes that 
CSIO’s innovations have empowered farmers with real -time, actionable data 

9 
 
and have also strengthened food safety, improved resource management, and 
enhanced productivity across th e agricultural value chain.   While significant 
progress has been made in precision agriculture and quality assurance, the issue 
of stubble burning remains one of the most complex and persistent challenges 
facing Indian farming today. Farmers often resort t o burning due to limited 
time between crop cycles, high costs of residue management machinery, labour 
shortages, and the lack of accessible, affordable alternatives for residue 
utilization. The resulting air pollution, soil nutrient loss, and greenhouse ga s 
emissions make stubble burning a problem of national significance . In view of 
this, the Committee recommends CSIR -CSIO to extend its proven expertise in 
the field of agrionics towards developing practical, low-cost, innovative, scalable 
and farmer-friendly technology-driven solutions for effective stubble 
management.

Prospective Research Frontiers for the Coming Years 
1.30 The Committee then sought information on some of the futuristic and cutting 
edge themes that CSIR -CSIO is focusing on. In response, the Committee was 
informed that  during the last few years, some new scientific frontiers including 
Semiconductor Chips, Quan tum Technologies, Artificial Intelligence have evolved 
aggressively and changed the technological landscape globally. Therefore, CSIR -
CSIO has focused on some of these cutting -edge R&D themes and invested heavily 
in infrastructure, scientific manpower in these areas. Some of these research domains 
are as follows: 
I. Next-Generation Display Technologies and Diffractive Optical Elements : 
One of the major research projects of CSIR -CSIO is focused towards the 
design and development of waveguide based Head -Up Displ ay (HUD). The 
waveguide optics for Head -Up-Display requires the nanofabrication of large -
area diffraction grating including input grating, turn -grating and out coupling 
grating for HUD. The nanoscale feature size will be fabricated and realized at 
Centre f or Nano -Optics Fabrication (CNOF) – recently established at CSIR -
CSIO Chandigarh. The in -house fabricated waveguide slab will also find 
applications for fighter aircrafts, head mounted display for strategic sector and 
AR/VR-based near -eye display for consu mer market. The futuristic research 
project on development of mini -/micro-LED display will drive the display 
industry in India.  
II. Quantum Photonic Chip and Photonics Integrated Circuits (PIC):  
Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs), unlike Electronic Integrate d Circuits 
(EIC), uses photons instead of electrons which enables high -speed, low-power 
optical data transmission and processing on a chip -scale platform. The 
development of silicon, silicon nitride, and indium phosphide platform will 
enable realization of  high-speed optical interconnects. The researchers at 
CSIR-CSIO Chandigarh are also focused on developing advanced PIC 
architectures including transceivers, MUX/DEMUX, photonic logic gates, and 

14 
 
quantum photonic chips. These quantum photonic chips are future of chip-scale 
quantum computing across the globe. 
III. Meta-Optics and Meta -surfaces: Meta-surfaces, which are subwave  length 
structures of desired shape, size, orientation and periodicity, artificially 
fabricated on a planar substrate, are capable of tailori ng amplitude, phase and 
polarization of incident light. The research teams at CSIR -CSIO are utilizing 
these capabilities to design and develop meta -lens, meta -surface absorber, 
meta-surface for AR/VR goggles and meta -surface-enabled THz nano antenna 
for reconfigurable intelligent.  
IV. 6G Components and Terahertz devices : After 5G , the world is moving 
towards 6G in commercial sector. The researchers at CSIR -CSIO are also 
focusing on the development of on chip terahertz emitters, detectors, and 
waveguides using plasmonics and photonic techniques. The CMOS compatible 
terahertz resonators and antenna array with 0.1 – 0.3 THz bandwidth are in 
R&D phase. Furthermore, the next generation on -chip optical sensors such as 
compact hybrid optical gyroscope (HOG) and on -chip biosensors will be 
crucial in the futuristic applications such as long -range drones and wearable 
healthcare devices.  
V. Hydrogen Generation Technology:  CSIR-CSIO is advancing hydrogen 
technology research to support India’s clean energy transition. The institute has 
taken some initiatives on developing efficient and scalable electrochemical and 
photo-electrochemical processes for hydrogen generation from water, 
including low-grade wastewater. Efforts include novel material development, 
system design, and ele ctrolyzer optimization in collaboration with EIL and 
Cheema Boilers. CSIR-CSIO is also working with TATA Motors on hydrogen 
sensing for H2 -IC engines and portable hydrogen storage systems. These 
initiatives aim to enhance indigenous hydrogen instrumentatio n capability, 
promote green hydrogen adoption, and contribute to India’s net-zero goals.  
VI. Advanced Manufacturing Technology for Medical Industry:  CSIR-CSIO 
has established the Innovative Additive Research & Manufacturing (iARM) 
facility as a dedicated hub for R&D and services in additive manufacturing of 
orthopaedic and maxillofacial implants, with integrated capabilities for design, 
metal AM production, and mechanical testing of titanium based implants. 
iARM lab houses end -to-end infrastructure including a  metal 3D printer for 
titanium implants, a polymer 3D printer for anatomical models and surgical 

15 
 
guides, a fatigue testing setup, and supporting auxiliary equipment to enable 
concept-to-clinic workflows. Patient -specific implants developed at iARM 
have bee n successfully implanted in patients at leading medical institutions, 
evidencing clinical translation across multiple indications and anatomical sites. 
The facility also offers additive manufacturing and testing services to industry 
partners, covering desi gn assistance, prototyping, and validation for medical 
applications. In addition, CSIR -CSIO has transferred its technology for 
advanced lattice -structured, additively manufactured implants to industry for 
commercialization, supporting wider clinical adopti on and Make -in-India 
objectives. Furthermore, CSIR-CSIO in collaboration with ALIMCO Kanpur is 
working towards Development of High Powered Spectacles for Low Vision 
Aid (HPS-LVA). CSIR-CSIO is working towards establishment of a Centre of 
Advanced Research for development of assistive technologies and elderly.  
VII. Drone-based Technologies for Various Applications : The teams at CSIR -
CSIO are working on design and development of modern techniques needed 
for drone automation such as AI based ground object detectio n and their 
localization, Vision -based navigation for GPS denied environment, and 
autonomous landing site detection for autonomous drones. Further, the team is 
working towards detection and mitigation of acoustic based cyber -physical 
attack on the UAVs. Ad ditionally, the teams are also working towards 
detection of drones autonomously using different sensing principles such as 
visual, thermal and acoustic and detection and tracking of one UAV from 
another UAV. The researchers at CSIR -CSIO also working towards the design 
and development of an advanced aerial electrostatic spraying technology for 
agricultural applications. Aerial electrostatic spray technology for agricultural 
applications integrates precision agricultural aviation (UAVs) and electrostatic 
spray technology. According to the current development of agricultural UAVs 
and the characteristics of the farmland environment in India, the UAV -based 
aerial electrostatic spray technology, which carries the airborne electrostatic 
spraying system on the plant  protection UAVs, has vast potential in the future. 
There is a boom in the use of drones for spraying agrochemicals and fertilizers 
in Indian agriculture sector. However, the application of UAV -based aerial 
electrostatic spray technology is unavailable in India and is yet to be 
developed. It is the first work of its kind, in which the advanced aerial 
electrostatic spraying will be developed at CSIR-CSIO, Chandigarh. 

16 
 
1.31 The Committee commends CSIR -CSIO for its forward -looking research 
initiatives in fronti er areas such as quantum photonics, next -generation display 
technologies, terahertz devices, hydrogen generation, advanced medical 
manufacturing, and drone -based automation, which have the potential to 
position India as a leading global player in instrumen tation sciences and high -
technology innovation. While acknowledging these remarkable strides, the 
Committee emphasizes that CSIR -CSIO must also direct its scientific 
capabilities toward addressing India’s most persistent environmental challenges, 
particularly air and water pollution, which continue to affect millions of citizens. 
The Committee is deeply concerned that Delhi continues to hold the unfortunate 
distinction of being the most polluted capital city in the world, and that the 
heavily contaminated Yamuna River despite crores of rupees spent over the past 
decades shows little tangible improvement. Given CSIR -CSIO’s strength in 
sensor development, environmental instruments, real -time monitoring systems, 
and analytical technologies, the Committee strong ly recommends that the 
institute to prioritize the development of indigenous, scalable, and cost -effective 
technological solutions aimed at mitigating air pollution particularly in the Delhi 
NCR region , cleaning polluted river stretches  particularly the Ya muna, and 
monitoring environmental quality.  
Transfer of technologies  
1.32 During the interaction, the Committee sought information on multiple aspects 
of technology transfer, including the transfer process, criteria for selecting user 
industries, the list of industries that benefited from technology transfers over the past 
five years, product commercialization, revenue from royalties and license fees, 
marketing and promotion of industry -ready technologies, and the conduct of third -
party audits of the technology transfer process. 
1.33 In response, CSIR -CSIO stated that t he technology is first offered for transfer 
by the concerned Project Investigator, after which the Technology Evaluation 
Committee validates the technology. Subsequently, the duly consti tuted ToT 
Committee finalizes the license fee, royalty, exclusivity, duration, and other related 
terms. Accordingly, an Expression of Interest (EoI) is published to identify potential 
industrial partners for the transfer of technology. Interested parties s ubmit their 
proposals, which are reviewed by a committee. Based on this review, shortlisted 

17 
 
industry partners are invited to deliver technical presentations before the Empowered 
Committee. Following the evaluation, the committee finalizes the selection of 
industry partners. 
1.34 On finalization of ToT, CSIR -CSIO receives license fee, royalty based on the 
agreed terms and conditions at the time of signing the ToT agreement, after the 
product is commercialized. The typical duration of license validity varies from 1 to 
15 years, depending on the case. After the expiry of the license, renewal is carried out 
by charging the applicable license fee on a case-by-case basis.  
1.35 CSIR-CSIO also actively engages with industries by showcasing its developed 
technologies at various events such as exhibitions, conferences, and workshops. 
CSIO has a dedicated Business Development Group that ensures the effective 
showcasing of technologies developed at CSIR -CSIO in collaboration with the 
concerned Project Investigator of each technology.

from the early stages of technology development.

Introduction 
2.1 CSIR-Institute of Genomics & Integrative Biology (IGIB) is a premier Institute 
of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), engaged in research of 
national importance in the areas of genomics, molecular medicine, bioinformatics and 
proteomics. Their mission is t o translate concepts developed in basic biological 
research to commercially viable technologies for health care. 
Study visit of the Committee  
2.2 The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on S cience and 
Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change undertook a local study visit 
to CSIR -IGIB on 7 th November, 2025 to understand, first -hand, the path -breaking 
research, operational challenges, and  significant potential of IGIB in the realm  of 
genomics and integrative biology.  As the work conducted  at IGIB is critical not just 
for advancing the frontiers of science  but also for its direct impact on public health, 
personalized medicine, and biotechnology in India , the Committee considered it 
imperative to w itness the  operations in their  state-of-the-art laboratories from  
fundamental genomic sequencing to the development of  innovative diagnostic tools  
and to grasp the on-ground realities of scientific innovation.  During the visit, the 
Committee interacted with the Director, IGIB, representatives of DSIR & CSIR and 
the scientists working at IGIB. The complete list of officials who were present during 
the meeting is at Annexure II.  
2.3 During the visit, the Committee inspected the following facilities at IGIB: 
i. Biobank facility for Phenome India project - IGIB has a state -of-the-art 
Phenome India National Biobank on the campus. The Committee was informed 
that the biobank stores and maintains biological samples collected for Phenome 
India project, a nationwide cohort study which involves collecting 
comprehensive genomic, lifestyle, and clinical data from over 10,000 
individuals across India. This initiative will aid in early diagnosis, therapeutic 

21 
 
targeting, and the fig ht against complex diseases such as diabetes, cancer, and 
rare genetic disorders. 
ii. Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) facility for gene therapy of sickle cell 
anemia- The Committee noted that, i n a mission to eradicate Sickle -Cell 
Anemia from the country, IGIB has created a Good Manufacturing Practice 
(GMP) Facility on its campus in collaboration with multiple stakeholders such 
as the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Niti Aayog, Serum Institute of India, and the 
Ministry of Science and Technology. The Committee was told that t his facility 
will provide  ex-vivo CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing therapy options that use the 
patient's own blood, thereby, reducing the risk of immune rejection. This 
facility will receive blood samples from patients wit h sickle cell anemia and 
edit them using CRISPR -Cas9 technology. The blood sample will then be 
transfused back to the same patient in the hospital. Once fully functional, this 
facility will offer the potential for a one -time treatment approach towards 
sickle-cell anemia. 
iii. Biosafety Level 3 ( BSL3) facility towards TB -Mukt Bharat- The Biosafety 
Level 3 facility (BSL -3) at CSIR -IGIB is dedicated primarily to Tuberculosis 
research. The facility is equipped with negative -pressure rooms, High 
Efficiency Particulate Air/High Efficiency Particulate Arresting (HEPA) filters, 
and biosafety cabinets that allow students to work safely with Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis. Biosafety PPE kits and masks are worn by researchers for safety 
while they work with bacteria in this fac ility. The Committee observed that 
research being undertaken at this facility will give a better understanding of 
Tuberculosis and how the host immune response plays a role in Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis pathogenicity and how these mechanisms can be exploit ed to 
develop host-directed therapies. 
iv. Zebrafish facility for genetics, cancer, drug discovery and neuro -
behavioural diseases –The Committee was informed that  CSIR-IGIB’s 
zebrafish facility is among the largest zebrafish  facilities in the country. It 
houses many strains of wild -type fish and even more transgenic lines. The 
facility specialises in disease modelling, genetic manipulation, behaviour 
testing and developmental studies. The Committee was apprised that the facility 
is primarily student -run and uses state -of-the-art water circulation and 
purification systems. It houses multiple strains of wild -type fish, including 
Assamese wild-type (ASWT), which is native to the Brahmaputra River. CSIR-

22 
 
IGIB was the first to perfo rm high -depth genome seq uencing of the ASWT 
strain and put it on the map as a model for genomic studies. A variety of 
transgenic lines, including neural markers, are also maintained. The facility 
specialises in disease modelling, gene manipulation, genetic , epigenetic, 
behavioural and developmental studies. Zebrafish serves as an animal model to 
understand the pathophysiology of multiple genetic disorders and to help 
elucidate the effects of genetic and chemical interventions in alleviating or 
preventing th e defects. Currently, IGIB is focusing on creating zebrafish 
models of neuro -developmental disorders resulting from defects in brain 
development and on understanding defects in neuronal development, function, 
and behaviour. 
v. Genomics facility for genome sequencing, cancer genomics and rare 
genetic disorders - Sequencing facility -IGIB has a stand -alone sequencing 
facility equipped with MiSeq and NovaSeq machines used for human genomic 
sequencing. The Committee was told that  NovaSeq is a high -throughput 
instrument that generates large amounts of data in terabytes, while the MiSeq 
generates about 500 Mb of data in a single run and is usually used for bacterial 
whole-genome sequencing. Both of these machines are used for collaborative 
Pan-India projects such a s the Indian Breast Cancer Genome Atlas (IBCGA) 
and Phenome India. IGIB generates whole -genome, transcriptome, and 
metagenome sequences for these projects. Around 6,000 gut microbiome 
samples have been sequenced under the Phenome India project.

Indian Population Genomics  
2.12 During the presentation, the Committee was informed that CSIR-IGIB played a 
pioneering role in creating the Indian Reference Genomes, the first comprehensive 
catalogue of genomic variations across diverse Indian populations in the year 2008. 
They have sequenced the entire genomes of 1008 Indians in 2020. Under the Genome 
India programme, initiated in collaboration with CSIR and DBT, IGIB has sequenced 
thousands of genomes to create an inclusive database representing the genetic 
diversity of India. CSIR -IGIB is one of the four whole genome sequencing centers 
and is responsible for the collection of 3390 samples and the sequencing of over 2500 
human genome samples for the Genome  India 10000 target. The data forms the 
foundation for personalized and precision m edicine, enabling better understanding of 
disease predispositions and drug responses among India. 
2.13 The Committee inquired about India’s global standing in genomic research and 
the steps taken by CSIR -IGIB and DSIR to establish India as a leader in this  field. In 
response, it was submitted that India has sequenced about 10,000 genomes, compared 
with several hundred thousand worldwide. IGIB is contributing through initiatives 
such as Genome India, Phenome India, microbiome atlas projects, breast cancer 
genomics, and CRISPR programmes. It was emphasized that consistent and enhanced 
funding is essential to position India as a global leader in this field. 
2.14 The Committee acknowledges the significant achievements of CSIR -IGIB 
in advancing genomics in India.  However, the Committee notes that I ndia’s 
current genomic coverage, approximately 10,000 sequenced genomes, remains 
far from global benchmarks and does not represent the extrao rdinary genetic 
diversity of this  country. For a population as large and as heterogeneous as 
India, the Committee recommends that CSIR -IGIB, in collaboration with 
national scientific agencies, develop a long -term roadmap for sequencing at least 
10 million genomes and lead efforts to create a comprehensive National 
Reference Genome that captures the full spectrum of India’s geographic, ethnic 

27 
 
and linguistic diversity. The Committee feels that this endeavour will enable the 
identification of genetic variations unique to Indian populations, support the 
development of population -specific diagnostics and personalized  and precision 
medicine and provide  a deeper  understanding of  population history  such as 
migrations, admixture eve nts and demographic bottlenecks which will facilitate 
effective disease mapping. The Committee recommends that DSIR should extend 
sufficient funding, policy support, and infrastructure to CSIR-IGIB to enable the 
sequencing of at least 10 million genomes. 
 
National Rare Disease Diagnostics Programme 
 
2.15 The Committee was informed that CSIR-IGIB has developed a comprehensive 
workflow integrating whole -exome sequencing (WES), whole -genome sequencing 
(WGS), and RNA -seq-based validation to provide rapid and accurate molecular 
diagnosis and that t his platform has been used to diagnose over 6000 rare disease 
cases across India, including neuromuscular disorders, inborn errors of metabolism, 
intellectual disabilities, and mitochondrial diseases.  The Committee observed that 
IGIB also operates a Rare Disease Diagno stic Centre, where families from 
economically weaker backgrounds receive genomic testing and counselling support 
free of cost or at subsidized rates.  The Committee was given to understand that p rior 
to IGIB’s intervention, rare disease patients in India faced an average diagnostic delay 
of 6 –8 years  and that  IGIB’s pipelines have reduced this to less than 6 months, 
offering early diagnosis and actionable medical insights. 
 
2.16  The Committee has also been informed that IGIB works in close partnership 
with All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Postgraduate Institute of 
Medical Education and Research (PGIMER, Chandigarh), and several state hospitals  
and that t hese collaborations enable bedside -to-bench translation, integrating 
genomics into clinica l practice. IGIB has also been designated as a nodal institution 
supporting the National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021) and contributes to the 
national registry of diagnosed cases. 
 
2.17 The Committee also noted that IGIB has developed multiple low -cost n ext-
generation sequencing (NGS) panels for specific disease categories such as muscular 
dystrophies, primary immunodeficiencies, and metabolic disorders.  IGIB’s in -house 

28 
 
computational tools apply artificial intelligence and populatio n-specific data to 
improve variant classification accuracy.  Genomic data generated at IGIB is being 
linked to electronic medical records in pilot hospitals, paving the way for digital rare 
disease registries aligned with the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission . The Committee 
further noted that IGIB also provides genetic counselling for affected families, 
explaining inheritance patterns, carrier risks, and reproductive options.  The institute 
also partners with NGOs and patient advocacy groups to improve awareness, ensuring 
affected fa milies have access to psychosocial and financial support mechanisms.  
Educational workshops and outreach sessions in collaboration with state health 
departments are conducted to sensitize clinicians and genetic counsellors nationwide.

knowledge to execute a  study on this very important topic, and support and research

2.20 The Committee commends CSIR –IGIB for its extensive research on the 
genomics o f sickle -cell anaemia and for developing BIRSA -101, India’s first 
indigenous CRISPR-based gene therapy for sickle -cell disease. The Committee 
notes with concern that certain isolated tribal communities, including those in 
the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, are facing the  threat of extinction due to

Phenome India Cohort and Population Health Studies 
2.21 During the interaction, the Committee was informed about Phenome India 
Cohort, a flagship initiative of IGIB which aims to integrate genomic, phenotypic, and 
environmental data across thousands of Indian participants.  The cohort provides a 
longitudinal platform to understand gene -environment interactions, disease risks, and 
metabolic health in Indians.  The data helps address non -communicable diseases 
(diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular disorders) by identifying unique Indian risk markers 
and therapeutic targe ts. The cohort forms a critical component of India’s precision 
health infrastructure and informs national health policy. 
 
2.22 The Committee sought information on the timeline of Phenome India Project 
and also inquired about the measures taken by IGIB to ensure comprehensive 
representation of India’s diverse ethnic and regional populations  in the cohort. In 
response, it was submitted that Phenome India is executed in three phases from 2022 
to 2027; two phases have been completed. Cross -sectional data is un der analysis. A 
20–25 year follow -up is needed to meet major goals. For India -specific health 

30 
 
standards, larger cohorts from rural and urban settings are required. IGIB is working 
to harmonise the existing national cohort datasets. 
 
2.23 The Committee ackn owledges the critical role of the Phenome India 
Project in identifying biomarkers and risk factors unique to the Indian 
population, thereby laying the foundation for the development of India -specific 
precision medicine. Given the immense genetic, geographi cal, and ethno -
linguistic diversity of the country, the Committee recommends that the cohort 
data must be broad -based, inclusive, and truly representative of India’s varied 
populations. The Committee notes that India can no longer rely solely on 
Western-derived health standards, which may not accurately capture the 
physiological, metabolic, and disease-risk profiles of Indian communities. In this 
regard, the Committee recommends that CSIR-IGIB should intensify efforts to 
generate robust, India -specific heal th reference standards  in a time bound 
manner and ensure comprehensive representation from across all regions.

CHAPTER –III 
Strengthening CSIR’s Global Competitiveness  
3.1  The Committee notes that scientists constitute the intellectual backbone of 
CSIR, and enhancing CSIR’s global competitiveness requires empowering them 
with greater autonomy, adequate resources, and operational flexibility. The 
Committee feels that CSIR’s i nnovation capacity is constrained by 
administrative delays, further compounded by an imbalance wherein 
administrative staff outnumber scientists. Timely and predictable funding, 
robust administrative support, streamlined approvals, and online administrativ e 
processes are essential for accelerating scientific output. In view of the above, the 
Committee recommends that CSIR should review and reform its existing 
institutional ecosystem to ensure that administrative mechanisms facilitate 
rather than hinder scie ntific work. The Committee further recommends that 
Directors of the 37 laboratories under CSIR be granted autonomy in the 
approval of research proposals and be made accountable for outcomes. The 
Committee also impresses upon CSIR to digitize all administra tive processes 
end-to-end to enhance efficiency, transparency, and responsiveness.        
3.2 The Committee observes that, extant rules often limit scientists from 
taking sabbaticals, pursuing faculty visits, or engaging in collaborative research 
with institutions such as MIT, Stanford, or Harvard and setting up start -ups. 
These restrictions lead t o the underutilization of global opportunities and limit 
the flow of knowledge and technology. The Committee feels that, inorder to 
compete globally, CSIR must modernize its policies related to international 
engagement and professional mobility. A proactiv e global outreach strategy 
should be adopted to position CSIR as a preferred international collaborator. 
The Committee, therefore recommends CSIR to reform its existing policies and 
strengthen global engagement. The Committee further recommends CSIR to 
empower its scientific workforce through improved flexibility and resource 
access, to begin with, by designating scientists as project heads with full 
budgetary control and access to adequate administrative support. 
3.3 CSIR must also foster a strong culture of innovation and 
entrepreneurship, by empowering its scientists to co -found startups within 
institutional incubators. Encouraging deeper industry collaboration, greater IP 

36 
 
generation, and vibrant startup activity will significantly strengthen CSIR’s 
ability to contribute to national priorities. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that CSIR may consider permitting its scientific and technical 
personnel to establish or co -found startups, similar to what is already practiced 
in the IITs. CSIR may also explor e launching structured entrepreneurship 
programmes and supporting such startups through initial funding, grants, and 
seed capital to help convert laboratory innovations into viable commercial 
enterprises. This approach would enhance technology transfer, dr ive socio -
economic impact, and expand CSIR’s role in the national innovation ecosystem. 
The Committee further suggests introducing peer -driven, deliverable -based 
evaluation of research output, along with cumulative Pro fessional Development 
Allowance on the lines of IITs, to incentivize excellence and sustained scientific 
productivity. 
3.4 The Committee also notes that the current budgetary allocation to 
DSIR/CSIR is inadequate to meet the growing demands of frontier scientific 
research, development of advan ced laboratories, global collaboration, and 
sustained innovation-led national growth. In an era where countries are rapidly 
scaling their R&D investments, India must ensure that CSIR remains globally 
competitive and capable of delivering strategic technolo gies of national 
importance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government of India 
to substantially enhance the budgetary allocation to DSIR/CSIR to strengthen 
scientific infrastructure, modernize laboratories, and support high -risk, high -
impact research. The Committee further observes that corporate participation 
in national R&D remains limited, despite the provisions for Corporate  Social 
Responsibility (CSR). The Committee, therefore,  recommends the Government 
to evolve a clear and robust mechanis m to facilitate greater CSR contributions, 
both from public  and private sector enterprises, towards DSIR/CSIR -led 
research, innovation, and technology translation programmes.

CHAPTER –I  
CSIR-CENTRAL SCIENTIFIC INSTRUMENTS ORGANIZATION (CSIR-CSIO) 
Budget  
The Committee observes that CSIO is one of the 37 laboratories 
functioning under the umbrella of CSIR, and the Council must allocate its 
limited financial resources across all its laboratories; therefore, it is  not realistic 
to expect a significant increase in CSIO’s budgetary allocation from CSIR alone. 
The Committee further notes with concern that during the year 2024 -25, only 
8% of the funds received from CSIR were actually utilized for R&D purposes . 
In view of these constraints, the Committee emphasizes that CSIO must strive to 
move towards greater financial self -reliance by substantially increasing revenue 
generation through industry collaborations, consultancy, testing and calibration 
services, technology t ransfer, and sponsored research projects. The Committee 
recommends that CSIO  should develop and implement a clear, time -bound 
strategy to enhance its external earnings and ensure that these internally 
generated resources are effectively channeled into strengthening R&D activities, 
upgrading scientific infrastructure, and building long -term institutional 
capacity.               (Para 1.10) 
Man Power 
The Committee notes with concern that CSIR -CSIO is operating at less 
than half of its sanctioned strength in 2 024-25. The Committee is of the 
considered opinion that an institution like CSIO, which is fundamentally driven 
by scientific and technical expertise, cannot function effectively without 
adequate manpower, and the current shortage poses a serious threat to  its 
research output, technological innovation, and  future potential . If existing 
vacancies are kept unfilled, CSIO’s performance and ability to deliver on 
critical projects will stand severely compromised.                                  (Para 1.13) 
The Committee is unable to comprehend the rationale behind advertising 
only 10 percent of vacancies in each cycle and leaving such a large number of 
posts unfilled for years, a practice that has clearly contributed to the present 

38 
 
crisis. The Committee is of the view that this staggered approach to recruitment, 
coupled with the issue of deemed -abolished posts, has been a significant 
administrative lapse. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that 
CSIR-CSIO should take all necessary action to ensure th at the advertised 
vacancies are filled up expeditiously. Further, DSIR should impress upon the 
Department of Expenditure to revive the deemed -abolished posts without any 
further delay, so that CSIO can restore its functional capacity and fulfil its 
strategic role in the national science and technology ecosystem.           (Para 1.14) 
Agrionics 
 The Committee commends CSIR -CSIO for its outstanding and sustained 
contribution to the emerging field of agrionics.  The Committee notes that 
CSIO’s innovations have empowered farmers with real -time, actionable data 
and have also strengthened food safety, improved resource management, and 
enhanced productivity across the agricultural value chain.   While significant 
progress has been made in precision agriculture and quality assurance, the issue 
of stubble burning remains one of the most complex and persistent challenges 
facing Indian farming today. Farmers often resort to burning due to limited 
time between crop cycles, high costs of residue management  machinery, labour 
shortages, and the lack of accessible, affordable alternatives for residue 
utilization. The resulting air pollution, soil nutrient loss, and greenhouse gas 
emissions make stubble burning a problem of national significance . In view of 
this, the Committee recommends CSIR -CSIO to extend its proven expertise in 
the field of agrionics towards developing practical, low-cost, innovative, scalable 
and farmer-friendly technology-driven solutions for effective stubble 
management.                                                                                               (Para 1.19) 
Instrumentation, devices, and technologies developed by CSIO 
 The Committee notes that CSIR -CSIO has developed an ‘Intelligent 
Elephant Movement Detection and Alert System’, a technology designed to 
prevent elephant deaths near railway tracks. The Committee was informed that 
this system combines seismic sensing and t hermal imaging to detect elephant 
movement in real time, and has been successfully deployed and piloted for over 
four years at the Rajaji Tiger Reserve in Uttarakhand, in collaboration with the 

39 
 
Wildlife Institute of India and the World Wildlife Fund. The C ommittee is 
deeply concerned that India continues to witness numerous elephant fatalities 
every year due to train collisions, habitat fragmentation, and increasing human–
wildlife conflict, underscoring the urgent need for a permanent and scalable 
technological intervention.  In this context, the Committee recommends CSIR -
CSIO to collaborate with the Ministry of Railways and the Ministry of 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change and explore the feasibility of scaling 
up the system beyond just two or three pilot sites to a nationwide rollout.                                   
                                                                                                                      (Para 1.29) 
Prospective Research Frontiers for the Coming Years 
The Committee commends CSIR -CSIO for its forward -looking research 
initiatives in frontier areas such as quantum photonics, next -generation display 
technologies, terahertz devices, hydrogen generation, advanced medical 
manufacturing, and drone -based automation,  which have the potential to 
position India as a leading global player in instrumentation sciences and high -
technology innovation. While acknowledging these remarkable strides, the 
Committee emphasizes that CSIR -CSIO must also direct its scientific 
capabilities toward addressing India’s most persistent environmental challenges, 
particularly air and water pollution, which continue to affect millions of citizens. 
The Committee is deeply concerned that Delhi continues to hold the unfortunate 
distinction of bei ng the most polluted capital city in the world, and that the 
heavily contaminated Yamuna River despite crores of rupees spent over the past 
decades shows little tangible improvement. Given CSIR -CSIO’s strength in 
sensor development, environmental instrumen ts, real-time monitoring systems, 
and analytical technologies, the Committee strongly recommends that the 
institute to prioritize the development of indigenous, scalable, and cost -effective 
technological solutions aimed at mitigating air pollution particularly in the Delhi 
NCR region , cleaning polluted river stretches  particularly the Yamuna , and 
monitoring environmental quality.                                                           (Para 1.31) 
 
 

40

The Committee notes with concer n that although CSIR -CSIO has 
transferred around 105 technologies to over 70 industries in the last five years, 
the total revenue generated amounts to only about ₹3.20 crore, which appears 
disproportionately low in comparison to the commercial potential of  many of 
these technologies. The Committee is of the view that CSIO is transferring 
technologies to private players at undervalued prices  and t hese partners are 
earning significant profits while the institute is receiving only a marginal share 
of the value created. The Committee therefore recommends that CSIO  may also 
consider adopting a more competitive and market -aligned pricing framework 
for technology transfer, ensuring that licensing fees and royalty structures 
appropriately reflect the true commercial  worth, uniqueness, and societal 
impact of the technologies developed through public funding.              (Para 1.39) 
 The Committee was informed that a major challenge faced by CSIR-CSIO 
during technology transfer to industry is the delay in product commercialization 
by the ToT partner , which often leads to the technology becoming obsolete or 
competitors introducing similar products in the market. The Committee feels 
that there is an urgent need to arrest this trend since such delays may, in some 
cases, r esult in nullifying all the efforts and time put in development of 
technologies by CSIR -CSIO. To prevent this, the Committee recommends that 
CSIR-CSIO should consider including a clause in the technology transfer 
agreement requiring the ToT  partner to commercialize the product within a 
specified timeframe.                                                                                 (Para 1.40)
