growth and profit contraction to be a matter of serious concern. The Committee recommends

deep concern, particularly in view of its strategic centrality to India’s three -stage nuclear 
power programme. The Committee recommends that Government  should introduce a 
milestone-linked budgetary relea se mechanism for BHAVINI, whereby future funding 
tranches are contingent upon regulatory certification of defined commissioning achievements, 
so as to align financial flows with actual technical progress. The Committee further 
recommends that BHAVINI should be encouraged to draw upon relevant international 
operational experience in fast breeder technology to reduce the risk of recurring technical 
delays.

3.24 The Committee observes with concern that actual expenditure under the Nuclear 
Power Projects head in 2025 –26 stood at only Rs. 503.59 crore up to January 2026 against a 
Budget Estimate of Rs. 2,086 crore — a utilization of merely 37.78 per cent even against the 
substantially reduced Revised Estimate of Rs. 1,332.83 crore. Juxtaposed against 2024 –25, 
when actual expenditure of Rs. 2,244.43 crore exceeded the Revised Estimate of Rs. 1,500 
crore by 149.63 per cent, this pattern reveals significant volatility in budgetary planning and 
execution under this head. The Committee recognises that the milestone -based nature of 
nuclear fuel procurement under inter -governmental arrangements introduces inherent 
variability; however,  the scale of the fluctuation — from significant overshoot to deep 
undershoot within successive financial years — indicates that the planning and estimation 
framework for this head is inadequate. The Committee recommends that the Department 
should institute a quarterly monitoring mechanism to track fuel delivery milestones and 
projected payment obligations and use this to arrive at more accurate Budget Estimates, 
thereby reducing the recurrence of large supplementary demands on the one hand and large 
unspent provisions on the other.

have a direct bearing on India’s nuclear fuel expenditure and electricity generation. The 
Committee recommends that the Government should set a clear policy objective of 
progressively reducing dependence on any single ex ternal source for nuclear fuel supply, and 
take concrete steps towards expanding domestic uranium production, fuel fabrication 
capacity, and supply agreements with a diversified set of partner nations.

3.31 The Committee observes tha t India possesses among the largest known reserves of 
thorium in the world, and the utilization of thorium as a nuclear fuel is central to the long -
term vision of India’s three -stage nuclear power programme. However, the transition to 
thorium-based fuel cy cles remains at an early stage of development, with significant 
technological and infrastructural challenges yet to be resolved. The Committee is of the view 
that a more accelerated and focused approach to thorium fuel cycle development is essential 
if India is to realize its long-term energy security potential from this indigenous resource. The 
Committee recommends that the Government  should accord higher priority to research and 
development in thorium utilization, strengthen the institutional capacity and  resource 
allocation of relevant research establishments engaged in this work, and put in place a clear 
developmental roadmap with defined milestones for the progressive introduction of thorium -
based fuel in India’s nuclear power programme.

4.34 The Committee observes that the regul atory framework governing

CHAPTER – 5 
THE SHANTI ACT, 2025 
The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India 
(SHANTI) Act, 2025, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15th December 202 5, passed by the 
lower house on 17th December 2025, and subsequently approved by the Rajya Sabha on 18th 
December 2025, before receiving presidential assent on 20th December 20 25. This legislation 
repeals the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, to 
create a unifie d legal framework enabling private sector participation in building, owning, and 
operating nuclear power plants. Key provisions include granting statutory status to the Atomic 
Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), introducing graded operator liability caps rangi ng from ₹100 
crore to ₹3,000 crore based on reactor size, and removing the statutory right of recourse against 
suppliers—limiting it to contractual terms or proven intent to cause damage  . The Government 
retains exclusive control over sensitive activities such as uranium enrichment and spent fuel 
management, while expanding the definition of nuclear damage to include environmental harm. 
The Act forms part of India's strategy to achieve 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047, representing 
approximately 10% of the country's projected energy needs. 
5.2 The Committee enquired from the Department that after the enforcement of SHANTI Act, 
How the AERB will ensure functional autonomy given its composition and reporting structure and 
what mechanisms are in place to prev ent conflict of interest between the DAE‘s promotional and 
regulatory roles. The Committee also asked how will transparency in regulatory decisions b e 
maintained, especially under s ection 39 and what objective criteria will be used to determine if an 
entity is ―inimical to national security‖ under section 7(4) of the Act. 
5.3 The Department informed the Committee that the SHANTI Act while preserving the de 
facto independence of AERB provides for its institutionalization and de jure independence. The 
composition of the Board, appointment of Chairman and members, their terms, etc. has now been 
provided in the Act itself. The Board has been provided with complete functional autonomy to 
frame its own set of procedures for transaction of business. It is empowered  to frame regulations, 
issue safety codes and standards, grant safety authorization and exercise oversight through 
continued safety reviews and inspections. It has also been empowered to conduct investigation, 
carry out search and seizure and take appropri ate enforcement actions including imposition of 
monetary penalties. The Board is free to engage with any academic institutions, appoint experts and 
consultants and coordinate with national and international bodies to maintain its competency. The 
Board for all purposes remains accountable to the Parliament and its Annual Report shall be laid to 
the Parliament. As required by the Board, the Central Government shall provide the Board with 
financial and human resources. In view of opening up of the nuclear sect or, the information 
regarded as ‗restricted information‘ under Section 39 has been limited to only those which are 
detrimental to national security and public interest. In order to ensure transparency, the Regulatory 
Board is also entrusted with the respon sibility under section 24(3) (h) for planned public outreach 
and engagement with interested parties on matters related to nuclear safety without disclosing 
restricted information. Nevertheless, any person aggrieved by the decisions of appellate tribunal or  
awards for settlement of any claims can approach to court. The criteria for section 7(4) for 
determining an entity is inimical to the society may be based on certain aspects which includes: If 
any conduct of the licensee poses an intentional threat to hea lth of the public or environment, or if 
the Central Government has a reason to believe that the licensee is dominated by any entity which 
poses a security risk or if there are any inputs from intelligence or law enforcement agencies 
against the licensee. 

38 
 
 
 
 
5.4 The Committee then sought to know how DAE will ensure timely processing of license and 
safety authorization applications. The Committee was informed that the Rules and Regulations will 
be framed under the SHANTI A ct which will provide for the forms and manner in which the 
license and Safety Authorization will be issued. 
5.5 The Committee also enquired regarding support mechanisms (financial, technical) that will 
be provided to private players to encourage investment. The Department replied that the Ce ntral 
Government provides necessary technical support to the Industry by carrying out stakeholders 
meeting, awareness programmes and technical discussions. As the SHANTI A ct has opened the 
nuclear energy sector to private industry, an ecosystem will be dev eloped based on the requirement 
of the industry. 
5.6 With regards to the Committee‘s query on management and monitoring of radioactive waste 
from private facilities, the Department informed that under section 32 of the Act, the Central 
Government will prov ide a policy on the radioactive waste management generated from nuclear 
facilities. 
5.7 The Committee desired to know regarding how will the liability cap in the Second Schedule 
be determined and will it be periodically reviewed. The Committee was informed  that as per the 
section 13(2) the maximum amount of liability of an operator in respect of each nuclear incident for 
different categories of nuclear installation shall be as specified in the Second Schedule. The Central 
Government has the power to amend t he second schedule (if required) to provide for a higher or 
lower amount of liability having regard to deployment of nuclear installations with advanced 
technology and enhanced safety features and other relevant criteria. 
5.8 Regarding the right to recours e against suppliers and its impact on international 
collaboration and insurance costs, the Committee learnt that a s per the international convention, 
300 million SDR is the minimum limit to be a signatory of CSC. The SHANTI Act has kept the 
same limit as India being a signatory to CSC can claim compensation from international funds, if it 
exceeds compensation for nuclear liability exceeds 300 million SDR. The SHANTI Act is special 
law dealing with the subject on civil liability for nuclear damage and section 11 of the Act make the 
operator liable for the nuclear damage and it is only after payment of the compensation in case of a 
nuclear incident, the operator may seek recourse to the extent such right is expressly provided for in 
a contract in writing betwe en operator and supplier. There is no provision in the Act which makes 
supplier liable. Further, section 87 of the Act provides for overriding effect of the Act. Thus, the 
SHANTI Act is compliant to the provisions of CSC and is consistent with the principle of exclusive 
channeling of the liability to operator (who is a licensee under the Act). With increased safety 
features in modern reactors and stringent framework for ensuring quality control of the supplied 
components (section 24(3)(c)(ii)), section 32(1 )(d)), inspection of manufacturing site (section 28 
(1) (b)(ii)), the likelihood of supply of substandard equipment or material is minimal. Thus, doing 
away with supplier‘s liability does not affect the compensation amount to be paid to the victims. 
5.9 The Committee also enquired that how the SHANTI Act aligns with international best 
practices in nuclear safety and emergency response. The Department replied that India has a robust 
system of implementation of Nuclear Safety in Nuclear and radiation Faciliti es. The responsibility 
for ensuring the safety of civilian nuclear facilities in India lies solely with the Atomic Energy 
Regulatory Board (AERB). The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) implements the national 
plan for nuclear safety, radiation protecti on, and nuclear security through a comprehensive 
Integrated Management System (IMS). This system consolidates all regulatory and management 
processes into a unified framework, ensuring coherence, consistency, and effectiveness in 
regulatory decision-making. To streamline regulation and promote uniform standards, AERB has 

39 
 
developed a comprehensive set of safety codes, guide, and standards that all operators are required 
to follow. Facilities must obtain the necessary licenses from AERB to operate these nucle ar 
installations legally. These licenses are contingent on strict adherence to the prescribed safety 
standards. AERB inspectors are authorized to conduct regular inspections of licensed facilities to 
verify compliance. In cases where non -compliance is iden tified, AERB provides corrective 
recommendations and technical guidance. In extreme situations of non -compliance, AERB holds 
the authority to suspend or revoke the operating license. Compliance with international nuclear and 
radiological safety conventions  across Indian nuclear facilities is systematically monitored and 
ensured by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) through a well -defined framework that 
integrates regulatory oversight, international cooperation, and alignment with globally accepted 
safety standards. This framework reflects India‘s commitment to maintaining high levels of nuclear 
safety, security, and transparency in accordance with its international obligations. The 
infrastructure requirements, for management of nuclear emergency in public domain as specified by 
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) for emergency response functions, are well established 
and maintained in coordination with Local, State and National Authority. Emergency preparedness 
and response plans have been formulated  as per requirements and guidance given by AERB to 
protect public in case of emergencies. These plans are tested periodically through exercises as well 
as revised periodically to be in line with the current requirements and situation. 
5.10 The Committee al so sought to know about w hat international treaties or conventions does 
the Act comply with, and h ow will updates be incorporated. The Committee was informed that t he 
Act has enabling provisions for the implementation of the safety, security and nuclear li ability 
which are aligned with their respective international conventions like CNS, CPPNM, CSC etc. to 
which India is a party. Any update in the international convention and its implication on the 
SHANTI Act shall be dealt based on the update. 
5.11 The Com mittee asked regarding public consultation processes befo re licensing nuclear 
facilities. The Department informed that public consultation is mandated for statutory clearances 
from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change . With regards to public accessibility 
of safety reports, inspection findings, and incident summaries , the Committee was informed that 
they may be made accessible to the public upon request, as long as they do not violate commercial 
confidence, trade secret or has national security implication. 
5.12 The Committee sought to know that h ow will the public be informe d in case of a nuclear 
incident. The Department informed that u pon the notification of nuclear incident, the Claims 
Commissioner designated for the area shall cause wide publicity to be given in such manner as may 
be deemed fit, for inviting applications for claiming compensation for nuclear damage.  As per 
section 65(2) of the SHANTI Act, the Claims Commissioner and the Claims Commission while 
discharging their functions  under this Act will exercise the same powers as are vested in a civil 
court under the Code of Civil Procedure. 1908. Further, Section 65(5) SHANTI Act provides that 
the Claims Commissioner and the Claims Commission shall be deemed to be a civil court for the 
purposes of relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Section 65(6) of 
the SHANTI Act further provides that every proceeding before the Claims Commissioner or the 
Claims Commission under this Act shall be deemed to be judicia l proceeding within the relevant 
sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Therefore, the awards of Claims Commissioner and 
Claims Commission are not administrative or executive orders but are judicial determination 
having the force of law and are bin ding on parties.  The procedures to be followed for the 
adjudication will be provided in the Rules framed under SHANTI Act. 
5.13 The Committee asked how the Government will balance national securities with innovation 
incentives in patent clauses . The Depart ment informed that t he SHANTI Act allows grant ing the 
patent only for those research & development and innovations which are for the peaceful uses of 
nuclear energy. The patents will be granted after technical evaluation of the patent applications. 
Any inn ovation which is sensitive in nature or having national security implications shall be 

40 
 
deemed to be non -patentable. Regarding guidelines on what constitutes ―sensitive‖ or ― security-
implicated‖ inventions, the Committee was informed that t he sensitive or s ecurity implicated 
inventions are those inventions which are related to activities exclusively reserved for the Central 
Government, as provided in Sect ion 3(5). In addition, Central G overnment has the power to notify 
any activity or facility as sensitive, if in its opinion the activity or facility has direct implications to 
the national security.  Regarding the appeal mechanisms for inventors whose  patents are deemed 
―sensitive‖, the Department informed that t he patents will be granted after technical evalua tion of 
the patent applications. In case if the inventions in the opinion of the Central Government, are 
sensitive in nature or having national security implications, then such invention shall be deemed to 
have been made or conceived by the Central Governm ent. The Controller General of Patents, 
Designs and Trademarks within the meaning of the Patents Act, 1970, has a final decision whether 
to grant or not grant the patent. The decision of the Controller can be appealed directly to high court 
having territorial jurisdiction over the ―appropriate office‖ where the patent application was signed. 
5.14 The Committee also enquired regarding c oordination between AERB, CPCB, and othe r 
regulators. The Committee was informed that AERB is an independent authority, and has the power 
to establish any coordination with other regulatory bodies as it may deemed fit, for its independent 
functioning and decision making. 
5.15 The Committee then asked h ow the SHANTI Act will interact with State Governments on 
land acquisition an d environmental clearances. The Committee was informed that t he land 
acquisition and environmental clearances are to be  obtained from other statutory a gencies. Upon 
the land acquisition and environmental clearances, the applicant will apply for license fro m the 
Central Government under the Act. 
5.16 The Committee also enquired regarding oversight role of the Parliament over exemptions 
and emergency powers granted under the Act. The Department replied that t he power of exemption 
from liability considerations  was already existing in the CLND Act, 2010 (Sec 45) with regard to 
small quantities of nuclear material if in the opinion of the Central Government, the risk involved is 
insignificant. The same reasoning has been extended to licensing and other provision s of the Act 
(section 44), and Central Government has  the power to notify such exemptions. However, the 
reason for all such exemptions needs  to be stated in the notification. The emergency power is to 
secure public health and safety and from security consid erations, Government assumes full control 
over the nuclear plants and materials during national emergency declared under Article 352 of the 
Constitution of India (section 46). 
5.17 The Committee asked that whether nuclear operators (including NPCIL) will be required to 
bear higher insurance premiums under the new framework, and if so, will these costs be  absorbed 
within existing budgetary support or passed on through tariffs  or will require additional budgetary 
allocation. The Department replied that t he li mits of liability for which operators have to obtain 
insurance would depend on the size of the reactors they would operate, as specified in the second 
schedule of the SHANTI Act. The exact premium would also depend on how the nuclear liability 
insurance market would evolve in future. The premiums paid by the  operators would be passed on 
through tariffs. 
5.18 The Committee also asked that whether  DAE faced any constraints (technical or financial) 
in achieving its goals so that it was forced to open t his sect or for private players and w hether 
private players can perform better than DAE in this sensitive a nd crucial field and if so, how. The 
Department replied that t he SHANTI Act has opened up the nuclear energy sector for peaceful 
purposes for wider participat ion including private entities as part of the whole of country approach 
leveraging the private sector capabilities for a rapid expansion of nuclear power generation capacity 
to 100 GW by 2047. This target is intended to be achieved through significant expa nsion of the 
nuclear power generation by government owned entities and private entities. DAE through its 
existing and upcoming nuclear power plants aims to augment the nuclear energy capacity in a 

41 
 
graded manner by ramping it to 22.8GW by 2032 and subsequen tly to around 50GW by 2047 
towards fulfillment of the  ambitious goal of 100 GW. The G overnment funding and financial 
support has been commensurate with DAE‘s expansion plans and has  not imposed any constraints 
to its programs. Adequate capacity and capabil ities are in place with DAE for achieving the share 
of around 50GW of nuclear power generation by Government owned entities out of the target of 
100 GW by the year 2047. 
5.19 The Committee also sought to know that since  the sector is now open for private players, 
does DAE need such a h uge funding of approximately 25 thousand crores. The Department replied 
that their current projections indicate a participation space of around 50GW out of the am bitious 
100GW announced by the G overnment by the year 2047. The  proposed funding of approximately 
25 thousand crores for DAE is to support their ongoing programs and efforts towards achieving this 
target.  
5.20 The Committee observes that while the SHANTI Act provides statutory and de jure 
independence to AERB, the st ructural relationship between DAE — which actively promotes 
nuclear energy expansion — and AERB remains a source of potential conflict of interest. The 
Department's response does not adequately add ress the concern that the same M inistry 
driving India's 100  GW nuclear ambitions may influence the composition and leadership of 
the body meant to regulate it. The Committee therefore recommends that the Central 
Government should establish an independent Appointments Committee for the selection of 
AERB's Chairman and Board members, comprising members drawn  substantially from 
outside DAE. This would create a structural firewall between the promotional and regulat ory 
arms of nuclear governance. 
5.21 The Committee observes that the current disclosure regime under Section 39 and 
Section 24(3)(h) places the burden of accessing safety information on citizens, making safety 
reports, inspection findings, and incident summaries available only "upon request" and 
subject to broad exceptions including commercial confidence and national security. This 
passive disclosure approach is inadequate for a sector that directly affects public health and 
environmental safety, particularly as private operators — who have stronger commercial 
incentives to suppress unfavourable findings — now enter the nuclear space. The Committee 
therefore recommends that AERB should be mandated through Rules framed under the 
SHANTI Act to proactively and periodically publish inspection findings, regulatory decisions, 
and incident summaries on a publicly accessible digital platform, with only a narrowly 
defined category of genuinely sensitive information withheld. This would bring India in line 
with international best practices followed by regulators such as the US Nuclear Regulatory 
Commission and France' s ASN, build public trust in the regulatory process, and act as a 
structural deterrent against both operator complacency and regulatory capture. 
 

42 
 
5.22 The Committee observes that while the Central Government retains the power to 
amend the liability caps sp ecified in the Second Schedule, this power is entirely discretionary 
with no mandatory timeline, triggering mechanism, or independent oversight requirement. 
The liability caps ranging from ₹100 crore to ₹3,000 crore risk becoming inadequate over 
time as re actor sizes increase, population densities around plant sites grow, inflation erodes 
the real value of compensation, and new reactor technologies introduce different risk profiles. 
The absence of a structured review cycle means caps could remain outdated f or extended 
periods without any institutional pressure for revision, leaving victims of a potential nuclear 
incident severely undercompensated. The Committee therefore recommends that the Rules 
framed under the SHANTI Act should mandate a statutory review of the Second Schedule 
liability caps at least once every five years, conducted by an independent expert committee 
comprising legal, technical, actuarial, and public interest representatives, whose 
recommendations should be placed before Parliament before any revision is notified. This 
would ensure that compensation limits remain meaningful, provide long -term planning 
certainty to private operators and insurers, and uphold the State's fundamental obligation to 
victims of the nuclear catastrophe. 
 
5.23 The C ommittee observes that the SHANTI Act's removal of the statutory right of 
recourse against suppliers — limiting it solely to contractual terms — eliminates a significant 
legal deterrent that previously incentivized suppliers to maintain rigorous component quality 
standards. While the Department has justified this change on the grounds of compliance with 
the Convention on Supplementary Compensation and the enhanced safety features of modern 
reactors, this reasoning presupposes the very quality control effect iveness that supplier 
liability was designed to enforce. As private operators begin procuring from a wider range of 
domestic and international suppliers, often under cost pressures, the risk of substandard 
components entering nuclear facilities without ade quate legal accountability is a genuine 
concern. The Committee therefore recommends that the removal of supplier liability must be 
compensated by making third -party independent auditing of supplier manufacturing sites a 
statutory requirement under Section 28, with audit findings reported directly to AERB 
rather than routed through the operator. This structural safeguard would preserve the 
quality assurance function previously served by the threat of legal liability, protect potential 
victims without burdening international nuclear commerce, and ensure that the channeling of 
liability exclusively to operators does not come at the cost of supply chain integrity. 
 

43 
 
5.24 The Committee observes that while the SHANTI Act opens the nuclear sector to 
private participation, the Act and the Department's responses do not specify any minimum 
financial, technical, or operational qualification thresholds that private entities must meet 
before receiving a licence  to operate in the sector . Unlike other infrastructure sectors opened 
to private investment, a failure in nuclear facility operation is not recoverable — it carries the 
risk of irreversible environmental contamination, transboundary harm, and long -term public 
health consequences. The experience of private sector participation in other sensitive 
infrastructure sectors in India has shown that without robust pre -qualification criteria, cost-
cutting and regulatory arbitrage can emerge, particularly in early years of a new framework. 
The Committee therefore recommends that the Rules framed under the SHANTI Act must 
prescribe clear, publicly available and non -negotiable minimum qualification criteria for 
private nuclear operators, including minimum net worth requirements, mandatory insura nce 
coverage, demonstrated technical competency, and operational track records, before any 
private licence is granted. Further, a dedicated continuous monitoring mechanism should be 
established specifically for private operators during their initial years of operation to ensure 
that commercial pressures do not compromise nuclear safety. 
 
5.25 The Committee observes that the Department's response on public information during 
a nuclear incident focused primarily on the Claims Commissioner's role in publicisin g 
compensation procedures under Section 65, entirely conflating the immediate public safety 
alert function with the subsequent claims settlement process. These are two fundamentally 
distinct needs — the former requiring real-time, wide-area communication within hours of an 
incident, and the latter being a judicial process that unfolds over months or years. The 
Committee is of the opinion  that delayed and fragmented public communication during a 
nuclear emergency significantly compounds the humanitarian impa ct, regardless of the 
quality of subsequent compensation mechanisms. The Committee therefore recommends that 
the Rules framed under the SHANTI Act must mandate a statutory real -time public alert 
protocol, specifying defined timelines for initial public not ification, designated responsible 
authorities at local, state, and national levels, and mandated communication channels — 
including digital, broadcast, and community -level systems — that are activated immediately 
upon a nuclear incident being declared, ent irely independent of the claims process. This 
protocol should be tested through mandatory periodic drills and reviewed annually by AERB 
in coordination with State Disaster Management Authorities. 
 

44 
 
5.26 The Committee observes that the SHANTI Act defers the framing of a radioactive 
waste management policy to a future Central Government notification under Section 32, 
without specifying any timeline or minimum standards that such a policy must meet before 
private operators are licensed to construct or operate n uclear facilities. This sequencing is a 
significant governance concern. Radioactive waste management is not an operational 
afterthought — it is a fundamental safety, environmental, and intergenerational 
responsibility that must be planned and regulated fro m the earliest stages of facility design. 
The original Atomic Energy Act, 1962, reserved spent fuel management exclusively for the 
Government precisely in recognition of its extreme sensitivity and long -term consequences. 
Allowing private operators to begi n construction or operation without a legally binding, 
comprehensive, and publicly available waste management framework in place risks the 
development of ad hoc, inconsistent, and potentially unsafe waste handling practices that 
could have irreversible env ironmental consequences. The Committee therefore recommends 
that the Central Government should frame and publicly notify the radioactive waste 
management policy under Section 32 as a mandatory precondition before the first private 
nuclear licence is grante d under the SHANTI Act. This policy should specify standards for 
waste classification, storage, transportation, reprocessing, and long-term disposal, and should 
be subject to periodic review by AERB in consultation with the Central Pollution Control 
Board and relevant State authorities.

ATOMIC ENERGY REGULATORY BOARD 
 
The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) was established by the Government of India 
through a statutory order issued under Section 27 of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, with its primary 
mandate being to perform the regulatory and safety functions outlined in  Sections 16, 17, and 23 of 
the Act. AERB carries out various regulatory and safety functions such as specifying regulatory 
requirements and providing guidance to meet these requirements, granting licenses to facilities and 
activities, carrying out regulat ory oversight through regular safety reviews & assessment and 
inspections, monitoring compliance, taking enforcement actions as necessary, and confirming 
satisfactory states of emergency preparedness and response. In addition, AERB carries out as well 
as p romotes safety and regulatory research and interacts with relevant agencies at national and 
international level, disseminates information to keep public informed on relevant safety issues and 
carries out safety promotion activities. 
6.2 The Committee enqui red the  role played by  AERB as a facilitator of Research and 
Development of indigenous medical device  used in the field of Radiology. The Department

facilitator of Research and Development of indigenous medical device used in the field of 
Radiology. However, AERB is open for providing guidance on safety and regulatory requirements

obtaining regulatory approvals. Moreover, user guide lines on regulatory processes are available on

6.10 The Committee enquired that h ow does the structure and autonomy of India's AERB 
compare with n uclear regulators in countries like the Unit ed States (NRC) or France (ASN). The

without any external influence in its regulatory decision making. The Integrated Regulatory Review 
Service (IRRS) mission of IAEA held in 2015 has acknowledged the functional independence of 
AERB as a regulator. The recently enacted SHANTI Act 2025 provides statutory status to AERB 
by embedding it in the law. This legal framework est ablishes an independent regulatory body for 
issuance of safety authorization, in line with other countries such as the US and France. 
 
6.11 The Committee also desired to know how AERB is preparing to regulate emerging 
technologies like nuclear fusion or ad vanced small modular reactors (SMRs). The Department 
informed that AERB safety and regulatory requirements for licensing of NPPs are mostly 
technology neutral. In light of the evolving developments in the field of SMRs, AERB has 
conducted review of its exi sting regulatory requirements and concluded that the same regulatory 
framework can generally be applied for safety regulation of advanced reactors such as SMRs, 
except a few technology specific aspects for which review may be required when details of 
proposed sites and design of specific SMR is submitted to AERB. AERB also participates in 
various international forums to keep itself abreast about the developments in regulation of SMRs 
and suitably adopt them when required. Commercial use for Fusion technolog y is not expected to 
be in the near future. 
 
6.12  The Committee sought to know that f or groundbreaking technologies (e.g., MR -LINAC 
systems, proton therapy machines), how does AERB's regulator y framework adapt. Does it engage in 
pre-submission dialogues with manufacturers to guide the development process against safety norms? 
The Department informed that i n the past, AERB has handled licensing for first -of-its-kind facilities 
such as Proton Therapy Facilities & MR-LINAC systems. The approach adopted is as follows: Based 
on the initial intent submitted by the user institute for establishing facilities incorporating new 
technologies (e.g., MR -LINAC systems, proton therapy machines), AERB engages with the 
manufacturer to discuss the relevant technical and regu latory aspects. Subsequently, AERB 
constitutes expert committees for specific areas (e.g., facility design approval, quality assurance 
aspects, etc.) and conducts further discussions with manufacturers and other relevant stakeholders, as 
required. AERB als o reviews international literature and regulatory practices for similar facilities in 
other countries to develop appropriate regulatory requirements. Using this approach, AERB has 
successfully licensed first -of-its-kind facilities such as Proton Therapy Fa cilities and MR -LINAC 
systems in the country. AERB remains open to a dialogue with manufacturers/suppliers to provide 
guidance on safety and regulatory requirements. 
6.13 The Committee also asked that in the context of public health needs, how does AERB manage 
the balance between ensuring rapid deployment of essential radiology machines (like in rural areas) 
and maintaining an uncompromising, often time -consuming, safety review process. The Department 
replied that AERB has implemented a digital regulatory p latform eLORA (e -Licensing of Radiation 
Application) covering all types of consenting processes, inventory management of sources & 
equipment, inspection activities and non -compliance management. Most of the consenting and safety 
review processes w ith respect to radiology equipment are processed faster using rules embedded in 
the eLORA system while ensuring that the safety aspects are duly covered. This in turns ensures 
effective regulatory oversight for rapidly expanding radiology facilities. 
6.14 The Commi ttee asked regarding AERB's policy on the import and installation of 
refurbished/used radiology machines and w hat additional safeguards and testing requirements are in 
place to ensure their safety and performa nce are comparable to new units. The Committee was 
informed that a s per AERB policy, only refurbished or used radiology equipment that is not more 

48 
 
than seven years old is permitted for import. However, if manufacturer support for refurbishment is 
available, equipment up to ten years old may also be imp orted. AERB issues an operational license 
for such refurbished or used equipment only after verifying that its performance (i.e.QA test) is 
satisfactory. The QA requirements are same irrespective of nature of machine i.e. new/refurbished. 
 
6.15 The Committ ee enquired regarding AERB's mechanism for monitoring the long -term 
performance and safety of radiology machi nes in the field. The department replied that AERB

informed that AERB's role is to carry out safety reviews and approvals based on compliance with the

AERB is open for providing guidance o n safety and regulatory requirements to manufacturers. 
AERB's regulatory approvals for Radiology equipment are issued through AERB's eLORA (e -
Licensing of Radiation Application) system. eLORA system provides convenience of submission and

6.17 The Committee also enquired regarding AERB‘s role  in promoting ―Make in India‖ in the

that of the r egulator for radiation safety and it has no direct role as a promoter. However, AERB is 
open for providing guidance on safety and regulatory requirements to manufacturers. AERB 
participates in professional forums, delivers technical talks and conduct NCRI (National Conference 
on Regulatory Interface), which are attended by the equipment manufacturer. Such openness 
approach of AERB is helpful to the manufacturer for understanding the regulatory requirement and 
further submission to AERB for obtaining regulat ory approvals. Also, as elaborated earlier, AERB's

6.18 The Committee observes that providing guidance and participating in professional 
forums is a passive approach. The development of indigenous medical devices requires 
proactive and structured support. The Committee therefore recommends that AERB should 
establish a formal "Innovation Facilitation Cell" or a "Regulatory Sandb ox" framework. 
This would allow developers of indigenous radiology and radiotherapy devices to engage in 
early, confidential, and structured pre -submission dialogues with AERB experts. This 
formalizes the ad -hoc expert committee approach used for Proton Th erapy and makes it 
accessible for domestic R&D, helping them navigate safety norms from the design stage itself, 
thus reducing time-to-market. 
6.19 The Committee also recommends that to build greater trust and identify process 
bottlenecks, AERB should publ ish more granular performance data on its public dashboard. 
This could include: (a) TAT broken down by type of application (import vs. license vs. type 
approval), (b) TAT for "first -of-its-kind" technologies vs. standard equipment, and (c) the 

49 
 
number of applications that went through multiple review cycles. This aligns with the global 
best practice of regulatory transparency and helps stakeholders manage their own planning. 
6.20 The Committee further recommends that AERB should move towards a more 
dynamic, risk-based post-market surveillance system. This could involve u tilizing data from 
the eLORA system to identify trends in equipment performance, recurring non -compliances, 
or specific manufacturers/models that may require more frequent oversight.  AERB should 
establishing a clear, mandatory, and simple mechanism for users (radiologists, technicians) to 
report any safety -related malfunctions or "near misses" directly to AERB, creating a 
national database for learning and preventative action. 
6.21 The Committee no tes that the current coordination of AERB with CDSCO needs a 
more proactive approach. To provide clarity to the industry and avoid duplication, the two 
agencies should formalize their coordination through a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 
or a Memorandu m of Understanding (MoU). This document should clearly map the

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
 
BUDGET ANALYSIS 
 
The Committee urges the Ministry of Finance to sympathetically consider the 
Department's requirements at the R.E. stage, particularly for time -sensitive nuclear 
programmes.                                                                                                         (Para 2.6) 
         
The Committee observes that the  capital expenditure utilization vis -à-vis the Revised 
Estimate has been consistently high — ranging from 97% to 109% over the five -year period 
from 2020-21 to 2024 -25. The Committee notes, however, a persistent pattern of significant 
downward revision between the Budget Estimate and the Revised Estimate in capital 
allocations. This pattern, which recurs across multiple financial years, suggests systematic 
over-estimation at the budget preparation stage. To enhance financial discipline and project 
execution, the Committee recommends that the Department should adopt the following 
corrective measures: firstl y, Budget Estimates for capital schemes should be prepared based 
exclusively on projects that have received formal sanction, while proposals pending approval 
are tracked separately as a forward pipeline to ensure transparency in future planning; and 
secondly, a mandatory pre -budget review should be conducted to evaluate procurement 
readiness and contractor availability prior to the finalization of capital provisions. 
(Para 2.11) 
         
 The Committee notes certain significant anomalies in the head -wise expenditure data. 
The Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) recorded actual expenditure of Rs. 2,885.65 crore against 
an original Budget Estimate of merely Rs. 263.20 crore for 2025 -26 — representing 
expenditure of over ten times the budgeted amount, met through Revi sed Estimate 
adjustments and supplementary provisions. Similarly, Heavy Water Pool Management 
recorded actual expenditure of Rs. 3,000 crore against a Budget Estimate and Revised 
Estimate of nil. The Committee recommends that the Department should ensure t hat 
anticipated extraordinary payment cycles of this nature are explicitly reflected in the Budget 
Estimates with adequate explanatory notes, so as to present a true and complete picture of 
planned expenditure. 
 (Para 2.13) 
 
The Committee observes that the  significant gap between BARC's capital R&D 
Budget Estimate and actual utilization reflects a recurring pattern of over -estimation at the 
budget preparation stage, compounded by procedural delays in project execution. The near -
doubling of the capital allocation to Rs.1,800 crore in B.E. 2026-27 is a welcome recognition of 
BARC's expanded research mandate, but the Committee cautions that enhanced allocations 
must be matched with commensurate improvements in execution readiness. The Committee 
recommends that the Department should ensure that BARC's capital Budget Estimates are 
henceforth prepared strictly on the basis of sanctioned projects with verified procurement 
readiness, and that a formal mid -year review mechanism be instituted to identify and resolve 
execution bottlenecks before they result in year -end underutilization. The Committee also 
recommends that the contractor empanelment initiative be implemented expeditiously and 
extended to all secured DAE installations, so that procurement constraints unique  to nuclear 
establishments do not continue to impede timely capital expenditure. 
(Para 2.15) 
Regarding the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), the Committee 
has observed significant underutilization of capital R& D allocations, with actual expenditure 

58 
 
amounting to just Rs.49.42 crore against a Budget Estimate of Rs.225 crore and a Revised 
Estimate of Rs.67.86 crore for 2025 -26. While the Department attributed this to the 
completion of most capital projects in 2023 -24 and the sanctioning of new projects only in 
October 2025, the Committee views this as indicative of a deeper structural issue. The gap 
between the conclusion of one project cycle and the initiation of the next has resulted in a 
prolonged expenditure vac uum at a premier nuclear research institution. To prevent such 
disruptions to institutional productivity, the Committee recommends that the Department 
should plan for a steady stream of projects at IGCAR. 
(Para 2.16) 
 
The Committee examined the financial performance of Raja Ramanna Centre for 
Advanced Technology (RRCAT) and noted with concern the sharp downward revision of its 
capital R&D allocation from Rs. 178.60 crore (B.E. 2025 -26) to Rs. 63 crore (R.E. 2025-26) — 
a reduction of 64.7%. The Department informed the Committee that this revision was 
necessitated by the fact that B.E. 2025 -26 was prepared on the basis of proposals for new 
projects that were in various stages of the approval process but could not receive f inal 
sanction in time. The Committee strongly recommends that RRCAT, and all DAE 
institutions, should align their Budget Estimates strictly with projects that have received full 
sanction and for which procurement activities are ready to commence.  
(Para 2.17) 
 
The Committee is gravely concerned about the underfunding of uranium exploration 
activities. Uranium discovery and resource delineation are long -gestation activities with lead 
times of eight to twelve years between exploration and mine production. Any  reduction in 
exploration investment today will translate into a fuel supply bottleneck for India's nuclear 
programme a decade hence. The Committee strongly recommends that the full shortfall of 
Rs.118.18 crore in AMDER's capital allocation be restored at the Revised Estimate stage of 
2026-27. The Committee further recommends priority -based funding for AMDER for 
increased uranium and rare metal exploration to secure a stable domestic supply of nuclear 
fuel in alignment with India's long-term energy security objectives. 
(Para 2.19) 
 
The Committee notes with concern that BRIT's persistent underutilization in capital 
projects occurs in a context of rapidly growing demand for radioisotope -based diagnostics 
and therapy in India. Radioisotopes play a critical role  in the management of cancer, cardiac 
conditions, and other life -threatening diseases. The Committee recommends that BRIT 
should implement a quarter -wise, milestone-linked execution plan for its Rs.76 crore capital 
allocation for 2026-27.  
(Para 2.21) 
The Committee examined the budgetary utilization of Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut 
Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), the implementing agency for the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor 
(PFBR) at Kalpakkam. The head -wise data reveals that BHAVINI utilized only Rs. 50 crore 
against an R.E. of Rs. 150 crore and B.E. of Rs. 374 crore for 2025 -26 - a utilization of merely 
33.3% of the Revised Estimate. The B.E. for 2026 -27 has been set at Rs. 200 crore. The 
Committee observes that BHAVINI's severe underutilization is particularly con cerning given 
that approximately 70% of the PFBR core has been loaded as on February 2026. As 
commissioning activities accelerate towards First Approach to Criticality, BHAVINI's 
expenditure requirements will increase significantly. The Committee recommend s that the 
Department should prepare a quarter -wise cash flow plan for BHAVINI's Rs. 200 crore 
allocation for 2026-27, tied to specific commissioning milestones. 
(Para 2.22) 
 

59

head - from 149.63% of R.E. in 2024 -25 to a significant shortfall in 2025 -26 - reflects India's 
considerable dependence on a single foreign supplier for an operationally critical input. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should prepare a com prehensive medium-term 
strategy for diversification of nuclear fuel supply for KKNPP, including assessment of the

recommends that payment schedules under the inter -governmental arrangement be
