RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
CHAPTER II 
ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY OF EARTH 
SCIENCES 
 
ANALYSIS OF THE BUDGETARY TRENDS OF THE MINISTRY OF EARTH SCIENCES  
 
         The Committee notes that the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES ) had projected an 
outlay of ₹4371.54 crore to the Ministry of Finance under Demand No. 24 for the financial 
year 2026–27. However, the Ministry of Finance approved an outlay of ₹3789.23 crore, which 
is about 86.67 % of the projected amount. The Committee is of the view that the pattern and 
extent of fund utilization during the current financial year significantly influence the 
allocation made in the subsequent year. A careful examination of the Ministry‟s expenditure 
pattern over the years indicates that i t has not been able to fully utilize the outlays sanctioned 
to it. For instance, the Ministry was allocated an outlay of ₹3658.08 crore at the BE stage in 
2025–26, which was subsequently revised downward to ₹3388.27 crore at the RE stage. 
Further, the Ministry has been able to incur an expenditure of only ₹2826.83 crore up to 31 st 
January, 2026. This relatively slow pace of expenditure appears to have contributed to the 
reduction in allocation made to the Ministry in BE 2026 –27 vis-à-vis the projected outlay. The 
Committee also observes that the gap between the outlay projected by MoES to the Ministry 
of Finance and the allocation approved has widened over the years. The outlay allocated to 
the Ministry in BE 2023–24 constituted 99.43% of the projected outla y. In BE 2024–25, the 
allocation was 107.90% of the projected outlay , while in BE 2025–26 it accounted for 97.69% 
of the projected outlay . However, the allocation for the forthcoming financial year represents 
only 86.67% of the projected outlay , indicating  a comparatively lower level of budgetary 
provision against the projected requirement.  In view of the above, the Committee urges the 
Ministry of Earth Sciences to take necessary measures to improve the rate of budget 
utilization and strive to achieve full utilization of the allocated funds in the coming financial 
year, so as to avoid any reduction in future budgetary allocations.                                                                                                                                 
(Para 2.7) 
 
ASSESSMENT OF THE PATTERN OF BUDGET UTILIZATION BY THE MINISTRY OF 
EARTH SCIENCES 
The Committee notes with concern  the persistent underutilization of budgetary 
allocations by the Ministry of Earth Sciences over the past few years. An analysis o f the 
pattern of expenditure indicates that the utilization of funds has ranged between 83% and 
93% in recent years , and the Ministry has not been able to utilize the full budgetary 
allocation in any of the recent years. The Committee is of the view that such a pattern reflects 
a slow pace of expenditure and limited capacity to absorb the funds allocated , particularly 
under the Capital Head.  The Committee further observes that the reduction in allocation at 
the Revised Estimates stage , as seen in 2025 –26, h as been attributed by the Ministry to 
procurement delays, implementation challenges, site finalization issues, and other technical or 
operational constraints . While acknowledging that certain scientific and technological 
projects may involve complex proced ures, the Committee is of the firm opinion that it is the 
responsibility of the Ministry to anticipate such challenges and establish effective mechanisms 
to overcome them in a timely manner . The Committee also notes that the capital allocation 
has shown a declining trend in recent years, partly due to lower utilisation and the completion 
of certain major capital procurements. In the Committee‟s view, the persistent shortfall in 

73 
 
utilisation has also contributed to a comparatively lower allocation in BE 2026 –27. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry strengthen its planning, project 
management and financial monitoring mechanisms so as to ensure timely and efficient 
utilisation of allocated funds . The Ministry should institute periodic reviews of expenditure, 
particularly under capital-intensive projects, and take proactive steps to address procedural, 
technical and operational bottlenecks that delay implementation.                            ( Para 2.14)   
CHAPTER III 
ASSESSMENT OF THE SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY 
PRITHVI VIGYAN (PRITHVI) 
 
The Committee recommends developing advanced indigenous technologies for desalination 
plants that run on non -renewable energy. Deployed in coastal areas and cities, these plants 
would augment fresh water supplies to help address existing shortages.                                    
(para 3.17)  
The Committee acknowledges the significant role played by the PRITHVI (Prithvi 
Vigyan) Scheme  in strengthening India‟s capabilities in Earth System S ciences through its 
integrated focus on atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, geosciences and societal applications. 
The Committee notes that several Low-Temperature Thermal Desalination (LTTD) plants  
have been established in the Lakshadweep islands under the PRITHVI-OSMART initiative to 
address the critical issue of potable water availability for island communities. While the 
Committee recognizes the importance of these plants in ensuring sustainable drinking water 
supply, it also notes that the desalination pla nts currently operate using electricity generated 
through diesel generator sets, which power the island systems. Considering the environmental 
sensitivity of island ecosystems and the broader national commitment towards clean and 
renewable energy, the Comm ittee is of the view that reliance on diesel -based power sources 
should be progressively reduced. The Committee therefore recommends the Ministry to 
explore the feasibility of making these desalination plants eco -friendly by using sustainable 
power sources  such as solar energy, Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), or other 
suitable renewable energy technologies.              (Para 3.18)
  
The Committee also examined the proposal for establishing Maitri-II, a new research 
station in Antarctica to replace t he existing Maitri station, which was commissioned in 1989 
and has now exceeded its designed operational life. The Committee notes the Ministry‟s 
submission that the present station is facing structural deterioration and limitations in waste -
management and environmental compliance systems, making the establishment of a modern 
replacement station necessary to ensure safety, operational sustainability, and India‟s 
continued year -round scientific presence in Antarctica in accordance with evolving 
environmental norms under the Antarctic Treaty System. However, the Committee notes that 
the architectural and design consultant for the Maitri -II project has been selected through a 
global design competition and that the winning consortium comprises Ramboll Deutschlan d 
GmbH and bofArchitekten, Germany. In this regard, the Committee recalls that India‟s first 
Antarctic research station, Dakshin Gangotri, was constructed with the involvement of the 
Indian Army, demonstrating indigenous capability in undertaking complex o perations in 
extreme polar conditions. The Committee is therefore of the view that greater consideration 
could have been given to Indian firms with relevant engineering and infrastructure expertise 
in cold-weather construction technologies. Such an approac h could have contributed to cost 
savings while also providing impetus to the objectives of Make in India and promoting greater 
self-reliance in specialized polar infrastructure development. The Committee recommends 
that, in future projects of this nature, the Ministry explore ways to ensure greater 

74 
 
participation of Indian companies, either independently or through collaborations, so that 
domestic capabilities in polar infrastructure and extreme -environment engineering are 
further strengthened.                                                           (Para 3.19) 
 
DEEP OCEAN MISSION 
The Committee notes that the Deep Ocean Mission , launched in 2021, with an 
approved outlay of ₹4,077 crore , for a period of five years, is a flagship initiative aimed at 
strengthening India‟s capabilities in deep -sea exploration, resource assessment, marine 
biodiversity research and development of advanced ocean technologies. While the Committee 
acknowledges the efforts made by the Ministry and its institutions in progressing with certain 
components of the Mission, it observes with concern that the overall progress achieved so far 
does not appear commensurate with the objectives and timelines originally envisag ed. The 
Committee further notes that key components of the Mission, including the Samudrayaan 
programme and the development of an integrated deep -sea mining system for polymetallic 
nodules, are still incomplete. It is also observed that against the approve d project cost of 
₹4,077 crore, only about ₹1,445 crore has been utilised so far, which constitutes roughly 35 
per cent of the total project outlay. In the Committee‟s view, the pace of progress under 
certain critical verticals of the Mission needs to be s ignificantly accelerated to ensure that the 
intended outcomes are achieved within a reasonable timeframe. In this regard, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry establish clearly defined and measurable milestones under 
each of the six verticals of the Deep Ocean Mission. The Committee further recommends that 
specific timelines be fixed for the achievement of these targets, along with a structured 
monitoring mechanism to periodically review progress and address implementation 
bottlenecks.                                                                                                (para 3.30) 
MISSION MAUSAM 
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry under Mission Mausam, 
which aims to transform India into a “Weather-ready and Climate-smart” nation through the 
deployment of advanced observational systems, next -generation modelling, and improved 
weather forecasting and early warning mechanisms. The Committee notes the progress made 
in strengthening Doppler Weather Radar networks, operationa lizing advanced forecasting 
systems, developing AI -based weather interpretation tools, and establishing platforms for 
hyper-local weather information dissemination.  At the same time, the Committee expresses 
concern over the increasing incidence of extreme weather events, particularly cloudbursts, 
which in recent years have caused significant loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and 
disruption of livelihoods in several parts of the country, especially in mountainous and 
ecologically fragile regions. The C ommittee notes the Ministry‟s initiative to establish a state-
of-the-art cloud microphysics laboratory  at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology 
(IITM), Pune, and to deploy specialised observing systems in cloudburst -prone regions such 
as the North-Eastern States, the Western Ghats, and the Western Himalayas. The Committee 
recommends that these research efforts should be strongly oriented towards developing 
reliable forecasting capabilities and an effective early warning system for cloudburst events so 
that timely alerts can be issued to vulnerable communities and disaster management 
authorities.                                                    (para 3.41)
  
           The Committee further notes that ocean –atmosphere interactions play a crucial role in 
influencing weather and climate patterns, including the formation and intensification of 
cyclones and extreme rainfall events. In this regard, the Committee takes note of the proposal 
under consideration for the development of floating radar systems mou nted on buoys  to 

75 
 
enhance meteorological observations over oceanic regions where land -based radar coverage is 
limited. The Committee believes that such systems could significantly improve monitoring of 
cloud formation and rainfall dynamics over the seas and  strengthen cyclone detection and 
tracking capabilities.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to accord due 
priority to the development and deployment of floating radar observation systems and 
provide adequate financial and institutional suppo rt for this initiative under Mission 
Mausam.                                   (para 3.42) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should coordinate with bodies like 
Central Water Commission and Survey of India to develop scientific models for analyzing 
riverine water flow. This initiative would enable accurate flood forecasting, thereby 
mitigating damage, particularly in the nation's flood-prone regions.                         ( para 3.43)
  
CHAPTER IV  
ASSESSMENT OF THE FUNCTIONING OF THE INSTITUTIONS OF THE MINISTRY 
OF EARTH SCIENCES 
V ACANCIES 
The Committee observes that the Ministry of Earth Sciences is currently implementing 
three major national missions, namely Deep Ocean Mission, Prithvi Vigyan and Mission 
Mausam, which are of critical importance for advancing the country‟s capabilities in ocean 
exploration, weather and climate services,  and earth system science. The successful 
implementation of these missions depends significantly on the availability of adequate and 
skilled human resources across the Ministry and its affiliated institutions. However, a 
substantial number of vacancies exi st across different categories of posts in the Ministry and 
its institutions. The Committee has been informed that the Recruitment Rules for the entry -
level posts of the scientific cadre in the Ministry and its affiliated offices are under finalization 
in consultation with the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) . Further, the finalization 
of the sanctioned strength of the scientific cadre  is under consideration with the Department 
of Expenditure . The Ministry has also submitted that the Department of Per sonnel and 
Training (DoPT) is the cadre -controlling authority for administrative posts of the Ministry, 
except in the case of Multi-Tasking Staff (MTS) . The Committee is of the view that such a 
large number of vacancies, particularly in scientific and technical posts, could adversely affect 
the effective implementation of these critical national missions. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry pursue the matter vigorously with the concerned authorities, 
including UPSC, the Department of Expe nditure and DoPT, to expedite the finalization of 
recruitment rules, sanctioned strength and recruitment processes.                             (Para 4.4) 
INDIAN METEOROLOGICAL DEPARTMENT (IMD), NEW DELHI 
           The Committee notes that numerous advan ced technologies, including Artificial 
Intelligence, are being utilized globally to enhance the accuracy and affordability of weather 
forecasting. In this context, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should conduct a 
detailed outcome analysis of the  budgetary allocations made to the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD).                                                                                                         (Para 4.12)
  
         The Committee is of the opinion that accurate and timely weather prediction is critically 
important for a country like India , where a large segment of the population depends on 

76 
 
weather-reliant economic activities . The Committee has been informed that 48 Doppler 
Weather Radars (DWRs) are currently operational ac ross the country . However, the 
Committee observes that the existing network does not provide adequate coverage across 
several parts of the country , which may affect the accuracy and timeliness of short -range and 
nowcasting services, particularly for locali zed severe weather events. The Committee is of the 
view that DWRs are critical components of a modern weather observation system , as they 
provide high -resolution, real -time information on rainfall intensity, wind patterns, 
thunderstorms and severe weather systems. Expanding the DWR network across the country 
would significantly enhance forecasting capabilities, strengthen early warning systems, and 
support more effective disaster preparedness and response mechanisms. The Committee notes 
that under Mission M ausam, the Government has proposed the installation of an additional 
84 DWRs across the country to address the existing coverage gaps. The Committee further 
notes that the estimated expenditure for this expansion is approximately ₹942.57 crore . In 
view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may take necessary steps to 
ensure that the proposed additional Doppler Weather Radars are installed at the earliest  so 
that most parts of the country are adequately covered by the radar network. The Co mmittee 
further recommends that the required financial resources may be provided to IMD in a 
phased manner to facilitate timely implementation of the proposed expansion.   
(Para 4.13) 
         The Committee also notes that a large section of the public is unaware of the existence of 
Mausam app developed by IMD. Moreover, the user interface of the app is not very user 
friendly and pales in comparison to other popular apps in this domain. The Comm ittee 
therefore recommends that IMD  should take steps for populariz ation of the app. The 
Committee also recommends that IMD should improve the overall U ser Interface of the app 
to make it more appealing to the general public.                                                        (Para 4.14 ) 
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TROPICAL METEOROLOGY (IITM), PUNE 
        The Committee recognizes the significant role played by the Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM), Pune, as a premier national research institutio n engaged in advanced 
studies on the atmosphere, ocean and climate systems, particularly in improving weather and 
climate forecasts for the tropics and understanding the dynamics of the monsoon over India. 
The Committee notes the research undertaken by IIT M under Mission Mausam to examine 
the meteorological factors contributing to severe air pollution in Delhi during the winter 
months. In view of the continuing severity of air pollution in Delhi and the National Capital 
Region, the Committee is of the opini on that scientific research findings such as those 
generated by IITM are extremely valuable for informed policy -making and mitigation 
planning. The Committee therefore recommends that the research findings and analytical 
insights generated by IITM should b e shared regularly with relevant regulatory and policy -
making bodies , including the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Delhi Pollution 
Control Committee (DPCC), and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), as 
well as other concerned agencies.                 (Para 4.18) 
 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM RANGE WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF), 
NOIDA 
            The Committee notes the important role played by the National Centre for Medium 
Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida , in developing and oper ating advanced 
numerical weather prediction models for short -range, medium -range, extended -range and 
seasonal forecasts, which are widely used by various user agencies including the India 

77 
 
Meteorological Department. The Committee appreciates the development  of the High-
Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) forecasting system , which is designed for short -range 
prediction of rapidly evolving weather systems, particularly in complex terrains such as the 
Himalayan region. Considering the increasing occurrence of extre me rainfall and cloudburst 
events in the Himalayan region and the serious damage caused by such incidents in recent 
years, the Committee is of the view that strengthening scientific capabilities for their 
prediction and early warning is of critical importa nce. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to provide sustained support to NCMRWF for further development 
and operationalization of high -resolution modelling systems such as HRRR, including 
enhanced assimilation of radar and satellite observati ons over mountainous regions. The 
Committee further recommends that efforts be made to integrate the outputs of these 
advanced models with early warning dissemination systems so that actionable and timely 
alerts can be provided to disaster management authorities and vulnerable communities.  
(Para 4.25) 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR SEISMOLOGY (NCS), DELHI 
 The Committee notes that the National Centre for Seismology (NCS), Delhi , 
established in 2015, plays a critical role in monitoring seismic activity across the coun try, 
maintaining the National Seismological Network, conducting earthquake hazard assessments, 
and supporting research in seismology, earthquake precursor studies, and deep borehole 
investigations. However, the Committee is constrained to note that even af ter nearly a decade 
of its establishment, the NCS does not have any sanctioned posts of its own and continues to 
function with personnel drawn on a loan basis from the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) 
and the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The Com mittee finds it difficu lt to 
understand why a specializ ed national institution entrusted with such crucial responsibilities 
is still operating without a dedicated cadre of scientific, technical, and administrative staff.  
While noting the Ministry‟s submiss ion that proposals for the creation of dedicated posts for 
NCS have been submitted under the PRITHVI scheme, the Committee strongly recommends 
that the matter be pursued on priority and that the approval process be expedited.                                      
(Para 4.29) 
INDIAN NATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN INFORMATION SYSTEM (INCOIS), 
HYDERABAD 
           The Committee recognizes the critical role played by the Indian National Centre for 
Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)  in providing ocean information and advisory services 
that support fisheries, maritime operations, coastal management and disaster preparedness. 
The Committee is of the view that a robust and comprehensive ocean observation network is 
essential for improving the accuracy and reliability of ocean forecasts, early warning systems 
and long -term marine research.  The Committee notes that there remain long -standing 
observational gaps in near  shore wave measurements along several parts of the Indian 
coastline. In this regard, the Wave Monitoring Along Near shore (WAMAN)  project has 
played an important role in generating real -time coastal wave observations that support 
operational wave forecasting, early warning services, maritime safety and scientific research. 
However, the Committee observes that the present WAMAN network covers only selected 
segments of the coastline. The Committee therefore recommends that the network of wave 
buoys under WAMAN be progressively expanded to cover the entire Indian coastline so that a 
more comprehensive and reliable near shore observation system can be established.                                                                        
(Para 4.38) 

78 
 
        The Committee also notes that coastal regions in the country remain relatively u nder-
observed, with limited availability of physico -chemical, biological and fisheries -related data. 
The absence of observations for several parameters constrains the accuracy of ocean 
information and advisory services and limits the effectiveness of forec asting systems. In this 
context, the Committee emphasizes the importance of establishing regional shore stations 
equipped with appropriate laboratory and monitoring facilities to support long -term coastal 
observations, data analysis, model validation and c apacity building. The Committee is of the 
view that strengthening coastal observation infrastructure through an expanded WAMAN 
network and the establishment of shore stations will significantly improve ocean forecasting 
capabilities and generate valuable l ong-term datasets. The Committee therefore recommends 
that the Ministry provide adequate financial support to INCOIS for strengthening the 
WAMAN network and for establishing the proposed regional shore stations in a time -bound 
manner.                                     (Para 4.39) 
CENTRE FOR MARINE LIVING RESOURCES AND ECOLOGY (CMLRE), KOCHI 
        The Committee notes that the Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel  (FORV) 
Sagar Sampada, which serves as the backbone of the Marine Living Resources programme 
implemented by the Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), was 
commissioned in 1984 and has been in service for more than four decades. The Committee is 
concerned that the ageing of the vessel has resulted in several operational limitations and that, 
in its current condition, the vessel may remain operational for deep-sea surveys for only about 
seven more years. In view of these limitations and considering the growing requirements of 
deep-sea research under programmes such as the D eep Ocean Mission and the PRITHVI 
Scheme, the Committee strongly feels that the country requires a modern and advanced 
Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel capable of supporting expanded scientific 
observations in deep and distant waters. Given that F ORV Sagar Sampada is already nearing 
the end of its operational life, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
necessary procedural formalities and take time -bound steps for the acquisition and 
construction of the new vessel. The Committee i s of the view that the new Fishery and 
Oceanographic Research Vessel should be built and commissioned at the earliest, preferably 
within the next two to three years, so that India‟s marine research programmes are not 
adversely affected due to the declining operational capability of the existing vessel.                                                                                              
(Para 4.44) 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR POLAR AND OCEAN RESEARCH (NCPOR), GOA 
        The Committee takes note of India‟s growing engagement in the Arctic through scientific 
expeditions, international collaborations, and the operation of the Himadri research station in 
Svalbard. The Committee observes that polar research has acquired increasing significance in 
recent years due to its direct relevance to global climate systems, ocean circulation, sea -level 
rise and their impact on weather patterns, including the Indian monsoon. The absence of a 
dedicated ice-class Polar Research Vessel has be en a major constraint in expanding India‟s 
polar research activities, particularly in the wider Arctic Ocean. The Committee notes with 
satisfaction that in -principle approval has already been accorded by the Department of 
Expenditure for the acquisition of a Polar Research Vessel with ice-breaking capabilities at an 
estimated cost of ₹2,329.40 crore. In view of the strategic and scientific importance of this 
project, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the remaining procedural 
formalities an d ensure that adequate financial resources are made available so that the 
project progresses in a time -bound manner. The Committee further recommends that, 
wherever feasible, Indian shipbuilding firms should be actively involved in the construction of 

79 
 
the Polar Research Vessel. Such an approach would not only strengthen domestic 
shipbuilding capabilities but also contribute to the objectives of promoting indigenous 
manufacturing and technological self-reliance in specialized marine infrastructure.                                                                                                                          
(Para 4.50) 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY (NIOT), CHENNAI 
         The Committee notes that the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) has 
transferred around 40 technologies between 2020 –26, generating a total revenue of ₹1.64 
crore. The Committee expresses concern that these technologies are being transferred at 
relatively low prices compared to their commercial potential. It is o bserved that private 
partners often earn significant profits from these technologies, while the originating public 
institutes receive only a marginal share of the value created. The Committee understands that 
there is no robust mechanism to verify whether the benefits of these low -cost technology 
transfers reach the intended target users, and that the fees for renewal of licenses after expiry 
remain undefined. In view of this, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Earth 
Sciences should adopt a more competitive, market-aligned pricing framework for technology 
transfer. Licensing fees should reflect the true commercial value, uniqueness, and societal 
impact of publicly funded technologies. The Committee further recommends the 
establishment of clear pro cedures and norms for technology valuation and licensing, with the 
National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and the technology developer jointly 
determining fees. To ensure transparency, accountability, and proper utilization of publicly 
funded technologies, all technology transfer agreements should be subjected to periodic third -
party audits, and the outcomes of such audits should govern future licensing and renewal 
terms.                                      (Para 4.58)

meeting on April 16, the modalities of the working of the Committee were discussed. On April 20, 21

queries raised by the Hon'ble Members on various aspects of the Space Progr amme to enable it to

                                                                                                REPORT 
General Background 
  
1.         The purpose of the Indian space programme  is to make India self-r eliant in regard to the 
applications of space technology thereby ensuring ra pid progress in socio-economic sectors: The space 
programme is broa d-based and its activities range from development of space launch systems,
sophisticated satellites, their o perations in the orbit to the conduct of extensive a pplications oriented

2.         Under the existing space programme s, space services in the areas of communication,
meteorology, resources surveys and. management, incl uding the development of  associated satellites,
launch vehicles, and ground system s are being looked after by th e Department of 8pace. The
Department of Space and the Space Commission were set up in 1972. 
 
3.         India has, by now, successfully launche d 16 satellites starting wi th Aryabhatta in 1975. INSAT
satellites have virtually revoluti onised telecommunications and TV and radio broadcasting in India,
enabling more than 75% of the country population to  have access to educat ional and entertainment
programmes on TV. The applic ation of IRS series of satellites is for carrying out remote sensing from
space for providing vital inputs for management-of land and water resources, and for enabling integrated
development of strategies at micro level for overall development of the nation. 
4.         A major achievement in India's space ca pabilities was demonstrated through the first successful
launch of SLV-3 in July, 1980. Th e successful launch of the Augm ented Satellite Launch Vehicle 
(ASLV) on May 20, 1992 is a very si gnificant milestone in the deve lopment of indigenous launch
capability. It has not only validated all the modifi cations carried out, base d on the detailed failure
analysis of the previous two un successful ASLV flights, but also  has proved, in flight, a number o f
important advanced, technologies needed for the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and the
Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV). 
5.         Despite some failures, our space pr ogramme has achieved new heights with the successful
launch and operationalisation of the indigenously built INSAT-2A whic h has enabled the Indian Space 
Programme to provide uninterrupted and enhanced services in the vital area of communications,
television, broadcast and meteorology including disaster warning. INSAT-2A was originally intended to 
be a test spacecraft as it was w holly developed and built in the country. However, on launch it has
proved to be so totally successful that it has now become a part of the INSAT operation system. 
6.         The Committee applauds the objective of  self-reliance in the space  programme and feels happy 
over the fact that the Department ha s learnt from its past  failures and carried out modifications for its
future system. The Committee has noted in particular, that the De partment of Space has evolved a
mechanism to go into various aspect s of the failure of the missions undertaken by it earlier and would
take suitable corrective measures while formulating future programmes.

 programmcs initiated by the Department. On its sitting held on April 5, the Secretary of the Department replied to the

REPORT
1. The Indian Space programme is geared to achieve to goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national development
 Its main thrust areas are: (a) satellite communications for various applications: (b) Satellite based radio and television,
 broadcast and networking: (c) Satellite remote sensing for resources survey and management, environmental monitoring and
 meteorological services: and (d) development and operationalisation of indigenous satellite and launch vehicles for providing
 these space services.
2. In his presentation while delineating the salient features of the Indian Space Programme, the Secretary of the Department of
 Space (DOS) assured the Committee that the Department of Space will continue to endeavour to make the best possible use of
 space technology in building a modern India by taking the benefits of space applications to the common man and to the
 remotest comers of the country. The Department has achieved significant success in the development and application of
 Space technology in such vital areas as telecommunications, television broadcast meteorological services including disaster
 warning and in providing information related to agriculture, forestry, water resources and mineral. Besides highlighting the
 achievements of the Department during the year 1993-94, the Secretary of the Department informed the Committee about the
 programmes/projects which the Department intends to undertake during the year 1994-95.
3. After listening to the presentation made by the Secretary of the Department, the Committee examined the budgetary
 allocations made for various programmes failing within the mandate of the Department. While examining the Demands for

4. The budget Estimates of the Department of Space for the year 1994-95 are placed at Rs. 755 crores, of which Rs. 600 crores
 constitute the plan component and Rs. 155 crores from the non-plan component. The total outlay projected for 1994-95 is Rs.
 36.93 crores more than the Revised Estimates for 1993-94. The increase in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 is mainly on
 account of additional provision made for GSLV project, IRS-p2 Project, indigenisation efforts, and general civil works and
 housing; the increased needs under the heads are partly offset by lesser requirements for PSLV, ASLV-C, IRS-IB, IRS-IC &
 ID projects and for advance action and parallel ordering. The Committee is happy to note that as high as 80% of the total
 budgetary outlay has been earmarked for plan expenditure and only 20% for non-plan expenditure.
5. While the voted grant, for the Department during the year 1991-92 was Rs. 509.30 crores, only Rs. 46.10 crores  could be
 utilised. Similarly, during 1992-93 only Rs. 490.92 crores could be utilised while the voted grant was Rs. 510.08 crores.
 During1993-94 the Department hoped to utilise the entire voted grant but had to surrender Rs. 14.00 crores at the end of the
 year. When asked about the reasons for the under utilisation of funds during these year the Committee was informed that the
 surrender of funds were mainly due to economy instructions issued by the Government in 1991-92, and postponement of
 various payments which the Department had to make because of unforeseen problems which were beyond the control of the
 Department. Rs. 14.00 crores had to be surrendered in 1993-94 due to sudden termination of the agreement for cryogenic
 technology transfer from Russia. As regards economy instructions under which the Department had to surrender money, the
 Committee would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation made in its First Report that any surrender of funds under
 economy drive should not starve the ongoing space projects under plan because any setback suffered by the projects Schedule
 will have a chain effect on the future programmes. 
 
* For summary of the Demands for Grants, See Schedule
 
            The committee is happy over the fact that the gap between budgetary allocation and actual utilization is gradually
 coming down.  From Rs. 49.20 crores in 1991-92 and Rs. 19.16 crores in 1992-93, the amount which could not utilized came
 down to Rs. 14.00 crores in 1993-94.  The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to utilize the budgetary
 allocation fully during the year 1994-95.
 
6. Out of the total approval Plan outlay of Rs. 1804.00 crores for the Department of Space for the Eighth Five Year Plan
 period, the total outlay for the first three years of the Eighth plan comes to Rs. 1530.38 crores. The Department is, therefore,
 left with a sum of Rs. 273.62 crores for the remaining two years of the Eighth plan period. The plan allocation for the year
 1994-95 (BE) of the Department is Rs. 600.00 crores. When a specific question was asked regarding the Plan outlay approved
 by the Planning commission for the Department of space for the Eighth Plan period, the Committee was informed that
 initially Rs. 1,804.00 crores was approved for this period, now the Planning commission has indicated that Rs. 3500/- crores
 will be made available to Department   through the annual plan allocations. Taking note of this the Committee reiterates its
 recommendation made in the first report while examining the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space that the
 Government should agree to the outlay of Rs. 3,500.00 crores projected by the Department of Space for the entire Eighth plan
 period.
7. The Committee sought further clarifications on the budgetary allocations for the various progmmmes/projccts/centres/units,
 etc. The Secretary, Department  of Space gave detailed replies and explained to the Committee that the Department of Space
 follows the concept of Zero Base Budgeting. Every year, very detailed reviews are carried out at different levels in the
 organisation, to arrive at the requirements of funds for each of the programme, scheme, etc. taking into account the progress
 achieved in the past, targets and schedules envisaged for the future and the minimum essential needs of cash flow for the
 current year. This review ensures proper prioritiisation  of the activities. For every project, the annual cashflow requirements
 are worked out based on the total cost and development schedule. In the initial period, the Secretary of the Department
 informed, the expenditure picks up slowly, followed by larger requirements in the subsequent period. The expenditure then
 tapers off towards the end of the project period. The committee was, satisfied by the explanation furnished by the Secretary of
 the Department and was happy to note that none of the programmes/projects of the Department is going to suffer adversely
 and this includes even those programmes for which there have been made comparatively lower allocations for the year 1994-
95.
POLAR SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE (PSLV)
8. The development of PSLV is an important component of the overall space proramme for acquiring indigenous capability for
 launching IRS satellites (100 kg. class) into Polar sun synchronous orbit. The Committee wanted to know whether a sum of
 Rs. 0.91 crores would be sufficient for taking care of the preparations for the next flight of PSLV D2 which is slated to be
 launched in 1994-95. The Secretary of the Department explained to the Committee that out of the sanctioned cost of Rs.
 414.96 crores for this project,          Rs. 409.58 crores had already been spent up to March 1993. He further informed that the
 PSLV D2 systems have already been realised and the launch is expected during 1994. With regard to the continuation of
 PSLV beyond D2 a separate project has been approved for PSLV-D3 at a cost of Rs. 48.00 crores. Rs. 5.00 crores have been
 provided in the budget for 1994-95 under the head PSLV-D3/D4.

9. The first development flight of PSLV took place on September 20, 1993 but could not place the IRS-IE satellite into the
 orbit as the flight became sub-orbital. When the Committee asked the reasons of the failure and expenses involved the
 Secretary of the Department said that the first flight of the PSLV was itself almost a success. He informed that the failure
 analysis committee set up by the Government after reviewing the entire gamut of flight results achieved from PSLV-D1
 launch, has concluded that "all the stages and their sub-systems have performed very well except for the software
 implementation error. The correction for the same, as well as other minor recommendations of the Expert Committee which
 went into the failure of PSLV-D1, have been incorporated. The total cost involved was about Rs. 45.00 crores. The Secretary
 told the Committee that through the successful development of PSLV, India will be for the first time, able to realise a state-of-
the-art satellite launch vehicle which will not only prove commercially viable in the global market but also pave the way for
 the realisations of 60% of the GSLV systems. In view of the details furnished by the Department, the Committee feels that the
 first developmental flight of the PSLV was, in fact, not a total failure as all the major rocket motors worked perfectly and
 practically all the secondary control motors worked very well. Though the mission of injecting IRS-IE into sun-synchronous
 orbit could not be achieved, most of the technologies developed for the PSLV were however, proven. The committee hopes
 that gaining from the findings of the failure analysis committee, the Department would initiate suitable remedial steps so as to
 achieve success in launching its next flight of PSLV for which preparations are already on.
 
Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV)
 
10. The Department is also working for the development, of the GSLV which is capable of launching 2,500 kg. class
 communication satellites into geostationary transfer orbit. About the progress of this project the Committee was informed that
 the work relating to the subsystem configurations and the requirements for the augmentation of the PSLV mobile service
 tower of SHAR are finalised. Also, actions have been initiated for hardware fabrication using Indian industries. The civil
 works at SHAR have already commenced and detailed design reviews of various systems have also been completed. The
 liquid hydrogen production facilities are established and commissioning trials are in progress. A sum Rs. 256.67 crores has
 been spent up to March 1993 towards fabrication, of the subsystem for  S125 Booster stage, L 40 strapons, Liquid Second
 Stage, Avionics, Stage Auxiliary systems, Control Power Plant, Test Facilities and Augmentation of the launch complex,
 including the milestone payments made to Russia for the cryo Engine and stage.
 
Cryo-technology
 
11. The Committee expressed its anxiety over the realisation of cryo technology indigenously and wanted to know about the
 present state of the programme. The Secretary of the Department informed that one of the objectives of the, Indian Space
 Programme is to achieve the capability to launch a satellite into geosynchronous orbit. Achievement of this capability is
 crucial for the propose of maintaining services like telecommunications, weather forecasting and broadcasting. As the country
 aims at launching several INSAT class of satellites in near future, it is necessary to develop our own cost-effective launches.
 For this, acquisition of hardware and  technology pertaining to cryogenic engine is of vital importance. Development of
 cryogenic technology has taken about 10 to 15 years in the developed countries and involves a huge investment.  It was,
 therefore, thought that if the segments containing cryo engine and related technology were obtained from other countries,
 India could acquire greater capability in about 5 years with hardly any risk of failure. This would also avoid delays. In 1986,
 with an allocation of Rs. 16.30 crore project activity started for developing cryo technology for GSLV and a one tonne class
 sub-scale engine using liquid oxygen and gaseous hydrogen was successfully fired. Studies have aim been undertaken in
 various related disciplines such as design of turbo pump, fabrication of milled thrust chamber, etc. In August 1990, the Space
 Commission approved a plan for the development of cryo engines and related technology as part of the GSLV programme
 relying on  indigenous  capabilities. At the  same time,  GLAVKOSMOS  of  the Soviet Union offered the technology to India
 including supply two stages for Rs. 235 crores. This was approved as the offer was within the scope of the originally
 envisaged GSLV project cost. In May 1992, however, USA imposed sanctions on ISRO and GLAVKOSMOS for a period of
 two years. ISRO and GLAVKOSMOS pointed out that the agreement did not come under the purview of MTCR and the use
 of cryogenic upper stage, as part of the GSLV, was only for launching geosynchronous satellites for peaceful purpose. Up to
 October 1993, the agreement with GLAVKOSMOS was progressing satisfactorily, but due to the pressure of US on Russia,
 GLAVKOSMOS invoked the force majaure clause on October 16,1993, as a result of which the transfer of technology and
 training stopped. Further negotiations between the GLAVKOSMOS and ISRO have now resulted in a modified agreement
 approved by both the Governments. Apprising the Committee of the details of the modified contract, the Secretary of the
 Department told that, in addition to the originally planned two cryo stages, two more flight stages and two ground models
 would be supplied in lieu of the technology transfer within the original agreement cost of Rs. 235 crores. ISRO has also
 exercised the option to buy 3 additional cryo stages at a cost of US $ 3 million each as negotiated in the original contract. The
 Committee was also informed that, for this programme, Government has approved an outlay of Rs. 245 crores after taking
 into account the provision already available for GSLV. The first indigenous built cryo stage, as informed by the Secretary of
 the Department, is expected in the year 1998-99. The Committee feels that with the experience and knowledge that the

Groundwater targeting
 
12.       Remote sensing is an important aspect of space technology which has proved useful in many areas such as flood
 monitoring, mapping forest cover and wastelands, drought assessment, groundwater targetting, fisheries forecast, etc. Several
 remote sensing application projects are being carried out by       the Department of Space and the user Departments as part of
 the Remote Sensing Application Mission (RSAM). The Committee evinced keen interest in application projects in the areas
 of groundwater targetting and fisheries forecast. As regards use of remote sensing in water resource management, the
 Committee was told that use of Space based imageries are of great importance in conservation and optimal use of water in
 India.  These are: predication of snow melt runoff; identification of ground water potential both in terms of quantity and
 quality; assessment of causes of pollution of water; sedimentation, etc.  It was also explained to the Committee that by the
 range of information obtained from Space imageries on types of soil, geomorphology, water, and wasteland. Watershed
 characteristics land use, agricultural, meteorological and forestry information, etc. a long-term strategy for land and water
 conservation can be chalked out to combat drought. The Secretary of the Department also informed  the Committee that under
 the Integrated Mission for Sustainable Development (IMSD), pilot studieson land and water resources in some drought prone
 districts were undertaken. Encouraged by the results,        this study was recommended to be extended to additional districts in
 the country which are perennially affected by drought, floods; as also certain other areas which fall within hill and tribal
 regions. These  districts have to be covered under three phases. In Phase-1, 6 districts have been covered for which data have
 already been generated and implementation taken up.* 15 Districts are proposed to be covered in Phase-II for which Action
 Plans am being finalised.** In Phase III, 136 districts are proposed to be covered for which study has been initiated and
 Action Plans would be finalised within a period of 3-4 years. *** The Committee was also informed that
 hydrogeomorphological maps obtained from remote sensing imagery have been utilised for identification of ground water
 potential zones for all the districts in the country on a mapping scale of 1:250,000 under the National Drinking Water Mission
 and these maps were given to the Ministry of Rural Development. For some of the problem districts, large scale maps have
 also been prepared. This activity of Department has led to a great success in identifying ground water. The Committee was
 told that as against the success rate of 40-45% achieved by the traditional method, borewells drilled on the basis of satellite
 data have led to a success rate of 90-95%. It proves the efficacy and commercial viability of the Space based data in this
 regard.While commending the efforts of the Department initiated under the IMSD which cover at present 45% of the
 geographical area of the country, the Committee feels that the Government should make available more funds through public
 finance institutions like banks, insurance companies etc. so that more area can be covered under this programme in view of
 the efficacy and the cost-effectiveness of the technology.
 
Potential Fisheries Zones (PFZs)
 
13. The Committee was informed that data derived from satellite imageries are also utilized to identify Potential Fisheries
 Zones (PFZs). The PFZs charts are prepared from the sea surface temperature data derived from satellite imageries. The PFZ
 information obtained from satellite imageries is, at present, disseminated through the AIR, in the local language, for the
 benefit of fishermen; and it has been found that generally fishermen who make use of this information are able to increase
 their catches by 2 or 3 times. The Department agreed with the Committee that adopting method for identifying the
 phytoplankton concentration would further improve the accuracy of prediction of PFZs. The Department of Space is
 coordinating its efforts with the Department of Ocean Development to develop an ocean colour monitor payload which can be
 incorporated on board the IRS Satellites. This could help in identifying phytoplankton which is the main source of food for
 many types of fishes. The Committee, while appreciating the efforts of the Department in the area of making available
 satellite based data for identifying PFZs, feels that the Department may also evolve a suitable programme to effectively tap
 the potential of space based information for deep-sea fishing. The Committee recommends that the Department should accord
 priority to the designing and developing the ocean colour monitor payload which could be put on board future IRS satellite as
 this would lead to more accurate predictions about PFZs.
 
Indigenisation
 
14. Space technology being one of the most advanced and useful area ideally calls for self-reliance and a significant effort to
 produce file systems, sub-systems and products indigenously. The Committee wanted to know as to how much of

 satellites and  launch vehicle, all systems are realised indigenously, including design, fabrication, testing and integration. In
 case of satellites the percentage of value of imported componcnts is about 50%. For the launch vehicle projects, the

The Committee is happy tonote that achieving self reliance in Space Technology is one of the vowed aims of the Department,

The Committee feels that in view of procurements of some of the components from abroad becoming increasingly difficult,

Linkages with Industries
 
15. Establishing linkages with industries has been one of the major thrusts of the Department of Space. The Department has
 transferred several technologies to Indian industries. The Committee wanted to know as to what specific actions have been
 initiated to strengthen the linkages with industries. The Secretary of the Department informed that, from the very beginning,
 concerted efforts have been made to involve the Indian industry, both in the private and public sector, in the Space
 programme . There are, at present, about 500 industries, most of them in the private sector, contributing to the space
 programme. Flow of funds from space programme to the industry is to the tune of Rs. 2.50 crores annually. Major space
 hardware for PSLV and GSLV, which includes hardware for the Cryogenic segment have been contracted to industry,
 including those in private sector such as L&T, Walchand Industries, Godrej, NOCIL, Andhra Sugar etc. So far, 216
 technologies/processes developed under the space programme have been transferred to industry. The expertise built up, and
 the infrastructure established, in these industries are now being commercially exploited. The Committee was further told that
 the Department had earned Rs. 15 lakhs in 1991-92, Rs 19 lakhs in 1992-93 and Rs. 25 lakhs in 1993-94 from royalties and
 nominal technology fee from recipients of the spin-off technologies. The Committee notes that though the earnings of the
 Department on this score appear to be meagre, this has, however, got a multiplier effect. The Committee is happy to note that
 the money so earned is being ploughed back for R & D and technology development.
 
Linkages, with Universities
 
16.  Space science research under the Indian Space Programme encompasses a wide spectrum of activities including study of
 cosmic rays, astronomical investigations, using space and ground based systems, study of meteorites and lunar samples and
 physical observations of sun. Another major branch of activity relates to the study of the earth's atmospheric system through
 rockets, balloons and orbiting space systems. When Committee asked if there was any programme for starting post-graduate
 courses in atmospheric sciences in Universities, the Secretary, Department of Space told that apart from what is already
 ongoing, post-graduate courses and research in atmospheric sciences have been taken up by the Gujarat University in
 Ahmedabad, Kerala University in Thiruvanthapurarm and SV university Tirupati, which draw support from the Centres of the
 Department of Space located at these places. About 100 universities participated actively in the workshop on atmospheric
 sciences, organised at Tirupati recently, as part of the utilisation programme of MST (Mesosphere-Stratosphere-
Troposlghere) Radar. The Committee was further informed that under the sponsored Research Programme-- (RESPOND) the
 Department of Space has been promoting research projects in space technology/science/applications since 1976. So far, more
 than 250 projects have been funded in 75 Universities from all parts of the country. Three space technology cells have already
 been established at Bangalore, Madras and Bombay for ensuring advanced research in some of the critical areas. Efforts have
 been made to establish space technology cells in IIT, Kharagpur and BIT, Ranchi. Space Science Education Centre has been
 established at Ahmedabad. The Punjab State Remote Sensing Centre has been established as part of the Punjab agricultural
 University. Under the scheme for promoting remote sensing technology in educational curricula, both at college and school
 level, action has been taken jointly with UGC and NCERT. Under the IRO Geosphere-Biosphere programme, Universities are
 being encouraged to work in several related research areas. Jadavpur University has been involved in some Space science and
 technology (including Onboard processor development) areas. The Committee, while appreciating the efforts of the
 Department in promoting academic linkages, emphasises that there is a need to cover more universities at least by starting
 post-graduate courses in space/atmospheric sciences with a view to preparing more and more scientists who could assist in the
 area of space R & D.

GRAMSAT
 
GRAMSAT is a satellite system which intends to provide useful information to the people particularly in the rural
 areas by broadcasting development oriented programmes in the field of education, rural development, health, etc. It is
 envisaged under this programme to provide 6 to 8 TV channels for this purpose. The Committee noted that the department
 could utilize a sum of Rs. 10 lakhs  which was only one-tenth of the total amount provided in the budgetary outlay for this
 programme for the year 1993-94. For the year 1994-95 budget estimates for this programme are kept again at Rs. 1.00 crore.
 The Committee wanted to know as to how the Department proposes to utilise the funds provided for this project.  The
 Secretary, Department of Space informed that since the GRAMSAT project is yet to be defined, and formally sanctioned by
 the Government, the budgetary provision is only notional. While it is possible to define the satellite now, it is to be ensured
 that the user ministries (Rural Development, Human Resources Development, Information & Broadcasting, Health etc.) are
 geared up with facilities and software on the ground for its utilisation. Efforts are under way in this regard. The Committee is
 of the view that the GRAMSAT project can play a meaningful role in the lives of our people, particularly those living in the
 remote and rural areas. The Committee, therefore, would like the Department of Space to give full information about the
 potential of this project to the Ministries/Departments (both at the Centre and the States), which are concerned with
 socio­economic development. Such a contact would enable the Department to develop proper formats for the utilisation of
 the GRAMSAT system, when it is implemented, hopefully soon.
 
Second launch pad
 
18. The committee noted that Rs. 3.00 crores provided for the development of second launch pad and common facilities at
 Sriharikota for PSLV and GSLV launches could not be utilised during the year 1993-94. Budgetary outlay for the purpose for
 the yea
r 1994-95 has been kept at Rs. 2.00 crores. The Committee enquired about the non-utilisation of the amount sanctioned
 during the year 1993-94 for developing a second launch pad. The Committee was informed that to meet the immediate
 requirement of the GSLV, the Department had decided to augment the existing PSLV launch pad by adding the Cryogenic
 fluid handling facility. However, in view of the increasing number of launches per year, the need to have a second launch pad
 cannot be ignored. The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that due priority should be accorded to the development of the
 second launch pad at SHAR.
 
Housing for staff
 
19. The Committee asked the Department as to why the percentage of satisfaction of housing for scientific and technical staff
 was only 29.8% and why the funds provided for this purpose for the year 1993-94 could not be utilised fully. The Secretary,
 Department of Space informed the Committee that the aim of the Department at present is to provide at least 50% satisfaction
 for its staff. The funds provided, however, could not be utilised fully because longer time was taken in planning the activity in
 procuring the necessary statutory clearances. The Committee is of the view that providing accommodation near the work
 place attracts high quality talents and increases the efficiency of personnel working in any organization. The Committee,
 therefore, feels that the Department should make earnest efforts to achieve the target of providing 50% satisfaction for its
 employee within a reasonable period of time.
 
20. After making a detailed Scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space and assessing the progress of
 various important Programmes and projects administered by it the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of
 Rs. 755.00 crores, as sought by the Department of Space for the year 1994-95, under demand No. 88, are in order and may be
 approved.

NEW DELHI;
April 24, 2002   
                      C. RAMACHANDRAIAH, 
Chairman,
Committee on Science & Technology,
Environment & Forests.
 
R E P O R T
1.         The Space Commission and Department of Space (DOS) were set up in 1972 to promote the development and application of
 Space science & technology for national development. The DOS is responsible for implementing the policies framed by Space
 Commission.  These are carried out through Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Grant-in-aid institutions.  ISRO has
 established Nine Centres/Units for carrying out research and development activities as well as for undertaking various projects and
 programmes in the area of Satellites, Launch Vehicles, Space applications and Space science research.
2.         The Indian Space programme is characterized by a vision to use space technology for national development.  The primary
 objective of the Space Programme has been to establish operational space services in a self-reliant manner in the thrust areas of
 satellite communications, satellite based information to assist in Survey/management of natural resources and satellite meteorological
 applications.  The indigenous development of satellites, launch vehicles and associated ground segment for providing these services
 is integral to these objectives.
3.         The Indian space programme has established two indigenously built operational space systems, namely, the Indian Remote
 Sensing Satellites (IRS) and the Indian National Satellite System (INSAT).  The constellation of Indian Remote Sensing Satellites
 comprises of five satellites viz., IRS-1B, IRS-P3, IRS-1C, IRS-1D and India’s first oceanographic satellite (IRS-P4) providing a
 range of spatial resolutions, spectral resolutions and coverage cycle.  The IRS system is among the best in the world for generating
 information useful for natural resources management besides providing data worldwide.  The multi-purpose INSAT satellite system,
 with currently four satellites in orbit viz., INSAT-2C, 2DT, 2E and 3B, is one of the largest domestic communication satellite
 systems in the world and is the mainstay for television broadcasting services, for remote areas and transmission of developmental
 programmes in rural areas, educational training of developmental programmes in rural areas and educational training.  India’s Polar
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) is well proven through four successive successful flights and provides launch capability to orbit
 Remote Sensing satellites of 1.2 ton class in polar sun-synchronous orbits.
4.         The first successful test flight of Geo-synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) from Sriharikota on April 18, 2001 was
 the most significant milestone of the Indian space programme during the year 2001-02.  The launch unequivocally demonstrated
 India’s capability to place satellites into geo-synchronous transfer orbits.  India is among the six nations in the world to achieve such
 a capability.  The launch of GSLV is the culmination of efforts of several DOS centers and other institutions that involved complex
 interfaces between scientific and technological disciplines, industries and research institutions.
5.         Another important milestone during the year was the successful flight of PSLV-C3 on October 22, 2001 from Sriharikota.  In
 this fifth consecutively successful flight, PSLV placed three satellites –– India’s Technology Experiment Satellite, TES, Belgian
 Project for on-Board Autonomy (PROBA) and German Bispectral and Infrared Remote Detection (BIRD) into their intended polar
 sun-synchronous orbit.  The requirement of a higher orbit for the Belgian PROBA compared to other two satellites was successfully
 met by a flight manoeuvre.  Both German and Belgian satellites were launched under commercial agreements.  The flight has clearly
 established the reliability of PSLV for launching not only the Indian remote sensing satellites, but also, multiple  satellites  thus
 making it an attractive  vehicle for the  international  space community to
launch their satellites.  PSLV is also planned to be used for a geo-synchronous transfer orbit mission for launching India’s METSAT
 in 2002-03.
6.         The INSAT system for telecommunication, television broadcasting and meteorology has received further boost during the year
 with the successful launch of INSAT-3C on January 24, 2002.  INSAT-3C will not only augment the present INSAT system but also
 continue the services of some of the satellites that need to be phased out at the end of their mission life.
7.         Besides, the remote sensing applications continue to expand to several new areas; the data has been used to assess damage due
 to floods, earthquakes, etc and for helping in relief operations.  The announcement of Remote Sensing Data Policy (RSDP) during
 the year will help to streamline the availability of remote sensing data from Indian and foreign satellites to users in India.
8.         In the field of space sciences, the cryogenic sampler that had been developed by ISRO for Geosphere-Biosphere Programme,
 has been used to detect micro-organisms in the stratosphere, which could have far reaching implications on the understanding of the
 origin of life on earth.  Detailed analysis of the samples collected were going on in scientific research laboratories in India and
 abroad.
9.         Educational and research institutions in India continue to participate in the space programme taking up projects under the
 Sponsored Research scheme of DOS.  During the year, 22 new projects were initiated under the scheme.  The task team constituted
 to study the feasibility and scientific objectives for undertaking an unmanned mission to the moon has made substantial progress in
 their work.
10.       The Committee  observes that  with sustained efforts of DOS end-to-end capability in space for vital application in
 communications, broadcasting, meteorology and natural resource information which have direct relevance for national development,
 has secured India a unique place in the International Community.  However, the committee is of the view that front ranking scientific
 investigations in the field of astronomy, atmospheric sciences and long term climatic research using satellites, balloons, sounding

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
11.        It has been stated that the Ninth five-year plan has witnessed significant progress and achievements in the space programmes.
     The total expenditure of the Department during the 9 th plan period would come to approx. Rs.7905 crores consisting of Plan
 component of Rs.6603 crores and Non-plan component of Rs.1302 crores against the approved  outlay of Rs.6511.72 crores.  Thus,
 the plan allocation for the Department for 9th plan was fully utilised.
The major missions planned during the Ninth Plan period and their current status are at Annexure I.
12.        Asked about the Programme/Projects where funds have remained unutilized during 2001-2002 and steps taken to complete
 them in 2002-03, the DOS  informed as follows ––
Taking note of the reduced ceiling for RE fixed by the Ministry of Finance and also the progress status of the projects, the
 provision in RE 2001-02 has been reduced in respect of GSLV project, IRS-P5, METSAT, GSAT-2 and certain new Projects
 like GSLV MKIII, GSLV Continuation & GSAT-3
 
The steps taken by the Department to complete them in 2002-03 include:
(a)    The provision in RE  in respect of GSLV project has been reduced by rescheduling of payments related to Cryo contract
 based on the revised milestone payment schedules. Provision has been incorporated in BE 2002-03 to complete these
 milestone payments.
(b)    The reduction in RE in respect of IRS-P5 project is based on the revised delivery schedules of certain contract items
 (imported) such as Data Compression System, Solid State recorder and hi-rel electronic components.  The progress in
 respect of these contract items is being monitored periodically to ensure the actual delivery of these items in 2002-03. 
(c)    The provision in respect of METSAT & GSAT-2 projects has been reduced in RE due to postponement of expenditure
 related to spacecraft testing, launch and post launch mission support based on the launch schedule. The Department has
 accelerated the work on METSAT & GSAT-2 projects and the payloads are in advanced stages of completion. METSAT
 & GSAT-2 are now targeted for launch during 2002-03. 
(d)    The provisional amounts shown in BE 2001-02 in respect of new projects like GSLV MkIII, GSLV-Continuation &
 GSAT-3, have been reduced in RE as these new projects have not yet been approved.  However, the budgetary support
 required for the pre-project R&D related to these initiatives have been met from the respective Centre’s budget. The
 project proposal for GSLV MkIII is in advanced stages of approval.  The formulation of proposals for GSLV
 Continuation & GSAT-3 are in progress and will be taken up for approval shortly.  It has been planned to complete the
 approval cycle and initiate the development work on all these new projects in 2002-03.
13.        The Budget Estimates 2002-03 works out to Rs.2264.99 crore with a Plan component of Rs.1951.10 crore and Non-Plan
 component of Rs.313.89 crore.  The details of this provision are set out in  Annexure-II.
14.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department continues  with the practice of having detailed reviews at various
 levels in the organization in order to arrive at the minimum essential cash flow for each Project, Programme and Centre/Unit, based
 on the programmatic priorities, total cost, scheduled targets, progress achieved  and the milestone planned for the budgeting period. 
 The Committee  finds that consistent with the programme directions and targets envisaged for the 10
th Five year Plan period, the
 specific activities/projects to be undertaken and the performance milestones to be achieved have already been prioritized while
 finalising  the Budget Estimates for 2002-03.
15.       The Committee observes that during 1999-2000, the Department had utilized the funds to the extent of 99.76 percent.  In
 2000-2001 the fund utilization  was about 99.56 per cent.    The Committee thus notes with satisfaction that the Department has made
 optimum utilization of the funds allocated to it during 1999-2000, 2000-2001 as also in 2001-2002.
16.        The Committee has been informed that the tenth five year plan proposals have been drawn up under the frame work of a long
 term plan after extensive interactions, detailed studies and consultations within the organisation as well as with user community.  The
 total budgetary requirement  for  the  missions  planned  for  the 10
th  Plan  as  well  as  the  advance  investments required for the
 missions planned for the beginning years of the 11 th Plan works out to be Rs.20.593 crores.  Out of this, the non-plan budgetary
 support expected during the 10 th Plan would be Rs.2000 crores approximately.  Thus, the plan outlay requirement for 10 th Plan
 period would be Rs.18, 593 crores.
GEO STATIONARY SATELLITE SERVICES
17.        The Geo-stationary Satellites which are placed in an orbit, about 36,000 km over the equator are used for telecommunication,
 television broadcasting and meteorological services.  India established the geo-stationary satellite system, namely, Indian National
 Satellite (INSAT) system in 1983.  INSAT is one of the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the Asia Pacific Region
 with five satellites, INSAT-2C, INSAT-2DT, INSAT-2E, INSAT-3B and INSAT-3C in operation.  INSAT system also includes
 eleven transponders that have been leased from other agencies to augment the INSAT capacity. Beside, INSAT-1D which was,
 launched in June 1990, is used for meteorological imaging and a few other services even after eleven years of its operation. INSAT-
2B launched in July 1993 which was decommissioned from regular services during the year, is still used for Satellite Aided Search
 and Rescue and Data Relay Services and two of its transponders are used for scientific experiments.
            One of the major accomplishments during the year was the realisation of INSAT-3C, and its launch on board an Ariane-4

 launch vehicle on January 24, 2002.  INSAT-3C being a communication satellite, is a replacement for INSAT-2C whose life ends by
 the end of 2002.
18.        METSAT is an exclusive meteorological satellite to be flown on PSLV.  It will support the India Meteorological Department
 by providing meteorological services from geostationary orbit, including Cyclone Warning Dissemination Services, Meteorological
 Data Collection and Weather Imagery on a continuous basis.  The meteorological payload on METSAT comprises a 3-band VHRR
 instrument for providing imageries in visible, thermal IR and water vapour bands and a weather data relay transponder.
19.        Asked as to whether the amount of Rs.35 crores sought in this year BE will be adequate to meet the stated objective of
 METSAT i.e. to design, develop, fabricate, test, launch an exclusive meteorological satellite with a very high resolution radiometer
 (VHRR) to provide meteorological data and weather imagery on a continuous basis.  The Department has informed that the total
 approved cost of METSAT project is Rs.75 crores. Out of this an expenditure of Rs.25 crores is planned in RE 2001-02. The budget
 provision of Rs.35 crores sought in BE takes into account the requirements towards fabrication charges, test consumables, pre-launch
 and post-launch mission expenses of METSAT and is consistent with the overall project cost estimates. Currently, the fabrication and
 testing of the METSAT payload is nearing completion.  The integration of the spacecraft is in progress.  With the projected budget
 for BE 2002-03 and the current status of progress, the METSAT is targeted to be launched and operationalised by Mid 2002-03
 providing the meteorological data for weather forecasting on a regular basis. 
20.       GSAT-1 are experimental satellites which were launched during the development test flights of India’s Geo-synchronous
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV).  The first satellite, GSAT-1 was launched by the first developmental GSLV flight in April 2001.
21.        GSAT-2 would be launched by the second development flight which would carry instruments  to  conduct experiments  like 
 total  radiation dose monitor, surface  charge  potential monitor, coherent radio beacon experiment and solar X-ray spectrometer. 
 During the year, assembly of flight structure and dynamic analysis have been completed.  Fabrication of solar array deployment
 mechanism components, C- band reflector components have been completed. All control simulations have also been completed.
22.        The Committee has been informed that planning of INSAT-4 series of satellites has been initiated.  It is proposed to have
 seven satellites in the series.  INSAT-4A through INSAT-4G with INSAT-4D as a spare.  The transponder capacity has been worked
 out after a detailed evaluation of the projected requirements by the various users.  It is expected that by 2007, INSAT would have 251
 transponders in various bands catering to a demand of up to 11 GBPS capacity.
23.       The Committee feels that the major thrust of the INSAT programme plan should be  towards augmenting the space segment
 capacity of the INSAT system with fourth generation INSAT-4 series of satellites to meet the increasing demands for transponders in
 various sectors including government and social sectors.  The Department should therefore interact with the users and service
 providers in both government and non-government sectors, and then endeavour to achieve space segment capacity of transponders in
 INSAT system. The Department should also endeavour to complete the ongoing INSAT-3E satellite followed by next generation
 INSAT-4 series (INSAT-4A to G) during the 10
th plan period.  The indigenous GSLV Mk II capable of launching 2000 kg INSAT
 type of satellites should be fully utilized for launching INSAT-4 satellites.  The Department should examine the feasibility of using
 low cost experimental GSAT satellites for the development flights of GSLV. Besides, an Advanced Communication Technology
 Satellite (ACTS) should be planned with a view to develop and demonstrate advanced communication techniques & technologies for
 future generation INSATs. 
24.        The Committee is of the view that an advanced meteorological satellite, should be planned to provide valuable inputs for
 climatic / numeric weather prediction model studies related to vertical profile of temperature & humidity. It would enhance the
 quality of the Meteorological services aimed at accurate weather forecasts.
25.        Telemedicine is a recent application of the satellite communications that makes specialized medical facility available to the
 remote areas of the country.  The expert consultancy could be obtained for the patients in remote areas from specialists in speciality 
 hospitals in cities.  Five VSAT terminals have been set up for telemedicine in Chamarajanagar, Kenchanahalli, Bangalore, Kolkata
 and Tripura which are networked with a hub on shared basis.  Port Blair in Andaman Nicobar islands, and Leh in Jammu & Kashmir
 and Lakshadweep are also being provided with telemedicine facilities.  ISRO has already provided its SPACENET terminals to a
 private hospital at Chennai and a rural Hospital at Argonda in Andhra Pradesh for telemedicine network.  The Hospital at ISRO’s
 SHAR Centre, at Sriharikota is also being connected to this spacenet for telemedicine.
26.        A Standard Time and Frequency Signal Dissemination Service (STFSDS), using a Radio Networking (RN) type of CxS
 carrier on INSAT-2B, is being operated by the National Physical Laboratory (NPL).  This service is available round-the-clock in a
 broadcast mode in S-band and it can be received on a system consisting of a 2.4 m diameter antenna, a front-end converter, an FM
