NEW DELHI;
April 29, 2003
 
 
 
 
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
Chairman,
Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests.
       
R E P O R T
           
Oceans have played a critical and decisive role in our history. Numerous invasions of India through land frontiers never
 turned our country into a colony. We fell to that status only when mastery of our seawaters was lost. Oceans,
 particularly the Indian Ocean is assuming importance in shaping the world order. In the 19
th century, Admiral Mahan
 of the United States of America, had predicted:
“Whoever controls the Indian Ocean dominates Asia.  This ocean is the key to the seven seas.  In the twenty first
 century the destiny of the world will be decided on its waters.”
Not only from the strategic point of view but also from the point of view of our very survival and development we will
 increasingly depend on oceans, particularly the Indian Ocean in the centuries ahead.
“Oceans sustain nearly half of all life on earth and provide us with vital resources.  They are a source of food, energy,
 commerce, medicine and recreation…. They shape our weather and link us to other nations.  In the twenty first century,
 we will look increasingly to the oceans to meet our every day needs.”
This declaration formed the cornerstone of the convention on the Law of the Sea and Oceans Conference held in 1998, a
 year that was designated as the U.N. Year of the Ocean.
2.         Recognising the importance of oceans for our all round development on a sustainable basis, the Department of
 Ocean Development was created in July, 1981 within the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the charge of the Prime
 Minister.  In March, 1982 it became a separate Department and has since been functioning as a nodal Department for
 organizing, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country, in line with the Ocean Policy
 Statement of 1982. The national level R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in

115TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/115threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:25:50]
 carrying out its multi-disciplinary plans and programmes. Marine research and capacity building are key areas of the
 Department to promote basic research in marine science for self-reliance.  The activities of the Department are targeted
 towards scientific research and technology development with orientation towards its applications and harnessing ocean
 resources.  The Department has also the mandate for international programmes arising out of international obligations
 and bilateral and multilateral cooperative ventures to create technological capacity building and human resources
 development for self-reliance.
3.         The Department witnessed a phenomenal growth with manifold expansion of its activities during the 9
th Five
 Year Plan period, involving a plan outlay of Rs.510.62 crores.  A wide range of subjects and activities introduced
 during the 9
th Five Year Plan period included Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), Assessment of the Marine
 Living Resources, Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management, Ocean Observation and Information Services,
 Delineation of Outer limits of Continental Shelf, etc.  They were directed towards development, dissemination and use
 of Ocean Science and Technology for socio-economic benefit of the country, with the active participation of a large
 number of national research laboratories, academic institutions etc.  In addition, two autonomous institutions, viz.,
 National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR) at Goa and Indian National Centre for Ocean Information
 Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad were established under the Department for carrying out and implementing
 programmes in the areas of Polar Science; and Ocean Observation and Information Services, respectively.  For
 implementation of the Environment Management Capacity Building project and the related infrastructure, R&D and
 training programmes, the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM) Project Directorate was
 established in Chennai, jointly funded by the International Development Association and the DOD.  The Sagar
 Sampada Cell of Kochi was renamed as a “Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology” for implementing the
 programmes relating to Assessment of Marine Living Resources in the Indian EEZ.  Some of the major achievements
 include the development and successful testing of a seabed mining system at a depth of 410m of Tuticorin in Tamil
 Nadu coast, as a forerunner to the development of deep sea mining system for operation at 6000 m water depth;
 deployment of 12 Met Ocean Data Buoys along the Indian coastline for collection and dissemination of oceanographic
 data on real time basis; establishment of Ocean Science and Technology Cells in 8 different disciplines for human
 resource development and capacity building in Ocean Science and Technology.
4.         The Vision statement highlighting the Perspective Plan 2015 of the Department was formulated and released
 during this year (2002-03).  The following objectives have been set by the Department in the Vision Statement for the
 coming decades :
i)          Promoting ocean science, supporting technology development and strengthening observations, so as to
 continuously improve our understanding of local and remote processes.
ii)         Modelling sustainable uses of the coastal zone and reliably predicting extreme events, for the socio-economic
 benefits of the coastal population.
iii)         Understanding the influence of the ocean on the monsoons and contributing to the capability to forecast it.
iv)        Strengthening programmes in the southern Ocean and Antractica that offer unmatched opportunities to study
 planet earth in its pristine state.
v)         Mapping ocean resources and evolving guidelines for proper stewardship so that they are sustainably utilized
 with minimal environmental impact.

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME
9.         The objectives of the Antarctic Research Programme are to identify and initiate programmes of scientific and
 economic significance besides establishing infrastructure.  The Antarctic Research Progamme has been designed to
 take advantage of the unique location and environment of the icy continent for understanding the key global processes
 which are manifested and controlled by this polar cap.  Antarctic is a pristine and natural laboratory, which enables the
 scientists to study, detect and monitor global phenomena, such as the atmospheric patterns and ocean circulations. 
 Glaciological and geophysical research provides a clue to the geological history and evolution of the earth.  In addition,
 Antarctica provides a singular platform for conducting studies on solar terrestrial interaction, adaptation of organisms,
 including human beings in the cold land isolated conditions.  The XXII scientific expedition with 48 members was
 launched successfully from Cape Town, South Africa on the 10
th January, 2003.  This expedition will carry out
 research in the fields of atmospheric, geological, biological, environmental, medical and engineering sciences and
 global change.
10.       The Committee was informed that the during the year 2003-04, preparatory exercise is proposed to be initiated
 of identifying the location of a second permanent Indian station in Antarctica, replacing “Maitri”.  With this year’s
 allocation of Rs.24.00 crores, the Department proposed to augment the research facilities at Indian Antarctic Station
 and also to actively undertake research in the Southern Ocean Oceanography area.
11.       The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and logistics prompted
 the Department to establish the first polar research lab of the country at Goa namely the National Centre for Antarctic
 Ocean Research (NCAOR) in 1998 which is responsible for carrying out all the activities relating to Antarctic
 expeditions. The research on polar science and expeditions to Antarctica was being planned, executed and launched
 annually on behalf of DOD by the Centre.  The Centre has a specific R&D mandate in the realm of polar science and to
 coordinate and launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre has a unique laboratory for low-temperature research
 on ice cores retrieved from Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It would also have the facility for the application of remote
 sensing techniques aimed at understanding the sea-ice-atmosphere interaction in the Polar Regions.  It would also have

POLYMETALLIC NODULES (PMN) PROGRAMME
17        Robert Heilbroner in his book ‘An Enquiry into the Human Prospects’ pointed towards a bleak future for
 humans in the process of approaching finite resources of the earth.  Later he did modify his assessment.  He wrote “I
 would like to take a more hopeful view of the mineral resources problem.  This is because I did not know when I wrote
 the book of the possibility of mining the seabed for mineral nodules which are estimated to exist in the order of
 hundreds of billions of tons”.
17.       The above paragraph indicates the potentiality of the oceanic world in terms of the sources of energy. 
 Manganese nodules of the deep seabed today have revolutionised the expectations of the industrialized countries.  The
 commercial exploitation, in the near future, of this nodule will not only provide the much needed scarce minerals but
 also change fundamentally the international mining market and its allied fields.  This will help the nations who have got
 technological superiority to explore and exploit the deep seabed.  Therefore, India has taken steps to extract
 Polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed. 
18.       The Polymetallic Nodules Programme (PMN Programme) is a national programme with international
 commitments which envisages eventual exploitation of the nodules from the allotted 1,50,000 sq. km. mine site in the
 Central Indian Ocean Basin. The programme consists of four components-Survey & Exploration of Polymetallic
 Nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB); Environmental Impact Assessment studies at CIOB; Technology
 Development for mining of nodules;  and  Technology  Development  for  extraction of  metals from  nodules. The
 work related to Survey and Exploration was mainly directed towards assessing relative concentration and quality
 characteristics of nodules as well as seabed topography.  Demarcation of grade of nodules in the Central Indian Ocean
 Basin was one of the main objectives.  Design and development of mining system has been re-oriented so that the
 intermediate applications of the technology could be achieved before developing the ultimate system for a depth of
 6,000 m.  Towards this design, development and testing of mining nodule complex has been undertaken. 
19.       The Committee was informed that a joint collaborative programme between NIOT, Chennai and Experimental
 Design Bureau of Oceanological Engineering (EDBOE), Russia, for design and development of unmanned
 submersibles capable of operation up to 6,000 m was likely to be taken up soon in pursuance of a MoU signed between
 DOD and Russian Academy of Sciences. Besides, a continuous demonstration pilot plant of 500 kg/day capacity for
 extraction of Copper, Nickel and Cobalt from nodules was set up at Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL), Udaipur.  An
 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) monitoring cruise is also proposed during 2003-04 as a part of continuing
 studies in the pioneer area for assessing the impact of the simulated mining at deep seabed at the site of nodules
 occurrence.
20.       The Committee was also informed that during the year, it is proposed to undertake the following major activities

DRUGS FROM SEA
25.       World wide researchers believe that oceans hold the key to a whole range of new drugs for chronic pain,
 epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease.  The current attempt to reap a chemical harvest from the seas is just a continuation of
 the bio prospecting that the big drug companies have been doing in jungles for the past few decades.  The National
 Project on Drugs from Sea is a multi-institutional project aiming at developing potential drugs and chemicals from the
 marine flora and fauna. This project has led to identification of five marine organisms showing potent activity as anti-
diabetic, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-cholesterol and spermicidal agents for developing new drugs. The exploratory
 attempts will be continued in an intensive manner during the 10
th plan period. The Department has fostered the search
 for novel drugs from the sea and will continue to encourage these activities, supporting extensive bioassay guided
 screening programmes.  The emphasis will be on following aspects:
Extension of inventory of organisms with bioactive potential.
In-vitro synthesis molecules recognized for their bioactivity.
Development and application of novel screening programmes for bioactivity.
Explore and understand at levels ranging from genes to organisms, unique properties of the production of novel
 compounds.
Understand interactions between organisms and their habitats.

 Rs.2.00 crores allocated both at B.E. and R.E. stages of 2002-03. The enhanced allocation would strengthen the

 compounds. Lead compounds for anti-diabetic and anti-cholesterol have been identified. The anti-diabetic lead has

COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS)
29.       Under the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) Programme, the Department of Ocean
 Development had taken up scientific monitoring of pollution at different locations. The programme aimed to assess the
 status and likely trends in coastal marine environment quality and contribute directly to the development of strategies
 for maximising the economic benefits derived from the intelligent and sustainable use of marine environment and
 resources. The programme had been continuing since 1991 for monitoring the level of various marine pollutants and its
 impacts on marine fauna and flora of the country. The data collected under the programme was made available to the
 Pollution Control Boards and periodically discussed with them. Any significant increase in pollutants at a particular
 location was brought to the notice of the Central Pollution Control Board for control as well as remedial actions.  The
 main objective of the Programme was to constantly assess the health of India’s  marine environment and indicate areas
 that needed immediate and long term remedial action.  Data on 25 environmental parameters were being collected at 82
 locations last year with the help of nine R&D institutions.  The Programme along with the modeling component would
 be continued during 2003-04. An allocation of Rs.2.00 crores has been sought for carrying out the activities under the
 programme for the year 2003-04
30.       At present the Department is monitoring pollution levels at 82 locations in our coastal waters and brings data to
 the notice of Central Pollution Control Board as well as concerned State Pollution Control Boards for mitigative
 measures. Enormous efforts are made to collect data through the coastal research vessels, i.e., Sagar Purvi and Sagar
 Paschimi. The data generated under this programme is reviewed periodically in the presence of Member Secretaries of
 Coastal Pollution Control Boards who are permanent members of the Steering Committee of the programme.

47.       The Committee notes that India is a signatory to the Ocean Charter which is not a legal entity, but which
 stipulates that all nations shall act in unison to protect the oceans.  India being a major maritime country in the Indian
 Ocean rim, it has a greater responsibility to take initiatives for bringing together all littoral countries for the
 development, protection and conservation of oceans.  The Committee notes with trepidation the observation of Dr. R.
 Sengupta, renowned oceanographer, “Of the three greatest water bodies, the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Indian Ocean,
 the latter was the cleanest.  But that is history now”.  The Committee therefore recommends that India must take a lead
 to protect its own interests and the interests of developing countries vis-a-vis their oceanic resources.
OCEAN OBSERVATION & INFORMATION SERVICES (OOIS)
48.       Recognizing the need to operationalise the oceanographic services in the new areas of Science & Technology,
 the Department has implemented the Ocean Observation and Information Services (OOIS) programme from the
 beginning of the 9
th Plan.  The objective of the Programme is to provide ocean information services for various
 applications in the ocean section.  OOIS is structured  around four major  themes  namely,  Ocean  Observing 
 Systems,  Ocean  Information
Services, Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) and Indian Ocean Modelling & Ocean
 Dynamic(INDOMOD).
49.       The Ocean Observing Systems envisage collection of sea truth data using moored data buoys, expandable
 bathythermographs (XBT), current meter arrays and tide gauges, and designed particularly for acquisition of real-time
 sea surface, meteorological and upper oceanographic parameters from the coastal and deep waters.  Validation of the
 satellite sensors has also been undertaken using the sea truth data generated under this programme.  The Data Buoy
 Programme was initiated in 1996 with partial financial assistance from Norwegian Agency for Development (NORAD)
 and National Institute of Ocean Technology (NOIT) has been entrusted with the responsibilities for deployment,
 operation and maintenance of the data buoys.
50.       The Ocean information service envisages generation and dissemination  of ocean data/data products on an
 operational basis.  The 14 National Marine Data Centres will be continued under the Ocean Information & Services.A
 dedicated centre “Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)” started functioning at Hyderabad
 from 1999 for  efficient development and dissemination of data products.   INCOIS is involved to synthesis, generate,
 promote, provide and coordinate various endeavours in the field of ocean sciences, ocean observations, satellite
 oceanography, and ocean information and advisory services.  INCOIS has a vision to emerge as a knowledge and

 information technology enterprise for the oceanic realm.  Synergy and knowledge networking with centers of
 excellence in ocean, atmospheric sciences, space applications and information technology as well as translating this
 scientific knowledge into useful products and services comprise the cornerstone of INCOIS.
51.       The Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) component envisages development of regional
 algorithms, data assimilation techniques and operational models which would be transferred to the Ocean Information
 and Service Centre for operational use.  The ocean modeling and dynamics project addresses basic issues on the ocean
 dynamic, climate variability, ocean state forecast, sea level variations, ocean flux studies etc.
52.       The Committee recommends that in order to improve Oceanography services, the Department should strengthen
 the observation platforms.  The moored buoy network should also be augmented to improve generation of data useful
 for the Coastal and off shore developmental activities.  The Department should also process the data collected from
 Array for Real-time Geotropic Oceanography (ARGO) Floats for obtaining temperature and salinity profiles from the
 Indian Ocean to study the long-term climate and Monsoon variability.
53.       The Committee desires that the Department should monitor the performance of the Indian National Centre for
 Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) for efficient dissemination of ocean data and data products to user communities
 on a regular basis.
54.       The Committee recommends that the Department should take initiatives in setting up information kiosks in the
 coastal states to facilitate the dissemination of data/data products to user communities.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY
55.       The National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) was established in November, 1993 as a registered society
 under the administrative control of the Department of Ocean Development with a view to developing technology in the
 ocean sector. The main aim of NIOT is to develop and  promote  technology  in mission  mode  for  specific  purposes 
 in  ocean  related  areas. The multifarious activities of NIOT are carried out as in-house technology development
 programmes and field demonstration projects. Initially NIOT’s spectrum of activities includes the four core mission
 activities i.e. Ocean Energy, Deep Sea Mining, Coastal and Environmental engineering and Marine Instrumentation.
 Subsequently, NIOT was also entrusted with the operation & maintenance of two CRVs by establishing a  Vessel
 Management Cell in 1996 and National Data Buoy Programme in 1997. In 1998-99, one more project on Island
 Development was added to the activities of NIOT and renamed as Ocean Science & Technology for Islands. NIOT is
 also entrusted to undertake Hi-tech consultancy service in ocean related activities.  During 2003-04, the major
 activities, ongoing as well as new, undertaken by NIOT are testing of 1MW Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
 (OTEC) Plant, design of mining system for depth upto 6000 m, preparation of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)
 guidelines for Coastal Ocean management, development of Under Water Marine Instruments and calibration of the
 same and continuing the project on enhancement of Marine Living Resources. For the project Ocean Science &
 Technology for Islands, NIOT has already made a headway in enhancement of marine living resources in the island
 groups by taking up technology development for breeding, rearing and fattening lobsters to begin with. The facilities
 both at the Island groups and at the mainland have been augmented for this purpose. It is proposed to expand the
 activities under this programme to other marine organisms on selective basis and also to coordinate the implementation
 of all the programmes of the Department in the island groups for the benefit of the island community.
56.       The Committee was informed that the budgetary allocation for the National Institute of Ocean Technology
 (NIOT) has been kept at Rs.25.00 crores as against last year's allocation of Rs.23.40 crores. The increase in allocation
 was caused due to new activities on Marine Archaeology under the Coastal and Environmental Engineering Group and
 inclusion of Ocean Science and Technology for Islands Programme as part of the core Mission Programmes of NIOT.
 Feasibility studies for establishment of 5 MW OTEC plant is being implemented during the year 2003-04 by the
 Department in pursuance of the recommendation made by the Committee in its 101
st Report.
57.       The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation to the Department to build energy plants of higher capacity
 as it feels that this might be cost effective in the long run and lessen the dependence on fossil fuel for power generation.
NEW PROGRAMMES
Comprehensive Swath Bathymetric Survey
58.       This new programme entails scientific mapping of this area to have an inventory of potential resources and to
 identify the causes of hazards.  The study would help to develop innovative concepts in the following areas:
Submarine fans and their role on accumulation of hydrocarbons.
Submarine canyons and their role in transport and distribution of pollutants.
Island-understanding of submarine landslides and stability of coastlines.
Sedimentary processes-effect on fisheries and biogeochemical cycling.

A financial allocation of Rs.12.00 crores has been sought for the year 2003-04.
59.       The Committee hopes that such activities of the Department yield good results.  The Committee strongly feels
 that the allocation for the Department for this area must be substantially enhanced. 
Gas Hydrates
60.       With ever increasing gap between demand and indigenous production of natural gas and the huge import bill
 incurred by India, it is necessary to look for alternative resources.  Gas hydrates have the potential of providing total
 energy security to our nation.  The programme consists of both scientific & technology development for gas hydrates.
61.       The Department, in association with CSIR and other laboratories, would focus on scientific research with special
 emphasis on resource extent evaluation and environmental impacts and development of technology for detection and
 qualification of gas hydrates in sediments.  Thereafter, exploratory drilling will be advised.  The steps in this
 programme will be to
Understanding the generation and accumulation of hydrates in sediments/
Estimate impact of gas dissolution on geological environment and climate.
Develop or adopt environmentally safe technology for production and transportation of gas from hydrates.
Draw up plans to monitor and manage environmental perturbation during hydrate harvesting.
62.       During the year it is proposed to examine the multi-channel seismic (MCS) data collected and carried out under
 special processing and analysis of MCS data acquired under Legal continental shelf programme.  It is also proposed to
 initiate the mapping of Bottom simulating Reflector (BSR) prone zone. A financial allocation of Rs.18.00 crores has
 been sought for the year 2003-04.
Acquisition of New Research Vessel
63.       The new vessel is meant for technology demonstration. A concept design of the vessel has been made and the
 technical specifications of the vessel have been drawn. In principle approval from the Planning Commission for
 acquisition of the vessel has been obtained. An EFC memo for acquisition of the vessel has been circulated to
 concerned Departments for comments.
64.       This vessel will serve as a platform for the programme envisaged in the X Plan and also serve as a utility science
 vessel which will augment the capacity need of the marine living and non-living resources programme of the
 Department.  The NIOT would be the nodal agency to implement this programme and to operate and maintain the
 vessel.  A detailed design and estimates for the vessel have been worked out and a detailed project report has been
 prepared, which is under active consideration of the Department. A financial allocation of Rs.2.00 crores has been
 sought for the year 2003-04.
 65.      The Committee has been recommending for a Research Vessel for the Department and therefore notes with
 satisfaction that the proposal for such a vessel has been approved in principle by the Planning Commission.  The
 Committee recommends that this proposal be implemented as soon as possible to enable the Department to do its
 important work in ocean development.
Geophysical Study of Laxmi Basin
66.       Under this programme the Department is planning to undertake detailed geophysical surveys along the entire
 west coast to establish conclusively the nature of basement in the Laxmi Basin. A financial allocation of Rs.2.50 crores
 has been sought for the year 2003-04.
67.       The Committee strongly recommends that all the new projects proposed by the Department should be taken up
 on a time bound basis.  The Committee also strongly recommends that sufficient allocations be made for the successful
 completion of these projects.
68.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and assessing the progress
 of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary
 allocation of Rs.199.33 crores, as sought by the Department for the year 2003-2004, under Demand No. 65, may be
 approved.
SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMMENDATIONS
 
1.         The Committee feels that the Department during 2002-03 had to scale down its activities due to reduction in its
 B.E. from Rs.175 crores to Rs.150 crores.  The Committee is constrained to note that in many cases major
 disproportionate variations is due to delay in getting the necessary Government approvals.  The Committee feels that
 these kind of hassles should be removed and strongly recommends higher allocations for activities of the Department

 which is doing a commendable job.  The Committee also feels that there is an urgent need to review the whole planning
 and budgeting process in the Department so that realistic physical and financial targets are projected in the Budget and
 planned projects are not hampered due to drastic cuts at R.E. stage.  It is equally important to prioritise the projects in
 the light of their potential benefit to the Nation.
(Para 8)
2.         Commencement of the Antarctic Programme in the eighties and its evolution and growth represent the
 excellence of our scientific and technological capabilities beyond the frontiers of our country. The study and research
 undertaken during Antarctic expeditions have produced a repository of data and information which are of immense
 importance not only for India but for the entire world. Pursuing this mission as part of the mainstream of the
 international endeavour to explore the icy continent has made invaluable contribution to promote international
 understanding. The Committee, therefore, feels that the Antarctic programme should not be allowed to suffer for want
 of funds.  Besides, with a view to strengthening our scientific base in Antarctica, there is a need for expanding the area
 of activities by installing many more research stations in different regions of Antarctica.
 (Para 14)
3.         The Committee is also of the view that the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) which is the
 nodal Department to execute the Antarctic programmes should also initiate its activities to establish the Country’s ice-
core repository and analytical facilities with focus on high-resolution histories of fact changes in climate, atmospheric
 composition and ice-cover in Antarctica.
 (Para 15)
4.         The Committee further recommends that the Department may take steps to conduct state-of-the-art experiments
 in Antarctica.
 (Para 16)
5.         The Committee hopes that the periodical review of the Polymetallic Nodules (PMN) Programme would continue
 to be undertaken to adopt new technologies in view of the fast changing technologies.  This project has tremendous
 potential in supplying adequate minerals for the benefit of our economy.
 (Para22)
6.         The Committee recommends that efforts to extract polymetallic manganese nodules from the deep seabed be
 assessed from the point of view of its impact on the ocean environment.
 (Para 23)
 7.        The Committee hopes that data generated from the R&D activities of the Department for extraction of
 manganese nodules could be studied in depth with the ultimate objective of designing a commercial plant.
 (Para 24)
8.         The Committee notes with satisfaction that under the Drugs from Sea Programme the Department has done
 commendable work.  The Committee trusts that the Department would continue the exploratory work relating to
 collection, identification and bio-evaluation of the marine flora and fauna from the Indian Coastal waters for the
 purpose of extracting drugs.
(Para 27)
9.         The Committee is of the view that possibly from marine resources some medicines could be extracted which
 otherwise are not available at present to treat some of the diseases affecting mankind.   Therefore, the Committee
 recommends that marine resources must be used in a sustainable way for the benefit of our people.
 (Para 28)
10.       The Committee recommends that the Department may augment its ongoing Coastal Ocean Monitoring and
 Prediction System to regularly monitor the condition of the coastal waters and adjoining areas. 
(Para 31)
11.       For strengthening ocean research centres in coastal universities, the Department is emphasising on quantum
 jump in our approach towards the ocean.  To achieve that purpose the Committee recommends that the Department
 should formulate an integrated approach and explore the possibilities of bringing all maritime educational institutions
 under one body such as a Maritime University. Since ocean sciences are multi-disciplinary sciences such an integrated
 approach, the Committee feels, will be of vital significance.  The Committee recommends that the Department should
 establish Oceanariums in different parts of the country.  If planetariums could promote knowledge and awareness about
 space, the Committee feels that Ocenariums could also create awareness about oceans and their resources.
(Para 36)
12.       The Committee observes that the Coastal Research Vessels(CRVs), with the participation of scientists of other
 related institutions, should cruise frequently to monitor pollution and do other multidisciplinary work.

#          Nominated w.e.f. 7th April, 2003.
INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One
 Hundred-Sixteenth Report of the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2003-2004) of
 the Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science and Technology) (Demand No.82).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on 1
st April, 2003 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of
 Biotechnology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on
 various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by
 the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants
 of the Department of Biotechnology.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 29
th April, 2003.
 
 
NEW DELHI;
April  29 , 2003
 
 
 
C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
Chairman,
Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests.
       
 
R E P O R T
 
            Focus on biology has brought about a paradigm shift in the understanding of human life and the entire
 ecosystem.  The hallmarks of the second half of the 20
th century were the discovery of double helix, DNA structure,
 transfer of genes from one unrelated organism to another and the sequencing of human genome.  Much before all these
 path-breaking scientific activities were undertaken, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru had written, with rare far sightedness in
 the Discovery of India.  “Perhaps new developments in biology……… and other similar sciences and the interpretation
 of biology may help man to understand and control himself more than he has done in the past”.  While 20
th century was
 the age of physical sciences, the 21st century has been perceived as the century of biology.  India, with its vast
 biological resources is poised to reap rich harvests in the century of biology.  Establishment of the Department of
 Biotechnology is a significant step in that direction.
2.         Biotechnology as a branch of modern biology is hardly two decades old and it is the fastest growing branch of
 modern science.   It is rapidly becoming the cornerstone of industrial development and leading us to the brink of bio-
industrial revolution.  In fact, we are now in biotech century and our way of life is likely to be more fundamentally
 transformed in the decades to come. The present day definition of biotechnology is the application of scientific and
 engineering principles to the processing materials by biological agents to produce goods and services.  The applications
 of biotechnology are so wide that virtually every industry including pharmaceuticals, textiles, aquaculture, chemicals,

116TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
 household products, manufacturing, environmental cleaning, food processing and forensics, are using such technology. 
3.         Biotechnology is emerging as a major player for enhancing the food productivity, nutritional status, sustainable
 utilization of biological resources, prospecting of new molecules and genes, identification and characterization of
 biological wealth, development of new vaccines, diagnostics and drugs, pollution abatement through biotechnological
 route, waste recycling, etc.  Bioinformatics and human resource development have given rich dividends in terms of
 highly skilled and trained human resource available in the country and a strong information network being utilized by a
 large number of scientists. The Department of Bio-technology under the Ministry of Science & Technology was set up
 in February, 1986 to give a greater impetus to the development of biotechnology in the country.  The objectives of the
 Department include development of products and processes and technologies whose large scale applications would
 result in societal and economic benefits.
4.         The main responsibilities of this Department are :
To evolve integrated plans and programmes in Biotechnology.
Identify, specific programmes of Research and Development and oversee related research and manufacturing activities
 for biologicals.
Identify, set up and support centres of excellence for research and development in biotechnology and ensure proper
 dovetailing of these activities with national priorities.
To act as a screening, advising and approving body of Government with regard to import and transfer of new
 technologies for the manufacture of biological and biotechnological products.
To evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology research, development and manufacturing in India.
To act as the Central agency for the import of genetically manipulated/modified materials, culture cells, specimens,
 tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type and for promoting their production in the country.
To serve as the inter-ministerial and inter-agency nodal point for all specific international, bilateral and multilateral
 research and development collaboration in the area of biotechnology and act as the nodal point for all technology
 transfers in the area of biotechnology.
For manufacturing and application of cell-based vaccines.
To evolve programmes of human resource development in the area of biotechnology.
To act as the administrative department for autonomous institutions
Serve as the authorised Department of the Government in respect of legislative Parliamentary requirements in all areas
 mentioned under Allocation of Business for the Department.
5.         The biotechnology programmes are being implemented through a number of autonomous and statutory
 institutions and Universities to which assistance is provided by the Department by way of grants-in-aid.  The
 Department is also looking after the work relating to the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and
 Biotechnology (ICGEB).  The autonomous institutions established by the department under Societies Registration Act,
 1860, include: National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi, National Centre for Plant Genome Research, New
 Delhi, National Centre for Cell Science (NCCS), Pune, Centre for DNA Finger Printing and Diagnostics, Hyderabad,
 National Centre for Plant Genome Research, New Delhi, National Brain Research Centre, New Delhi, Institute of
 Bioresources and  Sustainable Development (ISBD), Imphal, Institute of Life Sciences, Bhubaneshwar.  A Public
 Sector undertaking namely, the Bharat Immunologicals and Biologicals corporation Ltd. (BIBCOL), Bullandshahr is
 engaged in manufacturing Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) and other immunologicals under Prime Minister’s Technology
 Mission on Immunization, with a view to achieving self-sufficiency in manufacturing of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
6.         The major programmes /projects to be taken up during 2003-04 include: six new P.G. teaching programme in
 regions not represented, NMR facility at Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (IICB) Kolkata, upgradation of some of
 the major bioinformatics centres as centres of Excellence for undertaking advanced research and postgraduate
 education; collaborative mutli-institutional research projects on functional genomics of rice, biotechnology for
 improvement of semi-arid crops; post harvest biotechnology for improved shelf life, nanobiotechnology, development
 of cocktail diagnostic molecular tools for infectious diseases, drugs through combinatorial chemistry and high
 screening throughput, basic research on diarrheal diseases, sequencing and molecular typing of infectious agents,
 neurodegenerative diseases, edible vaccines and contraception mission programmes on h
erbal
Products development, new generation vaccines, vaccines research and development, food and nutritional security,
 bioenergy and biofuels, genomics, oncology, advanced research in stem cell biology, the genomic sequencing of
 microbes relevant to India, establishment of bio-villages, international collaborations as per agreements and work plans
. The proposals for establishment of biotech parks, biotech incubators and other centralized facilities specially from
 State Governments will also be taken up.

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
7.         Keeping in view the above programmes, recent trends and international developments, the Department had
 projected a requirement of Rs.450.00 crores for the year 2003-04 to the Planning Commission. However, an allocation
 (plan side) of Rs.260.00 crores has only been provided. During the year 2002-03, the plan allocation at B.E. and R.E.
 stages was Rs.225.00 crores and Rs.205.00 crores respectively. The enhanced allocation for 2003-04 will primarily be
 utilized on new programmes/initiatives. Functional genomics, vaccines and plant based products will be a priority.
8.         The Committee was informed that one of the recurring problems of the Department is the shortfall of the non-
plan budget. Recurrence of such problems on year to year basis, the Committee was apprised,  has created a compelling
 situation for the autonomous bodies whereby they had to cut down from plan funds to pay salaries to the scientists. The
 Committee is constrained to note that scientific institutions engaged in research in frontier areas of science have to
 confront such a situation. The additional requirement of the Department for non-plan expenditure is to the tune of
 Rs.5.00 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds may be provided to the Department to
 overcome this problem. It further underlines that the Departments dealing with science and technology should be
 accorded priority for allocation of funds  and  if  necessary,   special  provisions  may  be  made  for  them  so  that they
 do not face such problems.  Biotechnology era is waiting to dominate the World  economy in the next twenty years. 
 Investment in this field is not commensurate with the potential of this branch of Science.
9.         The new areas covered during 2002-03 are related to agriculture and plants, healthcare, bioresource conservation
 and utilization, societal development and biotech industrial growth.
10.       It has been informed that the proposed programmes are based on the Vision Document of the Department as well
 as Tenth Plan proposals. These programmes aim at enhancing the knowledge base and generating highly skilled human
 resource, nurturing leads of potential utilityby emerging bioscience enterprises areas of agriculture, health care and the
 environment and bringing bio-products to the marketplace for generation of wealth, import substitutions, export
 promotion and technological self sufficiency. The emphasis would be on excellence and relevance for socio-economic
 progress. Agricultural Biotechnology programmes such as rice genome sequencing, development of pest and disease
 resistant varieties, nutritionally rich crops, virus free tissue culture plants, improved biofertilisers and biopesticides will
 have great impact on farmers and consumers in terms of food, nutrition, health, environment and livelihood security. A
 mission mode project on food and nutritional security is under implementation.
11.       To a specific query of the Committee as to how the Department monitors and reviews the progress of its on-
going schemes before formulating/finalising proposals for budgetary support, the Department stated that elaborate
 mechanisms have been established to review its activities.  It has got specific area wise sixteen Task Forces on various
 disciplines to review the activities and progress of all the schemes and programmes at periodic intervals, 2-3 times in a
 year.  Besides, the Department stated that a multidisciplinary high level Biotechnology Research and Promotion
 Committee consisting of experts from research institutions, universities, industry and NGOs does the same exercise. 
 Further, the Department maintained that the Scientific Advisory Committee of the Department and Standing Advisory
 Committee (Overseas) with eminent NRIs Scientists assess the overall policy issues, identify priority areas and review
 major projects. In addition to these, the Planning Commission also undertakes review of plan schemes at quarterly
 intervals. 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
12.       The focus of the programme has been to train a large number of scientists/students. An integrated manpower
 development programme comprising M.Sc./M.Tech./Post doctoral courses in biotechnology at various universities/
 institutes of many states and union territories is in operation. Programmes such as Biotechnology national and overseas
 associates, short-term training courses, seminars and symposia, popular lectures, biology scholarships, publications etc.
 have been implemented.  Five bioscience career development awards and three women bio-scientists awards were
 given to eminent scientists. The main focus of the programme has been to generate a large number of highly trained
 scientists/students. 
13.       The method of selecting a University for starting a teaching programme in biotechnology was based on the
 scientific merit of the proposal.  A DBT-UGC joint Task Force considers the proposals based on the evaluation by
 experts.  Generally, the DBT insists that a strong faculty and diverse expertise in biotechnology should be available
 with the University before starting a teaching programme.  The Department also provides for guest faculty from
 neighbouring institutions to enable better type of teaching programmes in the absence of many well-trained faculty
 members.
14.       The Committee was informed that as a result of continued support to this programme, a large number of highly
 skilled manpower in the field at Postgraduate as well as Post Doctoral levels have been generated which is catering to
 the requirements of academics, R&D and Biotech industries including pharmaceutical sector.  The proposed
 activities/programmes will further strengthen human resource development to meet the growing needs of this sector and

116TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
 promote academic excellence at par with international standards. 
15.       During the year 2003-04 an allocation of Rs.13.00 crores has been earmarked for Human Resource Development
 programme as compared to last year’s allocation of Rs.10.00 crores which will be utilised for on-going PG Teaching
 (M.Sc./M. Tech/Diplomas) and Post Doctoral Fellowship Programmes with increased intake of students and supporting
 6 new PG Teaching Programmes (including Post MD/MS Training Courses).
16.       The Committee recommends the Department to accord high priority to the issue of Human Resource
 Development and should coordinate with the University Grants Commission to implement the programme all over the
 country. 
PLANT TISSUE CULTURE
17.       Tissue culture is an important tool of biotechnology which can be used to improve the productivity of planting
 material through enhanced availability of identified plant stock with desired traits.  The main object of the programme
 is to develop protocols for regeneration of economically important plant species covering Forest Trees, Horticulture and
 Plantation Crops.  Plant Tissue Culture technology is being used for mass multiplication of elite forest species and also
 for producing large quantities of planting material with desired characteristics.   The shortage of biomass and the
 increasing gap between supply and demand due to the mounting population pressure necessitated the mass propagation
 of trees through Tissue Culture.  The tree species identified cover a wide spectrum including trees of desert and arid
 zones, tropical and temperate zones.  DBT has supported programmes on priority crops to increase productivity per unit
 area by developing a strong R&D component concentrating on the production of high yielding and improved varieties
 and fresh methods of multiplication of elite plus trees.
18.       The Committee was informed that during 2003-04 the ongoing efforts in R&D programmes on tissue culture
 protocol standardization would continue for the identified priority crops.  Protocols for in vitro production of Saffron
 and Kalazira will be refined and scaled up.  Studies will continue for complete technology development for coffee, tea,
 spices, apple and citrus.  The Network programmes on Apple and Citrus will be launched and the germplasm will be
 characterized.  The certified virus free plants would be field planted and evaluated.  The novel orchid hybrids produced
 will be evaluated based on commercial parameters and an effort will be made to take these hybrids for commercial
 production.  Field demonstration of tissue culture raised Black pepper will be taken up in all identified sites.
19.       The Committee was apprised that under Plant Tissue Culture, 20 regeneration protocols have been developed
 and a molecular diagnostic kit for detection of Bunchy top Virus in Banana is in use at present.  The Micropropagation
 Technology Parks are serving as a platform for transfer of proven technologies and training in tissue culture.  So far,
 6.5 million plants have been produced and planted in 7500 hectares in 17 States.  Technologies for 10 species have
 been transferred to the industry.  A satellite park has been setup in North-East for popularization of technology and
 production of planting material for the region.  In addition, five Regional Hardening Units in different States are
 functioning well.
20.       The Committee is of the view that efforts should be made to make use of the tissue culture and floriculture
 technology in rural areas. Additional incentives should be given to persons willing to work in these areas.
BIO-INFORMATICS
21.       The plan scheme of bio-informatics envisages to provide a National Bio-informatics Network in the country
 designed to bridge the gaps in Biotechnology information and to establish links among scientists in Biotechnology. 
 The network aims to provide a single reference to various information resources of importance to biotechnology and
 modern biology including data banks of genetic importance published literature, patents and other information of
 scientific and commercial value.  It also aims to provide necessary infrastructural support for modern research in
 biology involving computationally intensive analysis.  The network consists of 11 Distributed Information Centers
 (DICs) and 46 sub-DICs computational facilities at the national level.  It has also established linkages with international
 institutions like International Centre for Co-operation in Bio-informatics (ICCB), a UNESCO based funded bio-
informatics programme and is also linked with EMB net, as well as international legume-data base and information
 services (ILDIS).  Educational and training activities in bio-informatics will also form part of the scheme.  National Jai
 Vigyan Mission on Mirror Sites for Genomic Research to establish four major databases have progressed well. These
 projects are being pursued at Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore; University of Pune; Jawaharlal Nehru University
 and Institute of Microbial Technology, Chandigarh.  New projects for establishing Centres of excellence in bio-
informatics will be taken up.
22.       The Committee was informed that there are 57 Bioinformatics centres at various research
 institutions/universities.  Each centre of the network has built up Bioinformatics resources in their specialized areas in
 the form of databases, software packages for application to Biotechnology and Molecular Biology, which are shared by
 the researchers in the country.  Towards the development of molecular modelling and simulation studies in

116TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
 biotechnology, six interactive graphic facilities have been established and they act as a National facility for the benefit
 of researchers in the country.   Four one-year Post-graduate Diploma courses on Bioinformatics  are being offered by
 major universities with a view to enhancing human resource in the field.  Every year more than 50 short-term training
 programmes are being conducted to promote awareness for the utilisation of Bioinformatics resources.  Under the
 National Jai Vigyan Science & Technology Mission, mirror sites of internationally recognized databases have been
 established for unhindered access to large amount information resources for the acceleration of R&D activities in
 genomics and proteomics.
23.       The Bio-informatics programme offers a single window information resource in the country covering inter-
disciplinary areas of biotechnology and molecular  biology.    Human resource development has been recognized as an
 important area for effective sustenance of the bioinformatics programme.  Towards meeting the needs for trained
 bioinformatics professionals, long-term courses are being run as part of this network in five reputed Universities. 
 About 50-60 short-term courses are being offered every year to train the researchers and scholars in bioinformatics.  Six
 National Facilities on interactive graphics are dedicated to the promotion of molecular modeling and other related
 activities.  The Biotechnology Information  System (BTS) centers have developed more than 100 databases on various
 aspects of biotechnology.  Several major International databases for application to genomics and proteomics have been
 established in the form of mirrors as part of the network.  A Virtual Private Network (VPN) has been established to link
 these databases through high speed and large bandwidth network to promote faster sharing of information. 
24.       The Biotechnology Information System Network (BTISnet) under the bioinformatics programme presently
 consists of sixty-one centres spread all over the country. Over the years, the network has created a resource base
 including computational infrastructure, databases and software. Six National Facilities on Interactive Graphics are
 dedicated to the promotion of molecular modelling and other related activities. The five one year advanced diploma
 courses and a M.Tech course on bioinformatics are being conducted through the reputed institutions for development of
 leadership quality in human resources on bioinformatics. About 100 subject specific databases have been developed
 through the BTISnet. Several major International databases for application to genomics and proteomics have been
 established in the form of Mirror sites as part of the network. These databases are being linked through high speed and
 large bandwidth network in the form of VPN, now termed as BIOGRID INDIA, to promote faster sharing of
 information as well as to encourage tandem research by various R&D labs and industrial units. At the micro level, the
 programme deals with the various issues related to the biological data. It covers the development of data analysis tools,
 modelling of biological macromolecules and their complexes, metabolic pathways, designing of new molecules such as
 drugs, peptide vaccines, proteins etc.
25.       During 2003-04, the Department proposes to upgrade five of the Distributed Information Centres (DICs) into
 Centres of Excellence (CoEs) on bioinformatics to generate high quality human resource and to carry out competitive
 R&D activities in the area of bioinformatics and computation biology for producing world class bioinformatics tools. 
 This will in turn help in revealing several applications in the area of molecular biology in general and genomics and
 proteomics in particular. It has also been recommended to upgrade five Sub-DICs in to the level of DICs to enhance the
 activities. More and more institutions have been proposed to be part of the Biogrid India in its second phase execution.
 At least three new Bioinformatics centres might be established to cover un-represented and remote institutions as part
 of the BTISnet.  More than 50 short-term courses have been proposed to be organized for training the researchers and
 scholars on the latest developments, which are taking place on bioinformatics.
26.       The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in the field of bioinformatics  which are expected
 to yield multidimensional results in variety of areas. The Committee, however, recommends that the Department should
 make all out efforts to ensure that biological data created in agricultural and other sectors is disseminated in a way that
 it also reaches the people working at grassroot levels.
JAI VIGYAN NATIONAL S&T MISSION
27.       Of the 21 National Jai Vigyan Missions initiated by Ministry of Science & Technology, four were launched by
 DBT in the areas of new generation vaccines, herbal product development, improvement of coffee and establishment of
 mirror sites of genomic databases in India. 
28.       The objectives of the programme include generating candidate vaccine(s) for diseases like cholera, rabies,
 Japanese encephalitis, tuberculosis, malaria and HIV.  The programme has been grouped under three categories. 
 Category (A) includes those ‘candidate vaccines’ where potential research leads are available and which now require
 clinical trials for generating pre-clinical data.  Under this category, vaccines for cholera and rabies are being attempted. 
 The programmes under category (B) are related to available leads on candidate vaccines where efficacy and
 immunogenicity need to be worked out.  The target vaccines are tissue culture-based Japanese encephalitis, DNA
 vaccines.  Under category (C), programmes require sustained R&D efforts with the possibility for development of

116TH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/116threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:26:51]
 candidate vaccine(s).  Under this category, efforts would be made to produce candidate prophylactic anti-HIV and
 DNA vaccines for tuberculosis.
29.       The Committee was informed that under the programme about 25 technologies have been transferred to different
 industries. These include, diagnostic kits for detection of HIV, Hepatitis, Dengue, assessment of reproductive
 hormones, Japanese Encephalitis, Vaccines for leprosy, drug formulation for septic shock, plant tissue culture
 protocols, formulation of biofertilizers, high protein gene from Amaranthus and bioremediation technology for mine
 spoiled dumps and crude oil spillage.  The Indo-US Vaccine Action  programme has led to development of two
 candidate vaccine strains (116E & I321) against rotaviral diarrhoea which is now entering into the phase of clinical
 trials. 
30.       The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in vaccine research and development. The
 Committee hopes that the research done by the Department on microbial genomes, especially pathogens, in view of the
 burden of   infectious diseases on our people, will result in the elimination of diseases like Malaria and Tuberculosis in
 a time bound manner.  The Committee understands that India is on the threshold of producing the first ever DNA
 vaccine in the world, for rabies.  It is appropriately said that “In the area of infectious diseases, drugs, vaccines and
 diagnostics are the ultimate products expected out of genomic information”.  While the Committee commends the
 efforts of the Department and notes such achievements with satisfaction, it hopes that vaccines/medicines would be
 priced reasonably so that these are within the reach of common people.
BIO-TECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
31.       Under this project, the Department is pursuing three programmes. Under Bio-technology programme for SC/ST,
 the aim is to provide the benefits for biotechnological processes and techniques to SC/ST people.  The projects funded
 under the programme are generally focused on technology transfer covering training, field demonstration and extension
 oriented activities on proven biotechnologies with the involvement of targeted groups.  The programme helps in
 increasing  skills  and income  of  the SC/ST people.  The  Bio-technology  based programme for Women aims to
 promote and use biotechnological processes and tools for entrepreneurship development and provide employment
 opportunities especially for women.  One of the objectives of the programme is to set up Women Biotechnology Park

 utilization, and impart training in relevant areas to develop a pool of skilled and well trained women.  It would also

 generation and better health care in rural areas; to use biotechnological process and tools for creating new avenues of
 employment for people living in rural areas; and to promote bio-village concept for socio-economic upliftment of rural

2004.

fertilizer. While it is important for the Department to augment their efforts in this regard, the Committee recommends

 prevalent in India and exploiting the knowledge created by available human, microbial and parasitic genomic sequences

 functional genomics, powerful computational capability for handling large scale human genome sequence data, robotic
 methodologies for genotyping and PCR based diagnostics for common genetic disorders have been developed.

 symposia, training, programmes of specialised nature in immunological methods and related areas. It also serves as a
 national reference centre for immunology and provides consultancy services. It promotes linkages between various

 collaborate with foreign research institutions, laboratories and other international organizations in the field relevant to

 include: transgenic animals, virology–HIV/AIDS and Japanese encephalitis, small animal facilities, technology
 incubator etc.

 number of emerging and re-emerging infections requiring development of suitable diagnostics and therapeutics. Several

Development of new generation vaccines for prophylaxis and therapeutic use.
Development of newer and alternate drug delivery system.
Production of important biological and bioactive molecules using suitable expression systems and modern fermentation

Programme support for creation of infrastructures in newer areas of biotechnological research.

EXPEDITIOUS CLEARENCE OF PROJECTS SUBMITTED BY THE DEPARTMENT
76.       The Committee was apprised that the proposals submitted by the Department are subjected to periodic review
 and assessment by different agencies including the Planning Commission. The Department further stated that it
 remained ever ready to subject itself and its activities to scrutiny. However, it informed the Committee that time taken

BUDGET PROPOSALS AT R.E.STAGE
77.       The Department informed the Committee that the reduction of its budget at the R.E. stage causes a lot of
 problem in resetting its priorities. It prepares its plan as per the budget proposals and accordingly prepares its schedule
 of activities. Time taken to re-do the priorities due to cut in R.E. stage is not less than three or four months. Such re-
planning for scientific projects deviates the Department from the set objectives. The Committee is constrained to note
 that such problems are confronted by the Department.
Professor G. Padmanabhan, the UNESCO Professor in Biotechnology Department of Biochemistry, Indian Institute of
 Science, Bangalore in an important article “Contrary to reports, India has not missed the biotech bus” has written about
 the budget requirements of biotechnology which is revealing:
“A single funding agency in the USA has a Rs.4,000 crores budget for genomics. In India, all the funding agencies
 together can mobilise about Rs.100 crores a year for research in this area. It is interesting to note that the country can
 still come up with new drugs, vaccines and diagnostics within this limited budget. If India plays its cards right, it can
 hope to become a world leader in modern vaccine manufacturing, since MNCs are not interested in this field due to
 poor economic returns. All that is needed is a commitment on the part of the Government to ensure availability of the
 committed amount for the next five years, release of grants in time, a mechanism for quick clearance of clinical trials to
 convert the results of the laboratory into commercial products”.
78.       Determination and will of the scientists to achieve the goal which is comparable to international standards and
 within a limited but committed fund is indeed heartening. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgets for
 all the Departments dealing with science and technology including that of the Department of Biotechnology may not be
 reduced at the R.E. stage.

SUMMARY OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS
 
1.         The Committee was informed that one of the recurring problems of the Department is the shortfall of the non-
plan budget. Recurrence of such problems on year to year basis, the Committee was apprised,  has created a compelling
 situation for the autonomous bodies whereby they had to cut down from plan funds to pay salaries to the scientists. The
 Committee is constrained to note that scientific institutions engaged in research in frontier areas of science have to
 confront such a situation. The additional requirement of the Department for non-plan expenditure is to the tune of
 Rs.5.00 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds may be provided to the Department to
 overcome this problem. It further underlines that the Departments dealing with science and technology should be
 accorded priority for allocation of funds  and  if  necessary,   special  provisions  may  be  made  for  them  so  that they
 do not face such problems.  Biotechnology era is waiting to dominate the World  economy in the next twenty years. 
 Investment in this field is not commensurate with the potential of this branch of Science.
(Para 8)
2.         The Committee recommends the Department to accord high priority to the issue of Human Resource
 Development and should coordinate with the University Grants Commission to implement the programme all over the
 country. 
(Para 16)
3.         The Committee is of the view that efforts should be made to make use of the tissue culture and floriculture
 technology in rural areas. Additional incentives should be given to persons willing to work in these areas.
(Para 20)
4.         The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in the field of bioinformatics  which are expected
 to yield multidimensional results in variety of areas. The Committee, however, recommends that the Department should
 make all out efforts to ensure that biological data created in agricultural and other sectors is
 disseminated in a way that
 it also reaches the people working at grassroot levels.
 (Para 26)
5.         The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in vaccine research and development. The
 Committee hopes that the research done by the Department on microbial genomes, especially pathogens, in view of the
 burden of   infectious diseases on our people, will result in the elimination of diseases like Malaria and Tuberculosis in
 a time bound manner.  The Committee understands that India is on the threshold of producing the first ever DNA
 vaccine in the world, for rabies.  It is appropriately said that “In the area of infectious diseases, drugs, vaccines and
 diagnostics are the ultimate products expected out of genomic information”.  While the Committee commends the
 efforts of the Department and notes such achievements with satisfaction, it hopes that vaccines/medicines would be
 priced reasonably so that these are within the reach of common people.
(Para 30)
 6.        The Committee is of the view that the farmers and other needy people from the target groups should be provided
 with latest biotechnologies for mushroom cultivation and vermi-composting. The Committee notes with satisfaction
 that the Department has started approaching the State Governments for getting their support for production of bio-
fertilizer. While it is important for the Department to augment their efforts in this regard, the Committee recommends
 that small and medium enterprises and industries may also be approached for this purpose. 
(Para 34)
7.         The Committee also recommends that under the programme for women, emphasis should be given to take up
 programmes in a comprehensive and an integrated manner for the benefit of women in remote areas such as islands,
 hilly regions and desert areas. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the first ever   bio-technology park for
 women established in Chennai in 1998 has become a huge success. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 Department may take initiatives to establish more such parks in different parts of the country for the benefit of women

8.         The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department to provide molecular diagnosis and counseling
 for the common genetic disorders prevalent in the country.   The Committee recommends that the Department may
 provide wide publicity to the programme through print as well as electronic media so that the benefits of these activities
 of the Department could percolate to the underprivileged and weaker sections of society.
(Para 38)
9.         The Committee feels that the country has the advantage of production of all four commercial silk varieties viz;
 mulberry, tusser, eri and muga.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department is according priority on
 Seri biotechnology with special focus on non-mulberry silk. It is heartening for the Committee to know that the Indian
 Institute of Science, Bangalore has, for the first time, done the important job of adopting control measures for pests of
 silk worm. As sericulture is suitable for marginal, small and landless farmers, it has tremendous scope for expansion in
 view of its employment generation potential.  Efforts should therefore be made to strengthen the linkages between
 extension and R&D units.  The technology delivery systems should be streamlined by providing need based training
 and effective field demonstration. Various communication channels should also be used to disseminate information
 about the new measures to improve Sericulture.
(Para 40)
10.       The Committee recommends that the technology developed at the laboratory stage under the programme should
 be brought to the level of pilot plant scale and should be transferred to the industry.  Moreover, the technology
 developed should be patented so as to safeguard the rights of those who develop it.
(Para 43)
11.       The Committee also recommends that some new projects in the area of microbial and industrial bio-technology
 should be started with emphasis on development of novel molecules for application in the pharmaceutical and industrial
 sectors.
(Para 44)
12.       The Committee recommends that the Department may explore the possibilities of applying for a patent at the
 midway stage of producing a product so as to safeguard the rights of scientists engaged in doing valuable research in
 biotechnology.
(Para 45)
13.       The Committee notes that biotechnology holds the key to food security as well as farmers’ security. Therefore,
 the            Committee recommends that the on-going and new initiatives concerning food biotechnology may be further
 augmented. It notes with satisfaction that the Department has developed a food which is so nutritious that One kg. of
 food is equivalent to five 5kg. of normal food. While producing more such foods, care must be taken to make the price
 affordable. The Committee understands that the technology for such foods is transferred to industry and therefore it is
 all the more important to remain vigilant about keeping the price of such products affordable.

 research activities on certain unexplored areas in the field of Immunodiagnostics.

15.       The Committee also recommends that the Department may explore the possibility of raising funds by
 collaborating with the industry for providing additional support to research activities. It will open opportunities for
 making the Institute self-sufficient.

16.       While the Committee notes with satisfaction the contributions of the Centre to forensic medicine and wildlife
 preservation, it recommends that in order to disseminate the DNA fingerprinting technology, a number of lectures and
 workshops should be conducted for the benefit of various police officers, judicial officers, forensic scientists and
 environmentalists.  This technology also needs to be included in the syllabus of National as well as State Police
 Training Academies & Institutions.
(Para 60)
17.       The Committee notes with satisfaction the research activities undertaken at the National Brain Research Centre
 (NBRC). 
(Para 64)
18.       Moreover, in order to inform Medical Colleges and concerned Departments of Neurology about the research
 findings of the NBRC, the Department should undertake activities in a networking manner with the existing

       The Committee was informed that while some of the national centres of excellence in India possess rich expertise
 in bamboo technology, the knowledge flow to the industry has not come up to the desired level.   As such it is high time to

THE PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT SUPPORT FUND (PRDSF)
40.       The emerging economic, trade and intellectual property scenario, nationally and internationally, necessitates a
 qualitative change in the industry, to drive Indian pharmaceutical industry away from manufacturing only known drugs to
 discovering and commercializing new molecules. The availability of trained scientific manpower of high quality, S&T
 infrastructure, accumulated knowledge of traditional medicinal system and large bio-diversity of our country offer a great
 opportunity to our industry. However, at present, most Indian drug firms, due to their small size compared to international
 operators and limited resources, are not in a position to invest in a viable new drug development programme. At the same
 time, several Indian academic institutions and national laboratories have established impressive infrastructure and
 developed excellent expertise in selected areas of drug development.
41.       The Committee was informed that the scheme aims at enhancing capabilities of the Indian drugs and
 pharmaceutical industry towards development of new drugs by synergising the strengths of publicly funded R&D
 institutions and the Indian Pharmaceutical drug industry for discovery and introduction of new drugs and practices in all
 systems of medicine.
42.       During the tenth plan the Department has a provision of Rs.150 Crores for the Pharmaceuticals Research and
 Development Support Fund (PRDSF).   This is the corpus fund.  The interest earned from this fund will be used for the
 purposes of supporting Research & Development (R&D) Programmes and setting up of the National facilities for
 furthering R&D activities in the country.  Since the interest on this corpus will be accrued only after a year, an initial
 budgetary support of Rs.10 crores has been provided for sustaining various activities during the financial year 2003-2004. 
 It is proposed to constitute a Drug Development Promotion Board to administer the fund.
43.       It was stated that under this scheme financial support would be provided to national labs and academic institutions
 for joint research programmes conceived by the industry and public funded R&D institutions. The broad objectives of this
 programme include: Development of new molecules and practices for diseases prevalent in the Indian climatic zone by
 bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in research institutions and industry; Promote R&D at any
 stage of development in all systems of medicine including alternative system of medicines and Creating state-of-the-art
 infrastructure facilities at par with international standards for the benefit of the Indian Industry and other users.
44.       The existing ongoing Plan Programme on Drug and Pharmaceuticals Research will be merged with this new
 activity.  The broad objectives of this fund are: -
1.         Funding research in all the systems of medicine in particular development of new molecules, natural products
 including plant, mineral and animal based preparations, development of new drug delivery systems,       application of
 genomics/proteomics and development of key chemicals/reagents used in drug research.
2.         To create an enabling infrastructure for promotion of R&D at all stages including clinical research.

 Leucoderma, Psoriasis, Gastro-intenstinal  disorders like Diarrhoea, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardiovascular disorders and
